cards.body: Feed an ALU result straight from the EX/MEM or MEM/WB latch to the next instruction's ALU input. In the classic 5-stage pipeline (IF ID EX MEM WB) forwarding removes ALU-to-ALU stalls, but a **load followed by a dependent instruction still costs 1 stall**.

cards.title: CPI with stalls
points: CPI = 1 + average stall cycles per instruction
Branch: CPI = 1 + (branch fraction × penalty)
Speedup = k / (1 + stalls per instruction) for balanced stages

cards.title: Branch penalty
cards.body: 20% branches with a 3-cycle penalty: CPI = 1 + 0.2 × 3 = **1.6**. Resolving branches in ID cuts the penalty to 1 cycle: CPI = 1.2 — a 1.33× improvement.

cards.q: A 4-stage pipeline (1 cycle per stage) runs 100 instructions with no stalls. Total cycles:
Classic 5-stage pipeline with full forwarding: LW R1, 0(R2) followed immediately by ADD R3, R1, R4. Stall cycles:
cards.explain: Load data is available only after MEM, one cycle too late for the next EX.

cards.q: 25% of instructions are branches with a 2-cycle penalty; ideal CPI is 1. Effective CPI:

notes.p:
A pipeline does not make one instruction faster — it raises **throughput**. With k stages and n instructions, the first finishes after k cycles and one more finishes every cycle after that, so total = (k + n − 1) cycles.

**Worked example 1.** Stages 150, 120, 160, 140, 130 ps, latch 10 ps, 1000 instructions.
Pipelined: (5 + 999) × 170 = 170,680 ps.
Non-pipelined: 1000 × 700 = 700,000 ps.
Speedup = 700,000 / 170,680 ≈ **4.10**. Unbalanced stages and latch overhead keep it below 5.

notes.h: Worked example 2: RAW stall without forwarding
notes.p:
I1: ADD R1, R2, R3
I2: SUB R4, R1, R5
Assume the register file is written in the first half of WB and read in the second half of ID.
I1: IF(1) ID(2) EX(3) MEM(4) WB(5)
I2: IF(2), but its ID must read R1 in cycle 5 → ID(5) EX(6) MEM(7) WB(8)
I2 is delayed **2 cycles**; the pair finishes in 8 cycles instead of 6. With forwarding from EX/MEM, I2's EX can run in cycle 4 — **0 stalls**.

notes.h: Worked example 3: stalls from an instruction mix
notes.p:
30% of instructions are loads; half of them are immediately followed by a dependent instruction (1 stall each with forwarding). 15% are branches with a 2-cycle penalty.
Stalls per instruction = 0.30 × 0.5 × 1 + 0.15 × 2 = 0.15 + 0.30 = 0.45.
CPI = **1.45**. Compared with an unpipelined machine that takes 5 cycles per instruction at the same cycle time, speedup = 5/1.45 ≈ **3.45**.
Read the register names, not the instruction names.
points: **RAW** (read after write): I2 reads what I1 writes — a true dependence; needs forwarding or stalls.
**WAR** (write after read): I2 writes what I1 reads — only a problem if I2 can write before I1 reads (out-of-order).
**WAW** (write after write): both write the same register — only a problem when writes can complete out of order.
Compilers reduce stalls by **instruction scheduling**: move an independent instruction into the load-delay slot.
Control hazards: predict not-taken, dynamic 2-bit predictors, delayed branches, or early branch resolution.

notes.p: Do not add the latch delay to the non-pipelined time. When a question gives stage delays and asks for the speedup 'for a large number of instructions', use the per-instruction ratio, not (k + n − 1). A structural hazard on a single memory port stalls whenever IF and MEM happen in the same cycle — separate instruction and data caches remove it.
Remember:
points: Cycles = k + n − 1; cycle time = max stage + latch.
Ideal speedup → k; real speedup lower.
CPI = 1 + stalls per instruction.
Branch CPI = 1 + f × penalty.
Forwarding kills ALU-to-ALU stalls; load-use still 1 stall.
No forwarding (split-cycle register file): dependent next instruction stalls 2.
RAW is the true dependence; WAR/WAW appear with out-of-order completion.

chapters.title: Cache memory: mapping, replacement & write policies

cards.title: Address split
points: Offset bits = log₂(block size)
Sets = lines / associativity; index bits = log₂(sets)
Tag = address bits − index − offset
Direct-mapped: 1 line per set; fully associative: 0 index bits

cards.title: 4-way set associative
cards.body:
32-bit address, 32 KB cache, 64 B blocks, 4-way.
Lines = 32 KB / 64 B = 512; sets = 512/4 = 128.
Offset 6, index 7, **tag 19** bits.

cards.title: Tag storage
points: Tag directory bits = lines × (tag + valid + dirty + LRU/other bits)
Example above, valid bit only: 512 × 20 = 10,240 bits

cards.title: Three Cs of misses
cards.body: **Compulsory** (first access), **capacity** (cache too small), **conflict** (too many blocks map to one set). Higher associativity cuts conflict misses; bigger blocks cut compulsory misses but raise the miss penalty.

cards.title: Write policies
cards.body: **Write-through**: update memory on every write (usually with a write buffer and **no-write-allocate**). **Write-back**: update only the cache, mark the line **dirty**, write it back on eviction (usually **write-allocate**).

cards.title: Average memory access time
points: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty
Two-level: H₁ + m₁ × (H₂ + m₂ × T_mem), m₂ = local L2 miss rate
Global L2 miss rate = m₁ × m₂

cards.title: Two-level AMAT
cards.body:
L1 hit 1 ns, miss rate 10%; L2 hit 10 ns, local miss rate 20%; memory 100 ns.
AMAT = 1 + 0.1 × (10 + 0.2 × 100) = 1 + 0.1 × 30 = **4 ns**.

cards.q: Direct-mapped cache with 8 blocks; block requests 0, 8, 0, 6, 8. Number of misses:
cards.explain: 0 and 8 both map to line 0 and keep evicting each other: every access misses.

cards.q: Same requests 0, 8, 0, 6, 8 on a fully associative 8-block cache with LRU. Misses:
cards.explain: 0 miss, 8 miss, 0 hit, 6 miss, 8 hit.

cards.q: 64 KB, 2-way set-associative cache with 32 B blocks. Index bits:
cards.explain: 2048 lines / 2 = 1024 sets → 10 bits.

notes.p: Every block address maps to set = (block number) mod (number of sets). **Direct-mapped** has one line per set: simple and fast, but suffers conflict misses. **Fully associative** lets a block go anywhere: no conflict misses, but every tag must be compared. **k-way set associative** compares k tags in parallel — the usual compromise (k comparators, each of tag width).

notes.h: Worked example 1: LRU on a 2-way cache
notes.p:
`def simulate(blocks, sets, ways):
    cache = [[] for _ in range(sets)]     # each list ordered LRU -> MRU
    misses = 0
    for b in blocks:
        s = cache[b % sets]
        if b in s:
            s.remove(b)
        else:
            misses += 1
            if len(s) == ways:
                s.pop(0)
        s.append(b)
    return misses
seq = [0, 4, 8, 0, 4, 12, 0, 8]
print("direct 8x1:", simulate(seq, 8, 1))
print("2-way 4 sets:", simulate(seq, 4, 2))
print("fully assoc 8:", simulate(seq, 1, 8))`

Output:
`direct 8x1: 6
2-way 4 sets: 8
fully assoc 8: 4`

In the 4-set, 2-way cache every block (0, 4, 8, 12) maps to set 0, so LRU thrashes the two ways; the direct-mapped cache misses 6 times, and the fully associative cache only takes the four compulsory misses. More ways help only when the conflicting blocks fit in one set.

int a[1024] (4 bytes each) is summed once with a cold cache and 64-byte blocks. Each block holds 16 ints, so the loop misses once per 16 accesses: **64 misses**, miss rate 1/16 = 6.25%.

Now a 2-D array int M[256][256] stored row-major and traversed **column by column**. Consecutive accesses are 256 × 4 = 1024 bytes apart, so each touches a new block. If the cache cannot hold 256 blocks at once (16 KB of blocks for a column pass), every access misses: 65,536 misses. Row-wise traversal needs only 65,536/16 = **4,096** misses.
Read the question's model carefully.
points: **Hierarchical** (memory accessed after a cache miss): T = h·t_c + (1 − h)(t_c + t_m).
**Simultaneous** (cache and memory started together): T = h·t_c + (1 − h)·t_m.
Example: h = 0.9, t_c = 10 ns, t_m = 100 ns → simultaneous 0.9 × 10 + 0.1 × 100 = **19 ns**; hierarchical 0.9 × 10 + 0.1 × 110 = **20 ns**.
With write-back, a miss that evicts a dirty line costs an extra block write: penalty × (1 + dirty fraction).

notes.p: The **index** comes from sets, not lines. Tag-directory size questions may include valid, dirty and replacement bits — count exactly what the question lists. Byte offset uses the block size in **bytes** (or words, if memory is word-addressable). A larger cache with the same block size can still have the same number of conflict misses if the access pattern strides by the cache size.
Remember:
points: Offset = log₂(block); index = log₂(sets); tag = rest.
Sets = lines / ways.
AMAT = hit + miss rate × penalty; nest it for L2.
Global L2 miss rate = m₁ × m₂(local).
Write-back + write-allocate; write-through + no-write-allocate.
Compulsory, capacity, conflict — associativity attacks conflict.
Row-major arrays: traverse rows in the inner loop.

chapters.title: Main memory, disks & I/O (interrupts and DMA)

cards.title: Building memory from chips
cards.body: To make an M × w memory from m × b chips you need **(M/m) × (w/b)** chips. Higher address bits feed a **decoder** that selects one row of chips; lower bits go to every chip.

cards.title: 4K × 8 from 1K × 4
cards.body: Rows = 4K/1K = 4, columns = 8/4 = 2 → **8 chips**. 12 address lines: 10 go to every chip, 2 drive a 2:4 decoder that enables one row.

cards.title: Interleaving
cards.body: **Low-order interleaving** puts consecutive words in different modules (module = address mod m), so a block can be fetched from m modules in parallel. High-order interleaving puts contiguous ranges in one module — good for expansion, not for bandwidth.

cards.title: Disk numericals
points: Capacity = surfaces × tracks × sectors × bytes per sector
Access time = seek + rotational latency + transfer
Average rotational latency = ½ × (60/rpm) s
Transfer time = bytes / transfer rate

cards.title: Disk access
cards.body: 7200 rpm → one rotation 8.33 ms, average latency **4.17 ms**. Seek 5 ms; reading 4 KB at 100 MB/s ≈ 0.04 ms. Total ≈ **9.2 ms** — seek and rotation dominate.

cards.title: I/O transfer modes
cards.body: **Programmed I/O**: CPU busy-waits on a status flag. **Interrupt-driven**: device interrupts the CPU per word/byte. **DMA**: a controller moves a whole block and interrupts once at the end. DMA modes: **burst**, **cycle stealing**, **transparent**.

cards.q: Address lines needed for a 64 KB byte-addressable memory:
cards.explain: 64 KB = 2¹⁶ bytes.

cards.q: Average rotational latency of a 6000 rpm disk:
cards.explain: One rotation = 60/6000 s = 10 ms; average is half.

cards.q: Which mode moves a whole block with only one interrupt to the CPU at the end?
cards.explain: The DMA controller handles the per-word transfer.

notes.p:
The 2027 syllabus phrases this topic as **memory interfacing and hierarchy**. Typical question: 'design a 16K × 8 memory using 4K × 4 chips — how many chips and what size decoder?'

**Worked example 1.** 16K × 8 from 4K × 4.
Depth: 16K/4K = 4 rows. Width: 8/4 = 2 chips per row. Total = **8 chips**.
Address lines: 16K = 2¹⁴ → 14 lines. Each chip takes 12 (4K = 2¹²); the top 2 lines drive a **2:4 decoder** that enables one row of 2 chips.

Main memory is usually **DRAM** (one transistor + capacitor per bit, dense, needs periodic refresh). Caches use **SRAM** (six transistors per bit, fast, no refresh).

A disk has 16 surfaces, 1024 tracks per surface, 64 sectors per track and 512 bytes per sector.
Capacity = 16 × 1024 × 64 × 512 = 2⁴ × 2¹⁰ × 2⁶ × 2⁹ = 2²⁹ bytes = **512 MB**.
Sectors = 2²⁰, so a sector address needs **20 bits**.
At 6000 rpm (10 ms per rotation), one track (64 × 512 = 32 KB) passes the head in 10 ms → transfer rate 3.2 MB/s, and one sector takes 10/64 ≈ 0.156 ms.

notes.h: Worked example 3: interrupt vs DMA overhead
notes.p:
A device delivers one word every 10 µs. Interrupt-driven I/O with a 2 µs interrupt service routine keeps the CPU busy 2/10 = **20%** of the time.
With DMA, the controller interrupts once per 4000-word block, and setup plus completion handling costs 20 µs. A block takes 4000 × 10 = 40,000 µs, so CPU overhead = 20/40,000 = **0.05%**.

**Cycle stealing**: the DMA controller takes the bus for one cycle per word, slowing the CPU slightly; **burst** mode takes the bus for the whole block, which is fastest for the device but blocks the CPU from memory meanwhile.

Hierarchy: registers → caches → main memory → disk/SSD, each level larger, slower and cheaper per bit. It works because of **temporal** and **spatial locality**. Effective access time for a two-level hierarchy with hit ratio h: T = h·t₁ + (1 − h)(t₁ + t₂) when the lower level is accessed only after a miss.

Interrupt handling basics: the CPU finishes the current instruction, saves the PC and status, identifies the source (**vectored** interrupts supply the ISR address; **daisy chaining** sets priority by position), runs the ISR and returns.

Disk rotational latency is **half** a rotation on average. Use the question's units: MB may mean 10⁶ or 2²⁰ — follow the convention stated. For chip counting, divide both depth and width; forgetting the width factor is the commonest slip.
Remember:
points: Chips = (M/m) × (w/b); top address bits → decoder.
Address lines = log₂(addressable units).
Low-order interleaving → parallel block access.
Disk access = seek + ½ rotation + transfer.
Capacity = surfaces × tracks × sectors × bytes.
DMA: one interrupt per block; cycle stealing vs burst.
DRAM needs refresh; SRAM does not.

cards.title: C parameter passing
cards.body: C is strictly call-by-value; passing a pointer lets the callee modify the caller's object. A swap(int a, int b) that swaps its parameters changes nothing in the caller.

cards.title: Scope and storage
cards.body: C uses static (lexical) scoping. static locals persist across calls; automatic locals are re-created each call. Watch for dangling pointers to returned locals.

cards.title: Array address (row-major)
points: A[i][j] in an R × C array: base + (i·C + j) × size
Column-major: base + (j·R + i) × size
Adjust i, j if the lower bound isn't 0

cards.title: Binary tree facts
cards.body: In any binary tree, leaves = (nodes with two children) + 1. A binary tree with n nodes has n + 1 NULL child pointers.

cards.title: Heaps
cards.body: Array storage: children of i at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 (0-indexed). Insert and delete-min O(log n). Building a heap bottom-up from n elements is O(n), not O(n log n).

cards.title: Hashing
cards.body: Chaining keeps lists per slot; open addressing probes (linear → primary clustering; quadratic; double hashing). Expected chain length = load factor α = n/m.

cards.q: int A[10][20] (4-byte ints, row-major) starts at address 1000. Address of A[2][3]:
A binary tree has 10 leaves. How many nodes have exactly two children?
cards.explain: Leaves = degree-2 nodes + 1.

cards.q: Time to build a binary heap from n unsorted elements (bottom-up heapify):
cards.explain: Most nodes are near the leaves and sift down only a little; the sum is linear.

notes.h: C programming as GATE tests it
notes.p:
GATE C questions trace small programs with **pointers, arrays, recursion, static variables, parameter passing and string arithmetic**. Read every line literally — the code often looks like it does one thing but does another.

Rules to remember: C passes arguments **by value** (pass a pointer to modify a caller's variable). A **static** local is initialised once and keeps its value across calls. `a[i]` ≡ `*(a + i)`; for a 2-D array `int a[3][4]`, `a + 1` skips a whole row of 4 ints, while `*(a + 1) + 2` points to `a[1][2]`. **Row-major** address of A[i][j] in an m × n array = base + (i × n + j) × element size.

**Stacks/queues:** a queue using two stacks; circular queue full when (rear + 1) mod n = front. **Binary trees:** a tree with n nodes has n + 1 NULL links; leaves = internal nodes with two children + 1; max nodes at height h (root at 0) = 2^(h + 1) − 1. **Heaps:** build-heap is **O(n)**, insert/delete O(log n); in an array heap, children of i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 (0-indexed). **BST:** number of distinct BSTs with n keys = Catalan(n).

**Hashing with linear probing (a GATE favourite).** Insert 12, 18, 13, 2, 3, 23, 5, 15 into a table of size 10 with h(k) = k mod 10:

`table = [None] * 10
for k in [12, 18, 13, 2, 3, 23, 5, 15]:
    i = k % 10
    while table[i] is not None:
        i = (i + 1) % 10
    table[i] = k
print(table)`

Output:
`[None, None, 12, 13, 2, 3, 23, 5, 18, 15]`

Clustering is visible: keys pile up from slot 2 onward (**primary clustering**). Quadratic probing and double hashing reduce it.

**Q: Postfix of A + B × C − D?** A: A B C × + D −.

**Q: Minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height 3 (root height 0)?** A: N(h) = N(h − 1) + N(h − 2) + 1 with N(0) = 1, N(1) = 2 → N(2) = 4, N(3) = 7.

**Q: Time to find the k-th smallest in a min-heap of n elements?** A: O(k log n) by k extract-mins (or O(k log k) with an auxiliary heap).

**Q: In `int a[10][20]` with base 1000 and 4-byte ints (row-major), address of a[5][7]?** A: 1000 + (5 × 20 + 7) × 4 = 1428.

**Q: Swap function `void swap(int a, int b)` — does it swap the caller's variables?** A: No; C passes copies.
Read carefully for:
points: Static variables changing between recursive calls.
Operator precedence: `*p++` increments the pointer, not the value.
`sizeof` on an array parameter gives the pointer size.
Short-circuit evaluation skipping side effects in `&&` and `||`.
Unspecified evaluation order of function arguments.

notes.p: Remember:
points: C is pass-by-value; static locals persist.
Row-major: base + (i × n + j) × size.
n nodes → n + 1 NULL pointers; leaves = degree-2 nodes + 1.
Build-heap O(n); heap ops O(log n).
Linear probing → primary clustering.
AVL minimum nodes follow N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1.

chapters.title: C: pointers, arrays, storage classes & recursion

cards.title: Pointer arithmetic
cards.body: p + 1 moves by **sizeof(*p)** bytes. a[i] ≡ *(a + i) ≡ *(i + a) ≡ i[a]. Subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of **elements** between them, not bytes.

cards.title: Arrays are not pointers
cards.body: An array name **decays** to a pointer to its first element in most expressions, but sizeof(arr) in its own scope gives the whole array size. As a function parameter, int a[] is really int *a.

cards.title: Strings
cards.body: char s[] = "GATE" is a 5-byte **modifiable array** (with '\0'): sizeof = 5, strlen = 4. char *p = "GATE" points to a **string literal** — modifying it is undefined behaviour.

cards.title: Parameter passing
cards.body: C passes **everything by value**. A function receives copies, so swap(x, y) cannot change the caller's variables; swap(&x, &y) can, because the copies are addresses.

cards.title: Storage classes
cards.body: **auto**: default local, garbage if uninitialised. **static** local: initialised once, keeps its value between calls. **static** global: visible only in its file. **extern**: declared here, defined elsewhere. Globals and statics start at 0.

cards.explain: p points to a[2] = 30; p − 1 points to a[1] = 20.

cards.q: void f(int n) { if (n > 0) { f(n / 2); printf("%d", n % 2); } } — f(10) prints:
cards.explain: It prints the binary representation of 10, most significant bit first.

cards.q: int m[3][4]; with 4-byte int, (char*)(m + 1) − (char*)m equals:
cards.explain: m + 1 skips one row of 4 ints = 16 bytes.

notes.p: C questions are **output-prediction** problems: pointer arithmetic, arrays of arrays, static variables, recursion and parameter passing. Trace with a table of variable values and a stack of active calls. Avoid code whose result is **undefined or unspecified** (for example i = i++ or two function calls with side effects in one printf) — GATE options are always well-defined, and so should your reasoning be.

notes.h: Worked example 1: one program, every idea

notes.p:
For int m[3][4]: m has type int (*)[4], so **m + 1 advances one row**. *(m + 1) is the row itself (decays to int *), and *(*(m + 1) + 2) is m[1][2]. Address of m[i][j] (row-major) = base + (i × 4 + j) × sizeof(int).

**Worked example 2.** int m[3][4] at base 1000, 4-byte ints. &m[2][1] = 1000 + (2 × 4 + 1) × 4 = **1036**. The expression *(m + 2) + 1 gives the same address.

Draw the call tree. Statements **before** the recursive call run on the way down (pre-order); statements **after** it run on the way back up (post-order). That is why f(n/2) followed by printf prints binary digits most-significant first; swapping the two lines would print 0101.

**Worked example 3.** int h(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; return n % 10 + h(n / 10); } — h(4729) = 9 + 2 + 7 + 4 = **22** (digit sum). Recursion depth = number of digits + 1 calls.
Five ways C output questions catch people:
points: sizeof is evaluated at compile time; sizeof(p) for a pointer is the pointer size (typically 8 on 64-bit), not the array size.
A static local is initialised **once**, even if the declaration line runs many times.
Integer division truncates toward zero in C99: −7/2 = −3, −7 % 2 = −1.
Order of evaluation of function arguments is unspecified — never rely on it.
Returning the address of a local variable gives a dangling pointer.

notes.p: Remember:
points: a[i] ≡ *(a + i) ≡ i[a]; p + 1 moves sizeof(*p) bytes.
Array parameters are pointers; sizeof differs inside the function.
char s[] = "GATE": sizeof 5, strlen 4.
C is call by value; use pointers to modify the caller's data.
static locals persist and start at 0.
Code before the recursive call runs top-down; after it, bottom-up.
Row-major: addr = base + (i·cols + j)·size.

cards.title: Stack
cards.body: LIFO; push, pop and top in O(1). Uses: function calls and recursion, expression conversion and evaluation, balanced parentheses, undo, DFS.

cards.title: Infix → postfix rules
points: Operand → output
'(' → push; ')' → pop to output until '('
Operator → pop while top has higher precedence, or equal precedence and left-associative; then push
^ is right-associative: equal precedence does not pop

cards.title: Queues
cards.body: FIFO. A **circular array** of size n, with the convention 'full when (rear + 1) mod n == front', holds at most **n − 1** items. A queue from two stacks has amortised O(1) dequeue; a stack from two queues makes push or pop O(n).

cards.title: Linked lists
cards.body: Insert/delete at the head: O(1). Search or access k-th: O(n). Deleting a node given only a pointer to it (not the last) in a singly linked list: copy the next node's data in, then bypass the next node. Doubly linked lists delete any given node in O(1).

cards.title: Stack-permutable sequences
points: Pushing 1, 2, …, n in order with pops in between can output Cₙ = (2n)!/((n + 1)! n!) sequences
n = 3 → 5 sequences; 3 1 2 is impossible

cards.q: Value of the postfix expression 2 3 1 * + 9 − :
Input 1, 2, 3 is pushed in order (pops allowed any time). Which output sequence is impossible?
cards.explain: To pop 3 first, 1 and 2 are on the stack with 2 above 1, so 1 cannot come before 2.

cards.q: A circular queue in an array of size 10 that keeps one slot empty can hold at most:
cards.explain: n − 1 = 9, so that full and empty are distinguishable.

notes.p:
**Worked example 1.** Convert a + b * (c ^ d − e) ^ (f + g * h) − i to postfix.
Read left to right, tracking the operator stack:
a → out. + → push. b → out. * → push (higher than +). ( → push. c → out. ^ → push. d → out. − → pop ^ (higher), push −. e → out. ) → pop −, remove (. ^ → push (higher than *). ( → push. f → out. + → push. g → out. * → push. h → out. ) → pop *, +. − → pop ^, *, + (all ≥), push −. i → out. End → pop −.
Result: **a b c d ^ e − f g h * + ^ * + i −**.

notes.h: Queues in arrays and with stacks
notes.p:
In a circular queue, front and rear advance as (i + 1) mod n. Empty: front == rear. Full: (rear + 1) mod n == front. The sacrificed slot is the price of telling the two apart without a counter.

**Worked example 2.** Queue with two stacks S1 (inbox) and S2 (outbox): enqueue pushes to S1; dequeue pops S2, and only when S2 is empty moves everything from S1 to S2. Each element is pushed and popped at most twice, so n operations cost O(n) total — **amortised O(1)**. Sequence enq 1, enq 2, deq → moves 2, 1 into S2 and returns 1; enq 3; deq returns 2 straight from S2.

Reversing a singly linked list in place uses three pointers (prev, cur, next) and O(1) extra space. Finding the middle uses slow/fast pointers. Detecting a cycle uses Floyd's algorithm. Merging two sorted lists of lengths m and n takes at most m + n − 1 comparisons.

Time summary: access by index O(n); insert after a known node O(1); delete a known node O(1) doubly, O(n) singly if you must find its predecessor (or O(1) with the copy-next trick when it is not the tail).
Remember:
points: Postfix: operators pop while top precedence is higher, or equal and left-associative.
^ is right-associative.
Stack-permutations of n items = Catalan Cₙ (n = 3 → 5).
Circular array queue holds n − 1 items with the empty-slot convention.
Two-stack queue: amortised O(1).
Linked list: O(1) at head, O(n) search.
Recursion depth = stack space used.

chapters.title: Binary trees, BSTs, AVL trees & binary heaps

cards.title: Binary-tree counts
points: Leaves n₀ = n₂ + 1 (n₂ = nodes with two children)
Max nodes at height h (root at height 0): 2^(h+1) − 1
Min height with n nodes: ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉ − 1
Unlabelled binary trees / BSTs on n keys: Catalan Cₙ

cards.title: Traversals determine trees
cards.body: **Inorder + preorder** or **inorder + postorder** identify a binary tree uniquely. Preorder + postorder do so only for **full** binary trees. A BST is fixed by its preorder (or postorder) alone, because inorder is the sorted order.

cards.title: BST operations
cards.body: Search, insert and delete cost **O(h)**: O(log n) if balanced, O(n) for sorted insertions. Deleting a node with two children: replace it with its **inorder successor** (smallest in right subtree) or predecessor.

cards.title: AVL trees
cards.body: Balance factor = height(left) − height(right) ∈ {−1, 0, 1}. Fix violations with **LL, RR (single)** or **LR, RL (double)** rotations. Minimum nodes for height h: N(h) = N(h − 1) + N(h − 2) + 1, N(0) = 1, N(1) = 2 → 4, 7, 12, 20 …

cards.title: Binary heaps
cards.body: A complete binary tree in an array; 0-based: children 2i + 1, 2i + 2, parent ⌊(i − 1)/2⌋. Insert and extract O(log n); **build-heap O(n)**; find-min in a min-heap O(1); the max of a min-heap is among the leaves.

cards.q: Number of structurally different BSTs with 4 distinct keys:
Maximum height (in edges) of an AVL tree with 7 nodes:
cards.explain: N(3) = 7 ≤ 7 < N(4) = 12, so height 3 is possible but 4 is not.

cards.q: A binary tree has 20 leaves. Nodes with exactly two children:

notes.p:
The leaf formula follows from counting edges: n − 1 = n₁ + 2n₂ and n = n₀ + n₁ + n₂ give **n₀ = n₂ + 1**. For a full k-ary tree with i internal nodes, leaves = (k − 1)i + 1.

**Worked example 1.** A complete binary tree has 100 nodes. Height = ⌊log₂100⌋ = 6. Leaves = ⌈100/2⌉ = 50 (in a heap array, indices 50..99 in 0-based numbering are leaves).

Preorder 50, 30, 20, 40, 70, 60, 80. The first key is the root; smaller keys form the left subtree, larger the right. Left subtree preorder 30, 20, 40; right 70, 60, 80.
Inorder = 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 (sorted).
Postorder = **20, 40, 30, 60, 80, 70, 50**.
Delete 50: its inorder successor 60 (leftmost node of the right subtree, here a leaf) moves into the root; the right subtree becomes 70 with only 80 as its child.

Insert 10, 20, 30 into an empty AVL tree. After 30, node 10 has balance −2 with the imbalance in its right child's right subtree → **RR case → single left rotation** about 10; 20 becomes the root with children 10 and 30.
Insert 30, 10, 20: imbalance at 30 is in its left child's right subtree → **LR case → double rotation** (left at 10, then right at 30); again 20 is the root.
AVL height is at most about 1.44 log₂ n, so all operations stay O(log n).

`import heapq
def max_heap_insert(h, x):
    h.append(x)
    i = len(h) - 1
    while i > 0 and h[(i - 1) // 2] < h[i]:
        h[(i - 1) // 2], h[i] = h[i], h[(i - 1) // 2]
        i = (i - 1) // 2
h = []
for x in [10, 20, 15, 30, 40]:
    max_heap_insert(h, x)
print(h)
from math import comb
print([comb(2 * n, n) // (n + 1) for n in range(1, 6)])
N = [1, 2]
for k in range(2, 6): N.append(N[-1] + N[-2] + 1)
print(N)
m = [9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2]; heapq.heapify(m); print(m[0], heapq.nsmallest(3, m))`

Output:
`[40, 30, 15, 10, 20]
[1, 2, 5, 14, 42]
[1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20]
1 [1, 2, 4]`

The heap matches the hand trace, Catalan numbers count BST shapes (1, 2, 5, 14, 42), and AVL minimum node counts are 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20.

Adjacency **matrix**: O(V²) space, O(1) edge test, O(V) to list neighbours — good for dense graphs. Adjacency **list**: O(V + E) space, neighbours in O(degree) — good for sparse graphs. BFS and DFS cost O(V + E) with lists and O(V²) with a matrix.
Remember:
points: n₀ = n₂ + 1.
Inorder + pre/post-order → unique tree.
BST ops O(h); delete with two children → inorder successor.
Heap: children 2i + 1, 2i + 2; build O(n); insert/extract O(log n).
BST shapes on n keys = Catalan Cₙ.
Adjacency list O(V + E); matrix O(V²).

cards.title: Master theorem: T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)
points: f(n) = O(n^(log_b a − ε)) → Θ(n^(log_b a))
f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)) → Θ(n^(log_b a) log n)
f(n) = Ω(n^(log_b a + ε)) + regularity → Θ(f(n))

cards.title: Apply it
cards.body:
T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n: n^(log₂4) = n² dominates → Θ(n²).
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n: equal → Θ(n log n).

cards.title: Greedy algorithms
cards.body: Activity selection (earliest finish), fractional knapsack (value/weight), Huffman coding, Kruskal and Prim MSTs, Dijkstra. Greedy fails for 0/1 knapsack.

cards.title: DP complexities
points: LCS of lengths m, n: O(mn)
0/1 knapsack: O(nW) — pseudo-polynomial
Matrix chain multiplication: O(n³)
Floyd–Warshall: O(V³); Bellman–Ford: O(VE)

cards.title: Lower bounds
cards.body: Any comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Finding both max and min of n elements needs ⌈3n/2⌉ − 2 comparisons.

cards.title: Graph algorithm costs
cards.body: BFS/DFS O(V + E); Dijkstra with binary heap O((V + E) log V); Prim with heap O(E log V); Kruskal O(E log E). DFS classifies tree, back, forward and cross edges; a back edge means a cycle.

cards.q: T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n² solves to:
cards.explain: n^(log₂8) = n³ dominates n².

cards.q: Minimum scalar multiplications for A(10×20), B(20×30), C(30×40):
Minimum comparisons to find both max and min of 100 elements:

notes.p: GATE expects you to compare growth rates (log n < n^ε < n < n log n < n² < 2ⁿ < n! < nⁿ) and to solve recurrences quickly with the **Master theorem**: for T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), compare f(n) with n^(log_b a).
points: Case 1: f(n) smaller polynomially → T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)). Example: T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n² → Θ(n³).
Case 2: f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) logᵏ n) → T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) log^(k+1) n). Example: merge sort 2T(n/2) + n → Θ(n log n).
Case 3: f(n) larger polynomially (with regularity) → Θ(f(n)). Example: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n² → Θ(n²).
T(n) = T(n − 1) + n → Θ(n²); T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + 1 → Θ(2ⁿ); T(n) = T(√n) + 1 → Θ(log log n).

notes.p:
DP classics with complexities: **matrix-chain multiplication** O(n³), **LCS** O(mn), **0/1 knapsack** O(nW), **Floyd–Warshall** O(V³), **optimal BST** O(n³). DP needs optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems; greedy needs the greedy-choice property.

Comparison sorting needs **Ω(n log n)** comparisons in the worst case (decision-tree argument: log₂(n!)). Quicksort worst case Θ(n²), average Θ(n log n); merge sort Θ(n log n) always; heap sort Θ(n log n), not stable. Selection of the k-th smallest is O(n) (median of medians). Counting/radix sort beat n log n because they are not comparison-based.

**Q: Solve T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n².** A: n^(log₂4) = n², equal → Θ(n² log n).

**Q: Minimum comparisons to find both max and min of n elements?** A: ⌈3n/2⌉ − 2.

**Q: Is the MST unique if all edge weights are distinct?** A: Yes.

**Q: Does Dijkstra work with negative edges?** A: Not in general; use Bellman–Ford.

**Q: P vs NP — what does NP-complete mean?** A: In NP and every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time (e.g. SAT, 3-SAT, vertex cover, Hamiltonian cycle).
Remember:
points: Master theorem: compare f(n) with n^(log_b a).
Kruskal O(E log E), Prim O(E log V), Dijkstra O((V + E) log V).
Bellman–Ford O(VE) handles negative weights.
Huffman cost = sum of merged weights.
Comparison sort lower bound Ω(n log n).
Max + min in ⌈3n/2⌉ − 2 comparisons.
NP-complete = NP + NP-hard.

cards.title: The five notations
cards.body: **O** (upper bound, ≤), **Ω** (lower bound, ≥), **Θ** (tight, both), **o** (strictly smaller), **ω** (strictly larger). f = Θ(g) iff f = O(g) and f = Ω(g). Worst-case time is usually stated with O or Θ.

cards.title: Growth order
points: 1 < log log n < log n < √n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < 3ⁿ < n! < nⁿ
log(n!) = Θ(n log n)
2ⁿ⁺¹ = Θ(2ⁿ), but 2²ⁿ = 4ⁿ ≠ O(2ⁿ)
Any polylog is o(nᵉ); any polynomial is o(cⁿ) for c > 1

cards.title: Comparing tricky functions
cards.body: Take logarithms. n^(log n) vs 2ⁿ: logs are log²n vs n, so **n^(log n) = o(2ⁿ)**. n^(√n) vs 2ⁿ: √n log n vs n, again smaller. Constants inside exponents matter; constant factors outside do not.

cards.title: Loop counting
cards.body:
for i = 1..n: for (j = 1; j ≤ n; j += i) → inner runs n/i times → Σ n/i = n·Hₙ = **Θ(n log n)**.
for (i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) for j = 1..i → 1 + 2 + 4 + … < 2n = **Θ(n)**.

cards.title: Recurrences beyond the Master theorem
points: T(n) = T(n − 1) + n → Θ(n²)
T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n → Θ(n log n)
T(n) = 2T(√n) + log n → Θ(log n · log log n)

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For recursion trees: total work = Σ (work per level) × (number of levels). If per-level work shrinks geometrically, the root dominates; if it is constant, multiply by the depth; if it grows, the leaves dominate.

cards.q: Which statement is FALSE?
cards.explain: 2²ⁿ = 4ⁿ, and 4ⁿ/2ⁿ = 2ⁿ is unbounded.

cards.q: for (i = 1; i ≤ n; i++) for (j = 1; j ≤ n; j += i) x++;  Time complexity:
cards.explain: Σ n/i = n·Hₙ = Θ(n log n).

cards.q: T(n) = 2T(√n) + log n solves to:
cards.explain: Put n = 2ᵐ: S(m) = 2S(m/2) + m = Θ(m log m).

notes.p: f(n) = O(g(n)) if there are constants c > 0 and n₀ with f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. Ω reverses the inequality; Θ requires both. Little-o means f/g → 0, little-ω means f/g → ∞. Useful properties: transitivity holds for all five; **O and Ω are reflexive, o and ω are not**; f = O(g) ⇔ g = Ω(f).

T(n) = 2T(√n) + log n.
Let n = 2ᵐ, so √n = 2^(m/2) and log n = m. Define S(m) = T(2ᵐ):
S(m) = 2S(m/2) + m → by the Master theorem S(m) = Θ(m log m).
Back-substitute m = log n: **T(n) = Θ(log n · log log n)**.
Similarly T(n) = T(√n) + 1 gives S(m) = S(m/2) + 1 = Θ(log m) → T(n) = Θ(log log n).

notes.h: Worked example 2: recursion tree with unequal splits
notes.p:
T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n.
Every full level sums to n (n/3 + 2n/3 = n). The shortest root-to-leaf path has log₃ n levels, the longest log₍₃/₂₎ n. So the total is between n log₃ n and n log₁.₅ n → **Θ(n log n)**.
Contrast T(n) = T(n/2) + T(n/4) + n: level sums are n, 3n/4, 9n/16 … — a geometric series bounded by 4n → **Θ(n)**.

`def count_harmonic(n):
    c = 0
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        j = 1
        while j <= n:
            c += 1
            j += i
    return c
def count_doubling(n):
    c, i = 0, 1
    while i < n:
        c += i
        i *= 2
    return c
for n in (1000, 2000, 4000):
    print(n, count_harmonic(n), count_doubling(n))`

Output:
`1000 8053 1023
2000 17498 2047
4000 37781 4095`

Doubling n slightly more than doubles the first count (n log n) while the second grows in step with n (the sum 1 + 2 + … + 2ᵏ < 2n).
Watch for these:
points: Θ(n) loop with an O(1) body is not automatically Θ(n) total if the body contains a hidden loop (e.g. a string copy).
Logs of different bases differ by a constant, so O(log₂ n) = O(log₁₀ n), but 2^(log₂ n) = n while 2^(log₄ n) = √n.
Worst-case Θ is not the same as 'always' — quicksort is Θ(n²) worst case and Θ(n log n) on average.
Space complexity counts the recursion stack.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Order: log n < √n < n < n log n < n² < 2ⁿ < n! < nⁿ.
Compare exponentials by taking logs.
Σ n/i = Θ(n log n); doubling loops sum to Θ(n).
T(n) = 2T(√n) + log n → Θ(log n log log n).
Unequal splits that sum to n per level → Θ(n log n).
Geometric level sums → root dominates.

cards.title: Searching
cards.body: Linear search O(n). **Binary search** on a sorted array uses at most ⌊log₂n⌋ + 1 comparisons (n = 1000 → 10). Interpolation search averages O(log log n) on uniform data but is O(n) in the worst case.

cards.title: Sorting cheat-sheet
points: Bubble / insertion: O(n²) worst, O(n) best (sorted input); stable
Selection: always Θ(n²) comparisons, at most n − 1 swaps; not stable
Merge: Θ(n log n) always, O(n) extra space; stable
Quick: Θ(n log n) average, Θ(n²) worst; in place; not stable
Heap: Θ(n log n); in place; not stable
Counting / radix: O(n + k) / O(d(n + k)); not comparison-based

cards.title: Inversions
cards.body: An **inversion** is a pair i < j with a[i] > a[j]. Insertion sort and bubble sort perform exactly one swap per inversion. A reverse-sorted array has n(n − 1)/2 inversions; merge sort can count them in O(n log n).

cards.title: Quicksort worst case
cards.body: With the first (or last) element as pivot, an already sorted array splits into sizes 0 and n − 1 every time: T(n) = T(n − 1) + n → Θ(n²) and recursion depth n. Random or median-of-three pivots avoid this in practice.

cards.title: Comparison facts
points: Merging sorted lists of sizes m and n: at most m + n − 1 comparisons
Any comparison sort: ≥ ⌈log₂(n!)⌉ comparisons worst case
Second largest of n: n + ⌈log₂n⌉ − 2 comparisons
k-th smallest: O(n) worst case (median of medians)

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: When a question names a specific input (sorted, reverse-sorted, all equal), simulate the algorithm on it rather than quoting the average case.

cards.q: Comparisons made by insertion sort on a reverse-sorted array of 5 elements:
cards.explain: Element i is compared with all i − 1 before it: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

cards.q: Worst-case comparisons of binary search on a sorted array of 1000 elements:
Which sort makes at most n − 1 swaps?
cards.explain: One swap per pass to place the minimum.

notes.p: GATE asks for **counts** (comparisons, swaps, passes), **properties** (stable, in-place, adaptive) and **behaviour on special inputs**. In-place: bubble, insertion, selection, heap, quick. Stable: bubble, insertion, merge, counting, radix (with a stable inner sort). Adaptive (faster on nearly sorted input): insertion and bubble with an early-exit flag.

`def partition(a, lo, hi):
    pivot, i = a[hi], lo - 1
    for j in range(lo, hi):
        if a[j] <= pivot:
            i += 1
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    a[i + 1], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i + 1]
    return i + 1
a = [7, 2, 1, 6, 8, 5, 3, 4]
p = partition(a, 0, len(a) - 1)
print(p, a)
def inversions(a):
    return sum(1 for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i + 1, len(a)) if a[i] > a[j])
print(inversions([5, 4, 3, 2, 1]), inversions([2, 4, 1, 3, 5]))`

Output:
`3 [2, 1, 3, 4, 8, 5, 7, 6]
10 3`

Pivot 4 lands at index 3, with smaller elements to its left and larger to its right. The reverse-sorted array of 5 has 10 inversions; [2, 4, 1, 3, 5] has 3 (2>1, 4>1, 4>3), so insertion sort makes exactly 3 swaps on it.

Merge sort recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n → Θ(n log n), independent of input order. For n = 8, there are log₂8 = 3 levels of merging. Worst-case comparisons when merging two sorted halves of size 4: 4 + 4 − 1 = 7; best case 4 (every element of one half is smaller). Total worst case for n = 8: 4 × 1 + 2 × 3 + 1 × 7 = **17** comparisons, which equals n⌈log₂n⌉ − 2^⌈log₂n⌉ + 1 = 24 − 8 + 1 = 17.

Binary search is a template, not one algorithm. To find the **first occurrence** of x, keep searching left after a match; to find the insertion point, return lo when the loop ends. Both stay O(log n).

**Worked example 3.** Sorted array of 31 elements: a successful binary search needs at most ⌊log₂31⌋ + 1 = **5** comparisons, and the search tree is perfectly balanced (1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 nodes). Average successful comparisons = (1·1 + 2·2 + 3·4 + 4·8 + 5·16)/31 = 129/31 ≈ **4.16**. Ternary search makes fewer iterations (log₃ n) but up to two comparisons per iteration, so it is not faster in comparisons.

A comparison sort is a decision tree with n! leaves, so its height is at least log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n). For n = 5, ⌈log₂120⌉ = **7** comparisons are necessary in the worst case.

Counting sort beats this by indexing on key values: O(n + k) time and space for keys in 0..k. Radix sort applies a stable counting sort digit by digit: d passes, O(d(n + b)) for base b. Sorting n integers in the range 0..n³ − 1 in base n takes 3 passes → **O(n)**.
Remember:
points: Binary search worst case ⌊log₂n⌋ + 1 comparisons.
Insertion/bubble swaps = number of inversions; reverse sorted → n(n − 1)/2.
Selection sort: ≤ n − 1 swaps, always Θ(n²) comparisons.
Quick sort worst Θ(n²) on sorted input with end pivot.
Merge: stable, Θ(n log n), O(n) extra space.
Comparison lower bound ⌈log₂(n!)⌉.
Counting/radix are linear but not comparison-based.

cards.title: Hash functions
cards.body: **Division**: h(k) = k mod m, choose m prime and not close to a power of 2. **Multiplication**: h(k) = ⌊m · frac(kA)⌋ with 0 < A < 1. A good function spreads keys uniformly and is cheap to compute.

cards.title: Chaining
cards.body: Each slot holds a linked list. With load factor **α = n/m**, a search takes Θ(1 + α) on average under uniform hashing. Deletion is easy; α can exceed 1.

cards.title: Open addressing
cards.body: All keys live in the table (α ≤ 1). Probe sequences:
points: Linear: (h(k) + i) mod m — primary clustering
Quadratic: (h(k) + c₁i + c₂i²) mod m — secondary clustering
Double hashing: (h₁(k) + i·h₂(k)) mod m — best spread; h₂(k) must never be 0

cards.title: Expected probes (uniform hashing)
points: Unsuccessful search / insert ≤ 1/(1 − α)
Successful search ≤ (1/α) ln(1/(1 − α))
α = 0.5 → at most 2 probes for a miss

cards.title: Deletion in open addressing
cards.body: You cannot just empty a slot — later searches would stop early. Mark it **deleted (tombstone)**: searches skip it, inserts may reuse it.

cards.q: A chained hash table has 10 slots and 25 keys. Its load factor is:
Keys 18, 41, 22, 44, 59 are inserted with h(k) = k mod 11 and linear probing. Where does 44 go?
cards.explain: 18 → 7, 41 → 8, 22 → 0; 44 mod 11 = 0 is taken, so it probes slot 1, which is free.

cards.q: With uniform hashing into m slots, the expected number of colliding pairs among n keys is:
cards.explain: Each of the C(n, 2) pairs collides with probability 1/m.

notes.h: Why hashing is O(1) on average
notes.p: Hashing maps a key to a slot in O(1); the cost of a lookup is the number of keys examined there. With chaining that is about 1 + α, so keeping α bounded (by resizing when it passes a threshold) keeps operations O(1) on average. The **worst case is still O(n)** when everything lands in one slot.

`def insert_all(keys, m, probe):
    t = [None] * m
    for k in keys:
        for i in range(m):
            s = probe(k, i) % m
            if t[s] is None:
                t[s] = k
                break
    return t
lin = lambda k, i: k % 10 + i
print(insert_all([43, 165, 62, 123, 142], 10, lin))
lin11 = lambda k, i: k % 11 + i
print(insert_all([18, 41, 22, 44, 59, 32, 31, 73], 11, lin11))
dbl = lambda k, i: k % 13 + i * (1 + k % 11)
print(insert_all([79, 69, 98, 72, 14, 50], 13, dbl))`

Output:
`[None, None, 62, 43, 123, 165, 142, None, None, None]
[22, 44, 73, None, 59, None, None, 18, 41, 31, 32]
[None, 79, None, None, 69, 14, None, 98, 72, None, None, 50, None]`

In the second table 22 takes slot 0, 44 collides at 0 and moves to **slot 1**, 59 (→ 4) is free, and later keys pile up around slots 7–10 and 0–2: primary clustering in action.

m = 13, h₁(k) = k mod 13, h₂(k) = 1 + (k mod 11). Insert 79, 69, 98, 72, 14, 50.
79 → 1. 69 → 4. 98 → 7. 72 → 7 taken; h₂ = 1 + 6 = 7 → 7 + 7 = 14 mod 13 = **1** taken → 1 + 7 = **8**. 14 → 1 taken; h₂ = 1 + 3 = 4 → 5. 50 → 11.
Final: 1: 79, 4: 69, 5: 14, 7: 98, 8: 72, 11: 50 — matching the program output. Because h₂ differs per key, colliding keys follow different paths, avoiding clusters.
Under simple uniform hashing each key lands in each slot with probability 1/m independently.
points: P(a given pair collides) = 1/m.
Expected colliding pairs among n keys = n(n − 1)/(2m).
P(no collision among n keys) = m(m − 1)…(m − n + 1)/mⁿ (birthday problem).
Expected empty slots after n insertions = m(1 − 1/m)ⁿ ≈ m·e^(−n/m).
Linear probing: the probability the next key goes to the slot right after a run of length r is (r + 1)/m — long runs grow faster.

notes.p: Remember:
points: α = n/m; chaining search Θ(1 + α).
Open addressing needs α ≤ 1; miss costs ≤ 1/(1 − α).
Linear → primary clustering; quadratic → secondary; double hashing best.
h₂(k) must never be 0 and should be coprime to m.
Delete with tombstones in open addressing.
Expected colliding pairs = n(n − 1)/(2m).
Worst case of any hashing scheme is O(n).

cards.title: Divide and conquer
cards.body: Split into subproblems, solve recursively, combine. Cost follows a recurrence such as T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n). Classics: binary search, merge sort, quicksort, max–min, closest pair (O(n log n)), Karatsuba and Strassen.

cards.title: Fast multiplication
points: Karatsuba: T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) → Θ(n^log₂3) ≈ n^1.585
Strassen: T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²) → Θ(n^log₂7) ≈ n^2.81
Naive matrix multiply: 8 half-size products → Θ(n³)

cards.title: When greedy works
cards.body: Greedy needs the **greedy-choice property** (a locally best choice is part of some optimal solution) and **optimal substructure**. Proofs use an exchange argument. It fails for 0/1 knapsack and general coin systems.

cards.title: Greedy classics
points: Activity selection: pick the earliest finishing compatible activity
Fractional knapsack: take items by value/weight ratio
Huffman: repeatedly merge the two smallest frequencies
Job sequencing with deadlines: highest profit first, latest free slot
Optimal merge pattern: always merge the two smallest files

cards.title: Fractional knapsack
cards.body: W = 50; items (value, weight): (60, 10), (100, 20), (120, 30). Ratios 6, 5, 4. Take the first two fully (weight 30, value 160) and 20/30 of the third (value 80): **240**.

cards.q: Strassen's algorithm runs in:
Optimal merge pattern for files of sizes 20, 30, 10, 5, 30: total record moves =
Which problem is NOT solved optimally by a greedy algorithm?
cards.explain: 0/1 knapsack needs dynamic programming.

notes.p:
**Max–min**: splitting in halves gives T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 2, T(2) = 1 → 3n/2 − 2 comparisons. **Closest pair of points**: split by x, recurse, then check a strip where each point needs at most a constant number of neighbours → O(n log n). **Counting inversions** piggybacks on merge sort.

**Worked example 1.** Karatsuba multiplies two n-digit numbers with three half-size products: (a·10^(n/2) + b)(c·10^(n/2) + d) needs ac, bd and (a + b)(c + d). For n = 1024 digits that is 3¹⁰ = 59,049 single-digit multiplications versus 4¹⁰ = 1,048,576 for the naive method.

Jobs (profit, deadline): J1 (100, 2), J2 (19, 1), J3 (27, 2), J4 (25, 1), J5 (15, 3).
Sort by profit: J1, J3, J4, J2, J5. Give each the latest free slot ≤ its deadline.
J1 → slot 2. J3 → slot 1. J4 → deadline 1, slot taken → skip. J2 → skip. J5 → slot 3.
Schedule J3, J1, J5, profit **27 + 100 + 15 = 142**.

Build a min-heap of frequencies, repeatedly merge the two smallest, and the merge tree gives prefix-free codes. Expected bits per symbol = Σ fᵢ × depthᵢ / Σ fᵢ.

**Worked example 3.** Frequencies a: 5, b: 9, c: 12, d: 13, e: 16, f: 45. Merges: 5 + 9 = 14; 12 + 13 = 25; 14 + 16 = 30; 25 + 30 = 55; 45 + 55 = 100. Code lengths: f 1; c, d, e 3; a, b 4. Total bits = 45·1 + (12 + 13 + 16)·3 + (5 + 9)·4 = 45 + 123 + 56 = **224** — the same as the sum of merged weights (14 + 25 + 30 + 55 + 100).
Remember:
points: Karatsuba n^1.585; Strassen n^2.81.
Max–min by D&C: 3n/2 − 2 comparisons.
Greedy needs greedy-choice + optimal substructure.
Fractional knapsack: by value/weight; 0/1 needs DP.
Activity selection: earliest finish time.
Job sequencing: highest profit into the latest free slot.
Huffman / optimal merge: merge the two smallest; cost = sum of merges.

cards.title: Two ingredients
cards.body: **Optimal substructure** (an optimal answer is built from optimal sub-answers) and **overlapping subproblems** (the same subproblem recurs). Memoise top-down or fill a table bottom-up; time = number of states × work per state.

cards.title: Core recurrences
points: LCS: L[i][j] = L[i−1][j−1] + 1 if xᵢ = yⱼ, else max(L[i−1][j], L[i][j−1])
0/1 knapsack: K[i][w] = max(K[i−1][w], vᵢ + K[i−1][w − wᵢ])
Edit distance: D[i][j] = min(D[i−1][j] + 1, D[i][j−1] + 1, D[i−1][j−1] + [xᵢ ≠ yⱼ])
Matrix chain: M[i][j] = min over k of M[i][k] + M[k+1][j] + pᵢ₋₁pₖpⱼ

cards.title: Complexities
points: LCS / edit distance: O(mn)
0/1 knapsack: O(nW) — pseudo-polynomial
Matrix chain, optimal BST: O(n³)
Floyd–Warshall O(V³); Bellman–Ford O(VE)
LIS: O(n²) simple DP, O(n log n) with binary search

cards.title: LCS
cards.body: LCS of AGGTAB and GXTXAYB is **GTAB**, length 4. LCS of ABCBDAB and BDCABA has length 4 (e.g. BCBA).

cards.title: Edit distance
cards.body: kitten → sitting: substitute k→s, e→i, insert g → **3**. sunday → saturday: insert a, t; substitute n→r → **3**.

cards.title: Subset sum
cards.body: S[i][t] = S[i−1][t] or S[i−1][t − aᵢ]. Like knapsack it is O(n·T) — polynomial in the **value** T, not in the input length, so subset sum stays NP-complete.

cards.q: 0/1 knapsack, W = 5, items (weight, value): (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 5), (5, 6). Maximum value:
cards.explain: Items of weight 2 and 3: value 3 + 4 = 7.

cards.q: Length of the LCS of AGGTAB and GXTXAYB:
cards.explain: GTAB.

cards.q: The 0/1 knapsack DP running in O(nW) is called:
cards.explain: W is a number; its input size is log W bits.

notes.h: How to set up any DP
notes.p:
1. Define the state in words (e.g. L[i][j] = LCS of the first i and j characters).
2. Write the recurrence by looking at the last decision.
3. Fix base cases (empty prefixes, capacity 0).
4. Choose the fill order so dependencies are ready.
5. Answer = a specific cell; trace back for the solution itself.
GATE often gives a recurrence and asks for a table entry, or gives code and asks what it computes.

notes.h: Reading DP code in GATE questions
notes.p:
GATE often shows a short C function with a table and asks what it computes or what a cell holds. Identify the state, the base row/column and which neighbours each cell reads.

**Worked example 3.** A function fills C[i][j] = C[i−1][j−1] + C[i−1][j] with C[i][0] = C[i][i] = 1. It is **Pascal's triangle**, so C[6][3] = 20 and the table has O(n²) cells. Another fills L[i] = 1 + max(L[j]) over j < i with a[j] < a[i] — that is the **longest increasing subsequence**; for 10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18 the answer is 4 (2, 3, 7, 18). Counting paths in a grid with only right/down moves uses P[i][j] = P[i−1][j] + P[i][j−1], giving C(m + n, n) paths for an m × n grid of moves.

**Bellman–Ford**: d_k(v) = min(d_{k−1}(v), min over edges (u, v) of d_{k−1}(u) + w(u, v)), for k = 1..V − 1. **Floyd–Warshall**: D_k[i][j] = min(D_{k−1}[i][j], D_{k−1}[i][k] + D_{k−1}[k][j]) — allowing vertex k as an intermediate. A negative value on the diagonal after Floyd–Warshall signals a negative cycle.
Remember:
points: DP = optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems.
Time = states × work per state.
LCS/edit distance O(mn); knapsack O(nW) pseudo-polynomial.
Matrix chain O(n³); parenthesisations = Cₙ₋₁.
1-D knapsack: iterate capacity downward for 0/1.
Floyd–Warshall O(V³); negative diagonal → negative cycle.
LIS in O(n log n) with patience sorting.

cards.title: BFS and DFS
cards.body: Both O(V + E) with adjacency lists, O(V²) with a matrix. **BFS** finds fewest-edge paths and gives levels. **DFS** gives discovery/finish times and classifies edges as tree, back, forward or cross; a **back edge ⇔ cycle**. Undirected DFS has only tree and back edges.

cards.title: DFS applications
cards.body: **Topological sort**: order by decreasing finish time (DAGs only). **Strongly connected components**: Kosaraju (two DFS passes, one on the transpose) or Tarjan, O(V + E). Articulation points and bridges via low-link values.

cards.title: Minimum spanning trees
points: Cut property: the lightest edge crossing any cut is in some MST
Kruskal: sort edges, add if no cycle (union–find) — O(E log E)
Prim: grow from a vertex with a heap — O(E log V)
Distinct weights ⇒ unique MST; Kₙ has n^(n−2) spanning trees

cards.title: Shortest paths
points: Dijkstra: non-negative weights, O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap
Bellman–Ford: negative edges allowed, detects negative cycles, O(VE)
DAG: relax in topological order, O(V + E)
Floyd–Warshall: all pairs, O(V³)

cards.title: Kruskal by hand
cards.body: Edges: AB 1, BC 2, AC 3, CD 4, BD 5, DE 6, CE 7. Take AB 1, BC 2, skip AC (cycle), take CD 4, skip BD, take DE 6. MST weight = 1 + 2 + 4 + 6 = **13**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: If every edge weight is increased by a constant, the MST does not change but shortest paths can. If weights are squared (all positive), MST is unchanged; shortest paths may change.

cards.q: MST weight for edges AB 1, BC 2, AC 3, CD 4, BD 5, DE 6, CE 7:
cards.explain: Kruskal picks 1, 2, 4, 6.

cards.q: A DFS of a directed graph finds a back edge. This means the graph:
cards.explain: A back edge points to an ancestor still on the recursion stack.

cards.q: Number of spanning trees of K₄:
cards.explain: Cayley: n^(n−2) = 4² = 16.

notes.p:
In BFS of an undirected graph, every non-tree edge joins vertices whose levels differ by at most 1. In DFS of an undirected graph there are no cross edges. In a directed graph, an edge (u, v) with d[u] < d[v] < f[v] < f[u] is a tree or forward edge; d[v] < d[u] < f[u] < f[v] is a back edge; f[v] < d[u] is a cross edge.

A DAG has at least one topological order; the order is unique iff there is a Hamiltonian path.

Graph: A→B 4, A→C 1, C→B 2, B→D 1, C→D 5. Source A.
Init: A 0, others ∞. Extract A: B = 4, C = 1.
Extract C (1): B = min(4, 1 + 2) = 3, D = 1 + 5 = 6.
Extract B (3): D = min(6, 3 + 1) = 4.
Extract D (4). Final **A 0, B 3, C 1, D 4**; order of extraction A, C, B, D.
With a negative edge (e.g. B→C −3 added), Dijkstra may finalise a vertex too early — use Bellman–Ford.
Facts that settle true/false options quickly:
points: With distinct weights the MST is unique; the heaviest edge of any cycle is in no MST.
The lightest edge of the graph is always in some MST.
Prim with an adjacency matrix and array is O(V²) — better for dense graphs.
A shortest-path tree is not necessarily an MST, and vice versa.
Max spanning tree: run Kruskal on edges sorted in decreasing order.

notes.p: Remember:
points: BFS/DFS O(V + E); back edge ⇔ cycle.
Topological sort = decreasing finish times; DAG only.
Kruskal O(E log E) with union–find; Prim O(E log V).
Dijkstra needs non-negative weights.
Bellman–Ford O(VE); one more relaxation round detects negative cycles.
Floyd–Warshall O(V³) all pairs.
Cayley: Kₙ has n^(n−2) spanning trees.

cards.title: Chomsky hierarchy
cards.body: Regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ context-sensitive ⊂ recursive ⊂ recursively enumerable. Machines: DFA/NFA, PDA, LBA, Turing machine (halting deciders for recursive).

cards.title: Finite automata
cards.body: DFA and NFA accept the same languages; subset construction can need up to 2ⁿ states. Minimise a DFA by merging equivalent states. 'Number mod k' languages need k states.

cards.title: Pumping lemma
cards.body: Used to prove non-regularity: aⁿbⁿ, palindromes, {a^p : p prime} are not regular. For CFLs: aⁿbⁿcⁿ and {ww} are not context-free.

cards.title: Closure properties
points: Regular: union, intersection, complement, concatenation, star, reversal, homomorphism
CFL: union, concatenation, star — NOT intersection or complement
CFL ∩ regular is CFL
DCFL: closed under complement, not union
Recursive: closed under complement; RE: not

cards.title: Decidability
points: Decidable: membership, emptiness, finiteness for CFGs; equivalence of DFAs
Undecidable: halting problem, equivalence of CFGs, ambiguity of a CFG, whether a CFG generates Σ*
Rice's theorem: any non-trivial property of the language of a TM is undecidable

cards.title: DFA for divisibility
cards.body: Binary numbers (MSB first) divisible by 3: states are remainders 0, 1, 2. On bit b, r → (2r + b) mod 3. Start and accept at 0 → 3 states.

cards.q: Which language is NOT context-free?
cards.explain: A single stack cannot match three counts.

cards.q: States in the minimal DFA accepting binary numbers divisible by 5:
cards.explain: One state per remainder 0–4, all distinguishable.

cards.q: Which problem is undecidable?
options: Membership of a string in a CFL
cards.explain: CFG equivalence is undecidable; the others have algorithms.

notes.p:
Languages form a hierarchy: **regular ⊂ deterministic CFL ⊂ context-free ⊂ context-sensitive ⊂ recursive (decidable) ⊂ recursively enumerable**. Machines: **DFA/NFA** (regular), **DPDA** (DCFL), **PDA** (CFL), **LBA** (CSL), **Turing machine that always halts** (recursive), **Turing machine** (RE).

NFA and DFA are equally powerful (subset construction may need up to 2ⁿ states). NPDA is **more** powerful than DPDA (e.g. even-length palindromes wwᴿ need non-determinism). Non-deterministic and deterministic Turing machines are equally powerful.

A language is regular iff some DFA accepts it iff some regular expression describes it. Non-regular examples: {aⁿbⁿ}, {ww}, {a^(n²)}, balanced parentheses — they need unbounded counting; prove it with the **pumping lemma** or Myhill–Nerode. The minimal DFA for binary numbers divisible by an odd n has exactly n states (even n, such as 4 or 8, can need fewer).

A DFA for 'binary strings whose value is divisible by 3' uses the remainder as the state: reading bit b moves state r to (2r + b) mod 3.

`def dfa_div(s, n=3):
    r = 0
    for b in s:
        r = (2 * r + int(b)) % n
    return r == 0

def even_zeros_odd_ones(s):
    state = (0, 0)                  # (zeros mod 2, ones mod 2)
    for c in s:
        z, o = state
        state = ((z + 1) % 2, o) if c == "0" else (z, (o + 1) % 2)
    return state == (0, 1)

print([x for x in range(16) if dfa_div(format(x, "b"))])
print(even_zeros_odd_ones("001"), even_zeros_odd_ones("0110"))`

Output:
`[0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15]
True False`

The second DFA has 4 states — one per (zeros mod 2, ones mod 2) pair, a standard product construction.
Closure questions are free marks if you memorise this:
points: **Regular:** closed under union, intersection, complement, concatenation, Kleene star, reversal, difference, homomorphism.
**CFL:** closed under union, concatenation, star, reversal, homomorphism; **not** under intersection or complement. CFL ∩ regular is CFL.
**DCFL:** closed under complement; not under union or intersection.
**Recursive:** closed under union, intersection, complement.
**RE:** closed under union and intersection, **not** complement. If L and its complement are both RE, L is recursive.

notes.p: **Decidable:** membership for CFG (CYK, O(n³)), emptiness and finiteness of CFLs, equivalence of DFAs, everything about regular languages. **Undecidable:** halting problem, whether a TM accepts any string, equivalence of two CFGs, ambiguity of a CFG, whether a CFG generates all strings (Σ*), Post correspondence problem. **Rice's theorem:** any non-trivial property of the **language** recognised by a Turing machine is undecidable.

**Q: Is {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 0} context-free?** A: No — it is context-sensitive.

**Q: Is {aⁿbⁿ | n ≤ 1000} regular?** A: Yes — it is finite, and every finite language is regular.

**Q: L₁ is regular and L₂ is CFL. Is L₁ ∩ L₂ CFL?** A: Yes, always.

**Q: Minimum states of a DFA accepting strings over {a, b} whose length is divisible by 3?** A: 3.

**Q: Is 'does TM M halt on the empty string' decidable?** A: No (reduction from halting).
Remember:
points: Regular ⊂ DCFL ⊂ CFL ⊂ CSL ⊂ REC ⊂ RE.
DFA = NFA in power; DPDA < NPDA.
Finite languages are always regular.
CFL not closed under ∩ and complement.
REC closed under complement; RE is not.
Rice: non-trivial language properties of TMs are undecidable.
CFG equivalence and ambiguity are undecidable.

cards.title: DFA, NFA, ε-NFA
cards.body: All three accept exactly the **regular languages**. The subset construction turns an n-state NFA into a DFA with at most **2ⁿ** states; ε-closures handle ε-moves. NFAs are often far smaller.

cards.title: Regex identities
points: r(sr)* = (rs)*r

cards.title: State counts to remember
points: #a's ≡ 0 (mod n): minimal DFA n states
Strings ending in a fixed string of length k: k + 1 states (e.g. (a + b)*abb → 4)
k-th symbol from the right is 1: NFA k + 1 states, minimal DFA 2ᵏ
Length exactly k: k + 2 states (including a dead state)

cards.title: Minimisation
cards.body: Remove unreachable states, then merge **indistinguishable** states by partition refinement: start with {final, non-final} and split groups whose members go to different groups on some symbol. **Myhill–Nerode**: the number of equivalence classes of the language = states in its minimal DFA.

cards.title: Pumping lemma (regular)
cards.body: If L is regular there is p such that any w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p splits as xyz with **|xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1**, and xyⁱz ∈ L for all i ≥ 0. Used to prove a language is **not** regular: aⁿbⁿ, ww, palindromes, a^(n²), a^prime.

cards.title: Regular or not?
cards.body: {aⁿbᵐ : n, m ≥ 0} = a*b* — regular. {aⁿbⁿ} — not regular. {aⁿbᵐ : n + m even} — regular (track parity). {w : #a(w) = #b(w)} — not regular.

cards.q: Minimal DFA states for strings over {a, b} whose number of a's is divisible by 3:
cards.explain: Track #a mod 3.

cards.q: Minimal DFA states for (a + b)*abb:
cards.explain: Track the longest suffix matching a prefix of abb: ε, a, ab, abb.

cards.q: Which language is NOT regular?
options: Strings with an even number of a's
cards.explain: Matching counts need unbounded memory.

notes.p:
NFA for strings over {a, b} ending in ab: states q0 (start), q1, q2 (final); q0 –a→ {q0, q1}, q0 –b→ {q0}, q1 –b→ {q2}.
DFA states (subsets):
A = {q0}: a → {q0, q1} = B; b → A.
B = {q0, q1}: a → B; b → {q0, q2} = C.
C = {q0, q2} (final): a → B; b → A.
Only **3** DFA states are reachable out of 2³ = 8 possible — the subset construction rarely hits its worst case, but the 'k-th from the right' family does.

DFA over {0, 1}: states A (start), B, C, D, E; final E.
A: 0→B, 1→C; B: 0→B, 1→D; C: 0→B, 1→C; D: 0→B, 1→E; E: 0→B, 1→C.
P₀ = {A, B, C, D} {E}.
On 1: D goes to E (final), others stay in the non-final group → split: {A, B, C} {D} {E}.
On 1 again: B goes to D, A and C go to C → split: {A, C} {B} {D} {E}.
No further split: **A and C merge**, minimal DFA has **4 states**. It recognises exactly the strings ending in 011 (B = 'last symbol 0', D = 'ends in 01', E = 'ends in 011').

`def run(delta, start, finals, w):
    s = start
    for ch in w:
        s = delta[(s, ch)]
    return s in finals
# binary numbers divisible by 3: state = value mod 3
d3 = {(r, b): (2 * r + int(b)) % 3 for r in range(3) for b in '01'}
print([n for n in range(16) if run(d3, 0, {0}, bin(n)[2:])])
dfa = {('A','0'):'B',('A','1'):'C',('B','0'):'B',('B','1'):'D',('C','0'):'B',('C','1'):'C',
       ('D','0'):'B',('D','1'):'E',('E','0'):'B',('E','1'):'C'}
from itertools import product
acc = [''.join(w) for n in range(1, 6) for w in product('01', repeat=n) if run(dfa, 'A', {'E'}, ''.join(w))]
print(all(w.endswith('011') for w in acc), len(acc))`

Output:
`[0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15]
True 7`

The divisibility DFA accepts 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, and every string accepted by the second DFA ends in 011.

It is a **necessary** condition, so it can only show non-regularity. Template for L = {aⁿbⁿ}: assume regular with constant p; choose w = aᵖbᵖ; since |xy| ≤ p, y = aᵏ with k ≥ 1; then xy²z = a^(p+k)bᵖ ∉ L — contradiction.

Closure is often faster: regular languages are closed under union, intersection, complement, concatenation, star, reversal, homomorphism, inverse homomorphism and quotient. If L ∩ a*b* = {aⁿbⁿ}, L cannot be regular.
Watch for these:
points: A **finite** language is always regular.
A subset of a regular language need not be regular ({aⁿbⁿ} ⊆ a*b*).
The union of infinitely many regular languages need not be regular.
Minimal DFA counts usually include the dead state — read whether the question wants a complete DFA.
Two regexes describe the same language iff their minimal DFAs are isomorphic.

notes.p: Remember:
points: DFA = NFA = ε-NFA = regex in power; subset construction ≤ 2ⁿ states.
(a + b)*w with |w| = k → k + 1 states.
k-th from right → 2ᵏ-state minimal DFA.
Minimise by partition refinement; Myhill–Nerode classes = states.
Pumping: |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1, all xyⁱz ∈ L.
Non-regular: aⁿbⁿ, ww, palindromes, a^(n²), a^prime.
Regular closed under ∪, ∩, complement, ·, *, reversal, homomorphisms.

cards.title: Grammars and ambiguity
cards.body: A grammar is **ambiguous** if some string has two parse trees (equivalently, two leftmost derivations). E → E + E | E * E | id is ambiguous for id + id * id. Some CFLs are **inherently ambiguous**, e.g. {aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = j or j = k}.

cards.title: Normal forms
cards.body: **CNF**: A → BC | a. A string of length n needs exactly **2n − 1** derivation steps. **GNF**: A → aα; a string of length n needs exactly **n** steps. Every CFL without ε has grammars in both forms.

cards.title: Pushdown automata
cards.body: NPDAs accept exactly the CFLs (by final state or by empty stack — equivalent). **DPDAs** accept the **deterministic CFLs**, a strict subset: ww^R is a CFL but not a DCFL; wcw^R is a DCFL. DCFLs = languages of LR(1) grammars.

cards.title: Closure
points: CFL: closed under ∪, concatenation, *, homomorphism, reversal, ∩ with a regular language
CFL: NOT closed under ∩ or complement
DCFL: closed under complement and ∩ with regular; NOT under ∪, ∩, concatenation

cards.title: Classic grammars
cards.body:
aⁿbⁿ: S → aSb | ε.
Palindromes over {a, b}: S → aSa | bSb | a | b | ε.
Equal numbers of a and b: S → aSbS | bSaS | ε.
aⁿbᵐ with n ≥ m: S → aSb | aS | ε.

cards.title: Decision problems for CFLs
cards.body: **Decidable**: membership (CYK, O(n³)), emptiness, finiteness. **Undecidable**: ambiguity of a CFG, equivalence of two CFGs, whether L = Σ*, whether two CFLs intersect, whether a CFL is regular.

cards.q: A CNF grammar derives a string of length 5 in how many steps?
Which language is NOT context-free?
cards.explain: Two independent equalities need more than one stack.

cards.q: Which statement is TRUE?
cards.explain: Swap final states of a (suitably normalised) DPDA.

notes.p:
Think about what must match. For aⁿbᵐcᵐdⁿ: the outer a/d pair wraps an inner b/c pair: S → aSd | T, T → bTc | ε. For aⁱbʲcᵏ with i = j + k: write aʲ⁺ᵏ as aᵏaʲ and match from outside in: S → aSc | T, T → aTb | ε.

**Worked example 1.** Show {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} is not context-free via closure. L₁ = {aⁿbⁿcᵐ} and L₂ = {aᵐbⁿcⁿ} are both CFLs, yet L₁ ∩ L₂ = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}. If CFLs were closed under ∩ this would be a CFL — it is not, so CFLs are **not closed under intersection**, and by De Morgan not under complement either.

Grammar (CNF): S → AB | BC, A → BA | a, B → CC | b, C → AB | a. Is 'baaba' in L?
CYK fills a triangular table bottom-up: length-1 cells get {B}, {A, C}, {A, C}, {B}, {A, C}; longer substrings combine pairs of shorter cells with matching rules. The top cell contains S, so **baaba ∈ L**. The table has n(n + 1)/2 cells and each combines O(n) splits — **O(n³)** overall (times grammar size).

If L is context-free there is p such that any w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p splits as uvwxy with **|vwx| ≤ p, |vx| ≥ 1** and uvⁱwxⁱy ∈ L for all i ≥ 0. For aⁿbⁿcⁿ with w = aᵖbᵖcᵖ, the window vwx spans at most two of the three letter blocks, so pumping unbalances the counts. Other non-CFLs: {ww}, {a^(n²)}, {a^prime}, {aⁿbᵐcⁿdᵐ}.
Regular ⊂ DCFL ⊂ CFL ⊂ CSL ⊂ recursive ⊂ RE.
points: Every regular language is a DCFL; aⁿbⁿ is a DCFL but not regular.
ww^R is a CFL but not a DCFL (the PDA must guess the middle).
aⁿbⁿcⁿ and ww are context-sensitive but not context-free.
A CFL ∩ a regular language is a CFL; a CFL ∪ a regular language is a CFL.
CFL over a one-letter alphabet is regular (Parikh).

notes.p: Remember:
points: Ambiguous = two parse trees for some string.
CNF: 2n − 1 steps; GNF: n steps.
NPDA ↔ CFL; DPDA ↔ DCFL ↔ LR(1).
CFL closed under ∪, ·, *, ∩ regular; not ∩, not complement.
DCFL closed under complement; not ∪ or ∩.
CYK membership O(n³); ambiguity and equivalence undecidable.
CFL pumping: |vwx| ≤ p, |vx| ≥ 1.

cards.title: Turing machines
cards.body: A TM has a finite control and an infinite read/write tape. Multi-tape, multi-head and nondeterministic TMs all have the **same power** as the basic TM (they may be faster). A TM may accept, reject or **loop forever**.

cards.title: Recursive vs RE
cards.body: **Recursive (decidable)**: some TM halts on every input with the right answer. **Recursively enumerable (semi-decidable)**: some TM accepts exactly L but may loop on strings outside L. If both L and its complement are RE, L is recursive.

cards.title: Closure
points: Recursive: ∪, ∩, complement, concatenation, star
RE: ∪, ∩, concatenation, star — NOT complement
co-RE = complements of RE languages

cards.title: Undecidable classics
cards.body: **Halting problem** HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w} is RE but not recursive; its complement is **not even RE**. Also undecidable: Post's correspondence problem, whether L(M) = ∅, whether L(M) is regular, CFG ambiguity.

cards.title: Rice's theorem
cards.body: Every **non-trivial property of the language** L(M) of a TM is undecidable. 'Non-trivial' = some TMs have it and some do not. Properties of the **machine** (number of states, halting within k steps) are not covered and may be decidable.

cards.title: Apply Rice
cards.body: 'Is L(M) empty?', 'Is L(M) finite?', 'Does L(M) contain 101?' — undecidable. 'Does M have more than 5 states?' — decidable. 'Does M halt on ε within 100 steps?' — decidable (simulate 100 steps).

cards.q: The complement of the halting problem is:
cards.explain: If it were RE, HALT would be recursive.

cards.q: If L and its complement are both recursively enumerable, then L is:
cards.explain: Run both recognisers in parallel; one must halt.

cards.q: Which question about a TM M is decidable?
options: Does M have an even number of states?
cards.explain: It asks about the machine's description, not its language.

notes.h: The hierarchy and the big table
notes.p: Type 3 regular ⊂ Type 2 context-free ⊂ Type 1 context-sensitive ⊂ recursive ⊂ Type 0 RE. The decidability table GATE keeps returning to:
points: Membership: decidable for regular, CFL, CSL, recursive; only semi-decidable for RE.
Emptiness: decidable for regular and CFL; undecidable for CSL and beyond.
Finiteness: decidable for regular and CFL; undecidable beyond.
Equivalence: decidable for regular (and DCFL); undecidable for CFL and beyond.
Universality (L = Σ*): decidable for regular; undecidable for CFL.

notes.p:
To prove B undecidable, reduce a known undecidable A to B: a computable f with w ∈ A ⇔ f(w) ∈ B. Then a decider for B would decide A. The direction matters: **A ≤ B transfers hardness from A to B and decidability from B to A**.

**Worked example 1.** Show E_TM = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅} is undecidable. Given ⟨M, w⟩, build M′ that ignores its input and simulates M on w, accepting if M accepts. L(M′) = Σ* if M accepts w, else ∅. So M accepts w ⇔ ⟨M′⟩ ∉ E_TM. A decider for E_TM would decide A_TM — impossible. (Rice's theorem gives the same result instantly.)
Decide each, with the reason:
points: 'Does M accept at least one palindrome?' — a non-trivial language property → **undecidable** (Rice); it is RE (search with dovetailing).
'Does M ever write a 1 on its tape when started on blank tape?' — undecidable (reduce halting), not a pure language property but still undecidable.
'Does M move left at least once within its first 50 steps on input ε?' — **decidable** (finite simulation).
'Is L(M) = L(M′)?' for TMs — neither RE nor co-RE.
'Given a DFA D and a CFG G, is L(D) ⊆ L(G)?' — undecidable (it contains CFG universality when D accepts Σ*).

notes.p: Partial deciders help classify: A_TM (M accepts w) is RE — simulate and accept if it accepts. Its complement is co-RE but not RE. A language that is RE and co-RE is recursive. Hence for each of the four combinations: recursive (both), RE only, co-RE only, neither. 'L(M) is infinite' and 'L(M) = Σ*' are neither RE nor co-RE.
Watch for these:
points: Rice applies to **TMs** only — for DFAs and CFGs many language properties are decidable.
A trivial property ('L(M) is RE') is decidable — the answer is always yes.
Nondeterminism does not add power to TMs, but it does to PDAs.
Decidable ≠ efficient: the question is about existence of a halting algorithm.

notes.p: Remember:
points: TM variants are equally powerful.
Recursive = halts always; RE = may loop on non-members.
L and L̄ both RE ⇒ L recursive.
HALT is RE, not recursive; its complement is not RE.
Rice: non-trivial language properties of TMs are undecidable.
Recursive closed under complement; RE is not.
CFG ambiguity, equivalence and universality are undecidable.

cards.title: Phases
cards.body: Lexical analysis → syntax analysis → semantic analysis → intermediate code → optimisation → code generation. The symbol table is shared by all phases.

cards.title: Counting tokens
cards.body:
printf("%d", x);
Tokens: printf ( "%d" , x ) ; → 7. A string literal is one token; whitespace and comments are not tokens.

cards.title: Top-down parsing
cards.body: LL(1) needs a grammar free of left recursion and left-factored, with disjoint FIRST sets per alternative (and FIRST/FOLLOW disjoint when ε is derivable).

cards.title: Bottom-up parsing
cards.body: Power: LR(0) < SLR(1) < LALR(1) < CLR(1). LALR merges CLR states with the same core, so it has as many states as LR(0)/SLR; merging can create reduce–reduce conflicts. YACC builds LALR(1).

cards.title: Syntax-directed translation
cards.body: S-attributed: only synthesised attributes, evaluated bottom-up. L-attributed: inherited attributes depend only on the parent and left siblings — evaluable in one left-to-right pass.

cards.title: Intermediate code & blocks
cards.body: Three-address code (quadruples, triples), SSA form. Leaders: first instruction, any jump target, and the instruction after a jump. Each leader starts a basic block.

cards.title: Optimisations
points: Constant folding & propagation
Common sub-expression elimination
Dead-code elimination
Loop-invariant code motion, strength reduction
Liveness analysis drives register allocation

cards.q: Number of tokens in: int a = b + 10;
YACC generates which kind of parser?
cards.explain: YACC/Bison build LALR(1) tables by default.

cards.q: Which must be eliminated before building an LL(1) parser?
cards.explain: Left recursion makes a top-down parser loop forever.

notes.p:
**Lexical analysis** (scanner) turns characters into **tokens** using regular expressions/DFAs; **syntax analysis** (parser) builds a parse tree using a CFG; **semantic analysis** does type checking; **intermediate code generation** produces three-address code; **code optimisation** improves it; **code generation** emits target code. The **symbol table** is shared by all phases.

**Token counting example:** `printf("i = %d, &i = %x", i, &i);` has **10 tokens**: printf, (, the string literal, ',', i, ',', &, i, ), ;. Text inside a string literal and comments are not split into separate tokens.

notes.h: FIRST and FOLLOW with a worked grammar

notes.p:
Bottom-up (shift-reduce) parsers in increasing power: **LR(0) < SLR(1) < LALR(1) < CLR(1)** (LR(1)). LALR merges LR(1) states with the same core, so it has as many states as SLR/LR(0) but may introduce **reduce–reduce** (never new shift–reduce) conflicts. Every LL(1) grammar is LR(1); no ambiguous grammar is LL(1) or LR(k). Operator-precedence parsers handle expression grammars.

**Syntax-directed translation:** **S-attributed** definitions use only synthesised attributes (evaluated bottom-up, fit LR parsers); **L-attributed** allow inherited attributes from the parent and left siblings (fit LL parsers). Every S-attributed SDD is L-attributed.

**Three-address code** has at most one operator on the right: `t1 = b * c; t2 = a + t1`. Representations: quadruples, triples, indirect triples. **Static single assignment (SSA)** gives each variable exactly one assignment. A **basic block** starts at a leader (first instruction, a jump target, or the instruction after a jump); a **control-flow graph** links blocks.

Optimisations: **constant folding** (3 * 4 → 12), **constant propagation**, **common sub-expression elimination**, **dead-code elimination**, **copy propagation**, **loop-invariant code motion**, **strength reduction** (x * 2 → x + x or x << 1), **loop unrolling**. **Liveness analysis** (a backward data-flow analysis) decides which variables need registers; register allocation is graph colouring of the interference graph.

**Q: Which parser is most powerful: SLR, LALR, CLR?** A: CLR(1).

**Q: Can LALR have shift–reduce conflicts that CLR does not?** A: No; merging can only add reduce–reduce conflicts.

**Q: Is a left-recursive grammar LL(1)?** A: No.

**Q: Minimum temporaries for a = (b + c) * (b + c) using CSE?** A: One: t1 = b + c; a = t1 * t1.

**Q: Which phase detects an undeclared variable?** A: Semantic analysis.
Remember:
points: Lexer → parser → semantic → ICG → optimiser → codegen.
String literal = one token.
LL(1): disjoint FIRSTs; check FOLLOW when ε is possible.
LR(0) < SLR < LALR < CLR.
LALR may add only reduce–reduce conflicts.
S-attributed ⊂ L-attributed.
Liveness is a backward analysis.

cards.title: Lexical analysis
cards.body: The **lexer** reads characters and groups them into **tokens** (identifier, keyword, constant, operator, punctuation, string literal). The matched text is the **lexeme**; the rule (usually a regular expression) is the **pattern**. Tokens are recognised by a DFA built from the regexes. Comments and whitespace are discarded.

cards.title: Maximal munch
cards.body: The lexer always takes the **longest** prefix that forms a token; ties go to the rule listed first (so `if` is a keyword, not an identifier). Hence `a+++b` is `a ++ + b`, and `x=-1` is `x = - 1`.

cards.title: Grammar transformations for LL(1)
points: Left recursion A → Aα | β becomes A → βA′, A′ → αA′ | ε
Left factoring A → αβ₁ | αβ₂ becomes A → αA′, A′ → β₁ | β₂
LL(1) condition: for A → α | β, FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅
If β ⇒* ε, also FIRST(α) ∩ FOLLOW(A) = ∅

cards.title: Bottom-up parsing
cards.body: Shift-reduce parsers find the **handle** and reduce it, tracing a **rightmost derivation in reverse**. LR(0) items drive SLR; LR(1) items (with lookahead) drive CLR; merging LR(1) states with the same core gives LALR(1).

cards.title: Power and size
points: LL(1) ⊂ LR(1); LR(0) ⊂ SLR(1) ⊂ LALR(1) ⊂ CLR(1)
States: LR(0) = SLR = LALR ≤ CLR
Merging into LALR can create reduce–reduce, never new shift–reduce, conflicts
Every ambiguous grammar fails every LL/LR test

cards.title: SLR fails, LALR works
cards.body: S → L = R | R; L → *R | id; R → L. In the state containing S → L·= R and R → L·, SLR reduces R → L on FOLLOW(R) ∋ '=', a **shift–reduce conflict**. LR(1) lookahead for R → L· there is only $, so LALR(1) and CLR(1) parse it.

cards.q: How many tokens does the C statement `int x = a+++b;` contain?
cards.explain: int, x, =, a, ++, +, b, ; — maximal munch takes ++ first.
