cards.q: Which ordering of parser power is correct?
cards.explain: Each adds more precise lookahead information.

cards.q: Merging LR(1) states with identical cores to form LALR(1) can introduce:
cards.explain: Shift actions depend only on the core, so a new shift–reduce conflict would already exist in CLR.

notes.p:
Lexical analysis is the only phase that touches raw characters. It removes whitespace and comments, recognises tokens with a DFA, enters identifiers into the **symbol table**, and reports errors such as an illegal character or an unterminated string. Keywords are usually recognised as identifiers and then looked up in a reserved-word table.

**Worked example 1: counting tokens.** `printf("i = %d, &i = %x", i, &i);`
Tokens: printf | ( | "i = %d, &i = %x" | , | i | , | & | i | ) | ; → **10**. The whole string literal is one token, however many symbols it contains.

`import re
TOK = re.compile(r'"[^"]*"|[A-Za-z_]\w*|\d+|\+\+|--|==|<=|>=|&&|\|\||[-+*/=<>&;(),{}]')
for s in ['printf("i = %d, &i = %x", i, &i);', 'int x = a+++b;', 'x = y<=z && w--;']:
    toks = TOK.findall(s)
    print(len(toks), toks)`

Output:
`10 ['printf', '(', '"i = %d, &i = %x"', ',', 'i', ',', '&', 'i', ')', ';']
8 ['int', 'x', '=', 'a', '++', '+', 'b', ';']
9 ['x', '=', 'y', '<=', 'z', '&&', 'w', '--', ';']`

The regex lists longer operators (`++`, `<=`) before single characters, which is exactly maximal munch.

**Worked example 2.** E → E + T | T, T → id.
Remove left recursion: E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε, T → id.
FIRST(E) = FIRST(T) = {id}; FIRST(E′) = {+, ε}.
FOLLOW(E) = FOLLOW(E′) = {$}; FOLLOW(T) = {+, $}.
Table: M[E, id] = E → TE′; M[E′, +] = E′ → +TE′; M[E′, $] = E′ → ε; M[T, id] = T → id.
No cell has two entries, so the grammar is **LL(1)**. A left-recursive or ambiguous grammar can never be LL(1).

An LR parser keeps states on a stack and consults ACTION (shift, reduce, accept, error) and GOTO tables. **LR(0)** reduces whenever an item A → α· is complete. **SLR(1)** reduces only on FOLLOW(A). **CLR(1)** reduces only on the item's own lookahead. **LALR(1)** merges CLR states with equal cores — as many states as SLR, almost the power of CLR; YACC/Bison generate LALR parsers.

**Worked example 3.** S → aSb | ab. The LR(0) items: I0 = {S′ → ·S, S → ·aSb, S → ·ab}; on a → I2 = {S → a·Sb, S → a·b, S → ·aSb, S → ·ab}. No state mixes a complete item with another item, so the grammar is **LR(0)** and therefore also SLR, LALR and CLR.
Diagnose a table quickly:
points: **Shift–reduce**: a state has A → α· and B → β·aγ with a in the reduce lookahead.
**Reduce–reduce**: two complete items whose lookaheads overlap.
Ambiguous grammar ⇒ conflicts in every LR table (YACC resolves them with precedence and associativity).
Operator-precedence parsing works only for operator grammars (no ε, no two adjacent nonterminals).
Error recovery: panic mode skips input to a synchronising token such as `;`.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Lexer: tokens via DFA, maximal munch, symbol-table entries.
A string literal is one token.
LL(1): no left recursion, no common prefixes, disjoint FIRST/FOLLOW sets.
LR parsers trace a rightmost derivation in reverse.
LR(0) ⊂ SLR ⊂ LALR ⊂ CLR; SLR and LALR have equal state counts.
LALR merging can add only reduce–reduce conflicts.
Ambiguous grammars are never LL(k) or LR(k).

chapters.title: Syntax-directed translation, runtime environments & intermediate code

cards.title: Attributes
cards.body: A **synthesized** attribute is computed from children (E.val = E₁.val + T.val). An **inherited** attribute comes from the parent or siblings (declarations pass the type down a list). **S-attributed**: only synthesized — evaluated bottom-up during LR parsing. **L-attributed**: inherited only from the parent and **left** siblings — evaluated in one left-to-right depth-first pass.

cards.title: SDT that prints postfix
cards.body:
E → E + T {print('+')} | T; T → T * F {print('*')} | F; F → id {print(id.name)}.
For a + b * c the actions fire in post-order: **a b c * +**. Actions placed at the end of a production run when that production is reduced.

cards.title: Activation records
cards.body: Each call pushes a record holding: actual parameters, return value, **return address**, **control (dynamic) link** to the caller's record, **access (static) link** to the enclosing scope's record, saved registers, local data and temporaries. Recursion needs stack allocation; purely static allocation cannot support it.

cards.title: Static vs dynamic scope
cards.body: **Static (lexical)** scope resolves a name by the program text — the nearest enclosing declaration. **Dynamic** scope uses the most recent active binding on the call stack. C, Java and Python use static scope.

cards.title: Intermediate representations
points: Three-address code: x = y op z, at most 3 addresses
Quadruple: (op, arg1, arg2, result) — easy to move code
Triple: (op, arg1, arg2), results named by position
Indirect triples: a list of pointers to triples — reorderable
SSA: every variable assigned exactly once; φ-functions at joins

cards.title: DAG removes repeats
cards.body:
a = b * −c + b * −c.
Tree 3AC: t1 = −c; t2 = b * t1; t3 = −c; t4 = b * t3; t5 = t2 + t4; a = t5.
DAG 3AC: t1 = −c; t2 = b * t1; t3 = t2 + t2; a = t3 — the common subexpression is computed once.

cards.q: An S-attributed definition uses:
options: Both, with inherited only from left siblings
cards.explain: S-attributed = synthesized only, so bottom-up evaluation works.

cards.q: Which field of an activation record points to the caller's activation record?
cards.explain: The control (dynamic) link chains records in call order; the access link follows lexical nesting.

cards.q: Which intermediate form makes it hardest to reorder instructions during optimisation?
cards.explain: Triples refer to results by position, so moving one changes every reference to it.

notes.p:
A **syntax-directed definition (SDD)** attaches attributes to grammar symbols and semantic rules to productions. A **syntax-directed translation scheme (SDT)** embeds actions inside the right-hand sides, so their position fixes when they run. Evaluation order must respect the **dependency graph**; a cycle means no order exists.

**Worked example 1.** D → T L {L.in = T.type}; T → int {T.type = int}; L → L₁ , id {L₁.in = L.in; addtype(id, L.in)}; L → id {addtype(id, L.in)}. Here `in` is **inherited** and `type` synthesized. Since L.in depends only on its left sibling T, the SDD is **L-attributed**, not S-attributed. For `int a, b, c` every identifier receives type int.

Three-address code (3AC) is the usual target. Boolean expressions and control flow use labels and jumps; **backpatching** fills in jump targets once they are known. Array references compute addresses: for A[i][j] in a row-major n₂-column array of w-byte elements, address = base + (i × n₂ + j) × w.

To count temporaries, generate 3AC for the expression tree; with a DAG, repeated subexpressions are shared, so fewer temporaries and instructions are needed.
Remember:
points: Synthesized: from children; inherited: from parent/left siblings.
S-attributed ⊂ L-attributed; S-attributed fits LR parsing.
Activation record: params, return value/address, control link, access link, locals, temps.
Control link = caller; access link = lexically enclosing scope.
Static scope uses text; dynamic scope uses the call stack.
Quadruples are movable; triples are not; indirect triples are.
DAGs expose common subexpressions.

chapters.title: Basic blocks, local optimisation & data-flow analysis

cards.title: Finding leaders
points: The first instruction is a leader
Any target of a (conditional or unconditional) jump is a leader
Any instruction right after a jump is a leader
A basic block runs from a leader up to, not including, the next leader

cards.title: Local optimisations
cards.body: Inside one basic block: **constant folding** (2 * 3 → 6), **constant propagation**, **copy propagation** (after x = y use y), **common subexpression elimination**, **dead-code elimination**, **algebraic simplification** (x + 0, x * 1) and **strength reduction** (x * 2 → x << 1).

cards.title: Loop optimisations
cards.body: **Code motion** moves loop-invariant computations out of the loop. **Induction-variable elimination** replaces i * 4 by a variable that is increased by 4. **Loop unrolling** reduces branch overhead; **loop jamming** merges adjacent loops over the same range.

cards.title: Data-flow equations
points: Reaching definitions: forward, union; OUT = GEN ∪ (IN − KILL)
Live variables: backward, union; IN = USE ∪ (OUT − DEF)
Available expressions: forward, intersection
Constant propagation: forward, meet over a lattice (constant / not-a-constant)

cards.title: Uses of the analyses
cards.body: **Liveness** drives register allocation (variables live at the same point interfere) and dead-store elimination. **Reaching definitions** find use–def chains for constant and copy propagation. **Available expressions** justify global common subexpression elimination.

cards.title: CSE trap
cards.body:
a = b + c; b = a − d; c = b + c; d = a − d.
The last statement repeats a − d with a and d unchanged → **d = b**. But b + c in line 3 is **not** common with line 1, because b was redefined in between.

cards.q: Basic blocks in: 1: x = 0; 2: if x > 5 goto 5; 3: x = x + 1; 4: goto 2; 5: y = x
cards.explain: Leaders 1, 2 (target), 3 (after a jump), 5 (target): blocks {1}, {2}, {3, 4}, {5}.

cards.q: Live-variable analysis is:
cards.explain: A variable is live if it may be used on some later path.

cards.q: Replacing i * 8 by i << 3 is called:
cards.explain: A costly operation is replaced by a cheaper one.

notes.p:
Optimisation starts by cutting the 3AC into **basic blocks** — straight-line code entered only at the top and left only at the bottom — and joining them into a **control-flow graph (CFG)**.

**Worked example 1.**
1: i = 1
2: j = 1
3: t1 = 10 * i
4: t2 = t1 + j
5: a[t2] = 0
6: j = j + 1
7: if j <= 10 goto 3
8: i = i + 1
9: if i <= 10 goto 2
10: halt
Leaders: 1 (first), 2 and 3 (jump targets), 8 and 10 (after jumps). Blocks: B1 = {1}, B2 = {2}, B3 = {3–7}, B4 = {8–9}, B5 = {10} → **5 blocks**. B3 loops to itself; B4 loops back to B2.

`blocks = {   # name: (use, def, successors)
    'B1': ({'a', 'b'}, {'c'}, ['B2']),           # c = a + b
    'B2': ({'c'}, {'d'}, ['B3', 'B4']),          # d = c * 2 ; if ...
    'B3': ({'d', 'a'}, {'a'}, ['B2']),           # a = d - a
    'B4': ({'d'}, set(), []),                    # return d
}
IN = {b: set() for b in blocks}; OUT = {b: set() for b in blocks}
changed = True
while changed:
    changed = False
    for b, (use, defs, succ) in blocks.items():
        out = set().union(*[IN[s] for s in succ]) if succ else set()
        inn = use | (out - defs)
        if (inn, out) != (IN[b], OUT[b]):
            IN[b], OUT[b], changed = inn, out, True
for b in blocks:
    print(b, 'in', sorted(IN[b]), 'out', sorted(OUT[b]))`

Output:
`B1 in ['a', 'b'] out ['a', 'c']
B2 in ['a', 'c'] out ['a', 'c', 'd']
B3 in ['a', 'c', 'd'] out ['a', 'c']
B4 in ['d'] out []`

The equations are applied until nothing changes. **a** is live into B2 because B3 may read it on the loop path; **c** stays live around the loop because B2 reads it and B3 never redefines it; **b** is dead after B1, so its register can be reused.

**Worked example 3.** x = 4; y = x * 2; z = y + x; if (z > 10) w = z else w = 0.
Propagate x = 4 → y = 8 (folding) → z = 12 → the condition 12 > 10 is always true → the else branch is **dead code** and w = 12. Constant propagation is a forward analysis whose meet treats 'two different constants' as not-a-constant.

Global CSE needs **available expressions**: e is available at a point if every path computes e and none of its operands is redefined afterwards — hence the intersection meet.
Watch for these:
points: A jump target is a leader even if it is the instruction right after another leader.
Liveness flows backward: IN depends on OUT, not the reverse.
Do not treat an expression as common after one of its operands is reassigned.
Dead code = result never used, not just unreachable code (both are removed).
Register count from liveness = maximum number of simultaneously live variables (for straight-line code).

notes.p: Remember:
points: Leaders: first instruction, jump targets, instruction after a jump.
Local: folding, propagation, CSE, dead code, strength reduction.
Loop: code motion, induction variables, unrolling.
Reaching definitions: forward, union.
Liveness: backward, union; IN = USE ∪ (OUT − DEF).
Available expressions: forward, intersection.
Liveness → register allocation by graph colouring.

cards.title: fork() counting
cards.body: Each fork() doubles the number of processes. A loop calling fork() n times creates 2ⁿ processes in total (2ⁿ − 1 children). A printf after the loop runs 2ⁿ times.

cards.title: Scheduling metrics
points: Turnaround = completion − arrival
Waiting = turnaround − burst
Response = first run − arrival
SRTF minimises average waiting time (given known bursts)

cards.title: Critical-section requirements
cards.body: Mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting. Peterson's solution meets all three for 2 processes. Semaphores: wait/P decrements (blocks if < 0), signal/V increments.

cards.title: Deadlock resource bound
points: n processes, each needs at most k units:
Minimum units guaranteeing no deadlock = n(k − 1) + 1
Banker's algorithm checks for a safe sequence before granting

cards.title: Paging numbers
points: Pages = virtual space / page size; page table size = pages × PTE size
EAT with TLB (hit ratio h, single-level): h(t + m) + (1 − h)(t + 2m)

cards.title: Page replacement & disks
cards.body: FIFO (Belady's anomaly possible), LRU, Optimal. Disk scheduling: FCFS, SSTF (starvation), SCAN/elevator, C-SCAN, LOOK/C-LOOK — count head movement carefully.

cards.title: Page-table size
cards.body: 32-bit virtual address, 4 KB pages → 2³² / 2¹² = 2²⁰ pages. With 4-byte entries: 2²⁰ × 4 B = 4 MB per process — the reason multilevel page tables exist.

cards.q: 3 processes each need up to 4 units of a resource. Minimum units that guarantee no deadlock:
TLB hit ratio 80%, TLB access 10 ns, memory access 100 ns, single-level paging. EAT = ?
for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) fork(); — total processes including the original:

notes.p:
GATE OS questions are mostly numerical. For scheduling, draw a **Gantt chart**, then use **TAT = completion − arrival** and **WT = TAT − burst**. **SRTF** (preemptive SJF) gives the minimum average waiting time; **Round Robin** behaves like FCFS when the quantum is very large and has high context-switch overhead when it is very small.

**Example 1 (SRTF).** P1 (arrival 0, burst 8), P2 (1, 4), P3 (2, 9), P4 (3, 5). Gantt: P1 0–1, P2 1–5, P4 5–10, P1 10–17, P3 17–26. Waiting: P1 9, P2 0, P3 15, P4 2 → average **6.5**.

A correct critical-section solution needs **mutual exclusion**, **progress** and **bounded waiting**. Peterson's algorithm satisfies all three for two processes. **Semaphores:** P (wait) decrements and blocks if the value goes negative; V (signal) increments. If a counting semaphore starts at 10 and undergoes 6 P and 4 V operations, the final value is 10 − 6 + 4 = **8**. A negative value −k means k processes are blocked.

**Deadlock** needs mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. With n processes each needing at most k instances of a resource, the minimum number of instances that guarantees no deadlock is **n(k − 1) + 1**. The **Banker's algorithm** grants a request only if a safe sequence still exists.

**Page table size** = number of pages × entry size. With 32-bit logical addresses, 4 KB pages and 4-byte entries: 2²⁰ entries × 4 B = **4 MB** per process — the reason for multi-level page tables. **Effective access time** with a TLB: EAT = h(t_TLB + t_mem) + (1 − h)(t_TLB + 2t_mem) for a single-level table.

**Disk scheduling** for requests 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67 with the head at 53 (cylinders 0–199):

`reqs, head = [98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67], 53

def fcfs(r, h):
    return sum(abs(b - a) for a, b in zip([h] + r, r))

def sstf(r, h):
    r, total = list(r), 0
    while r:
        nxt = min(r, key=lambda x: abs(x - h))
        total += abs(nxt - h); h = nxt; r.remove(nxt)
    return total

def scan_up(r, h, end=199):           # move toward 199, then reverse
    return (end - h) + (end - min(r))

print(fcfs(reqs, head), sstf(reqs, head), scan_up(reqs, head))

def bankers(avail, alloc, need):
    work, done, order = list(avail), [False] * len(alloc), []
    progress = True
    while progress:
        progress = False
        for i in range(len(alloc)):
            if not done[i] and all(n <= w for n, w in zip(need[i], work)):
                work = [w + a for w, a in zip(work, alloc[i])]
                done[i] = progress = True
                order.append("P%d" % i)
    return order if all(done) else "unsafe"

alloc = [(0, 1, 0), (2, 0, 0), (3, 0, 2), (2, 1, 1), (0, 0, 2)]
mx = [(7, 5, 3), (3, 2, 2), (9, 0, 2), (2, 2, 2), (4, 3, 3)]
need = [tuple(m - a for m, a in zip(M, A)) for M, A in zip(mx, alloc)]
print(bankers((3, 3, 2), alloc, need))
print(pow(2, 32) // 4096 * 4 // (1024 * 1024), "MB")`

Output:
`640 236 331
['P1', 'P3', 'P4', 'P0', 'P2']
4 MB`

FCFS moves 640 cylinders, SSTF 236 (but can starve far requests), SCAN toward 199 then back to 14 moves 331. The Banker's example (the textbook one) is in a **safe state**.

**Q: 3 processes each need 2 units of a resource. Minimum units for deadlock freedom?** A: 3(2 − 1) + 1 = 4.

**Q: `for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) fork();` — how many processes print a message placed after the loop?** A: 2³ = 8 (n sequential forks give 2ⁿ processes, 2ⁿ − 1 of them children).

**Q: TLB hit ratio 90%, TLB 10 ns, memory 100 ns. EAT?** A: 0.9 × 110 + 0.1 × 210 = 120 ns.

**Q: Which page replacement algorithm suffers from Belady's anomaly?** A: FIFO.
Frequent mistakes:
points: Forgetting context-switch time when the question gives it.
Counting the original process in fork() questions (total vs children).
Mixing logical and physical address widths in page-table questions.

notes.p: Remember:
points: TAT = CT − AT; WT = TAT − BT.
SRTF minimises average waiting time.
n fork() calls → 2ⁿ processes.
Deadlock-free resources ≥ n(k − 1) + 1.
Page table size = pages × PTE size.
EAT with TLB uses one extra memory access on a miss.

cards.title: System calls
cards.body: A **system call** is the controlled way a user program asks the kernel for service (I/O, memory, process creation). It executes a **trap** instruction that switches the CPU from **user mode** to **kernel mode**, runs the handler, and returns. Examples: fork, exec, wait, exit, open, read, write, pipe.

cards.title: Process states
cards.body: **New → Ready → Running → Terminated**, with **Running → Waiting** (I/O or event) and **Waiting → Ready** (event done). Running → Ready happens on preemption (timer interrupt). The kernel keeps each process's state, PC, registers, memory maps and open files in its **PCB**.

cards.title: fork() rules
points: fork() returns 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent (−1 on failure)
n unconditional forks in sequence → 2ⁿ processes
fork() && fork() → 3 processes; fork() && fork() || fork() → 5
exec replaces the image; wait collects a child's exit status

cards.title: Threads
cards.body: Threads of one process **share** code, data (globals), heap and open files; each has its **own** stack, registers and program counter. Switching threads is cheaper than switching processes. **User-level** threads are fast but one blocking call can block all (many-to-one); **kernel-level** threads can run in parallel on multiple cores (one-to-one).

cards.title: IPC
cards.body: **Shared memory**: fastest after setup, but processes must synchronise. **Message passing** (pipes, message queues, sockets): kernel copies data, simpler and works across machines. A **pipe** is unidirectional; **signals** deliver asynchronous notifications.

cards.title: Zombie and orphan
cards.body: A **zombie** has exited but its parent has not called wait() — its PCB entry remains. An **orphan** is a running child whose parent has exited; it is adopted by init (PID 1), which reaps it.

cards.q: Which of these is NOT shared by threads of the same process?
cards.explain: Each thread has its own stack, registers and PC.

cards.q: How many processes exist after: fork() && fork() || fork(); (including the original)?
cards.explain: Original: fork #1 and #2 return non-zero, so || stops. The fork-#2 child and the fork-#1 child each run fork #3: 3 + 2 = 5.

cards.q: A process moves from Running to Ready when:
cards.explain: Preemption by the timer sends it back to the ready queue; I/O sends it to waiting.

notes.p:
A **program** is a passive file; a **process** is a program in execution with its own address space (text, data, heap, stack), PCB and resources. The kernel switches between processes with a **context switch**: save the old PCB's registers and PC, load the new one's. Context-switch time is pure overhead, which is why scheduling questions sometimes add it explicitly.

**Mode switch vs context switch:** a system call changes mode (user → kernel) but need not change the running process.

**Steps of a system call:** the library wrapper puts the call number and arguments in registers, executes the trap instruction, the CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps to the handler via the trap table, the kernel validates the arguments and does the work, then the return instruction restores user mode with the result (or an error code). Because the kernel never trusts user pointers, every buffer passed to read() or write() is checked first.

`printf("hi "); fork(); printf("there\n");`
When output goes to a terminal it is line-buffered; when it goes to a file or pipe it is fully buffered. Here "hi " has no newline, so it is still in the user-space buffer when fork() copies the address space. Both processes eventually flush "hi there" — the string appears **twice**. Calling fflush(stdout) before fork() prints "hi " once. GATE uses this to test that fork duplicates the whole address space, including stdio buffers.

**Many-to-one** (all user threads on one kernel thread): no true parallelism, a blocking call blocks the process. **One-to-one** (Linux, Windows): parallel, but each user thread costs a kernel thread. **Many-to-many**: multiplexes user threads over a smaller or equal number of kernel threads.

IPC choices: shared memory plus semaphores for speed, message passing for simplicity and distribution. `pipe(fd)` gives fd[0] for reading and fd[1] for writing; after fork, parent and child close the ends they do not use.
points: Context switch between threads of one process keeps the same page tables.
A thread crash (e.g. segmentation fault) kills the whole process.
exec() keeps the PID but replaces code, data, heap and stack.

notes.p: Remember:
points: System call = trap to kernel mode; fork, exec, wait, exit, open, read, write.
States: new, ready, running, waiting, terminated.
fork returns 0 to the child, child PID to the parent.
n sequential forks → 2ⁿ processes; use short-circuit rules for && and ||.
Threads share code, data, heap, files; not stack, registers, PC.
Zombie: exited, not reaped; orphan: parent gone, adopted by init.
Shared memory is fastest; message passing is simpler.

cards.title: Definitions
points: Turnaround (TAT) = completion − arrival
Waiting = TAT − burst (− I/O time if any)
Response = first time on CPU − arrival
Throughput = processes completed / time
CPU utilisation = busy time / total time

cards.title: Non-preemptive algorithms
cards.body: **FCFS**: simple, suffers the **convoy effect** (short jobs wait behind a long one). **SJF**: shortest next burst first — optimal average waiting time among non-preemptive schedules, but needs burst prediction. **Priority**: may starve low-priority jobs; **aging** raises their priority over time.

cards.title: Preemptive algorithms
cards.body: **SRTF**: preemptive SJF, optimal average waiting time overall. **Round Robin (RR)**: each process gets a time quantum q, then goes to the tail of the ready queue. Large q → FCFS; tiny q → too many context switches.

cards.title: Other policies
points: HRRN: response ratio = (waiting + burst) / burst; pick the highest
Multilevel queue: fixed queues (system, interactive, batch)
Multilevel feedback queue: processes move between queues by behaviour
Burst prediction: τₙ₊₁ = α tₙ + (1 − α) τₙ

cards.title: HRRN choice
cards.body: At t = 10, A has waited 8 with burst 4 → (8 + 4)/4 = 3. B has waited 3 with burst 1 → (3 + 1)/1 = 4. C has waited 9 with burst 9 → 2. HRRN runs **B**. Short jobs are favoured, yet long waits keep growing the ratio, so nothing starves.

cards.title: Exponential averaging
cards.body:
α = 0.5, initial guess τ₀ = 10, actual bursts 6 then 4.
τ₁ = 0.5 × 6 + 0.5 × 10 = 8.
τ₂ = 0.5 × 4 + 0.5 × 8 = **6**.

cards.q: Processes (arrival, burst): P1 (0, 6), P2 (0, 2), P3 (0, 4), all non-preemptive SJF. Average waiting time:
cards.explain: Order P2, P3, P1: waits 0, 2, 6 → 8/3.

cards.q: Round Robin with a very large time quantum behaves like:
cards.explain: Every process finishes within one quantum, in arrival order.

cards.q: Which algorithm can cause starvation?
cards.explain: A long job can keep being preempted by newly arriving short jobs.

notes.h: How to solve any scheduling question
notes.p:
Draw the **Gantt chart** first, carefully applying the tie-breaking rule the question states (usually lower process ID or earlier arrival). Then fill a table with completion, TAT and waiting time for each process. Check: the Gantt chart's busy time must equal the sum of bursts; idle gaps appear when no process has arrived.

For **Round Robin** the usual convention is that a process arriving at the same instant a quantum expires joins the queue **before** the preempted process. State your assumption if the question does not.

`from collections import deque
procs = {'P1': (0, 5), 'P2': (1, 3), 'P3': (2, 1), 'P4': (3, 2)}   # arrival, burst
q, t, rem, done, gantt = 2, 0, {p: b for p, (a, b) in procs.items()}, {}, []
order = sorted(procs, key=lambda p: procs[p][0])
ready, i = deque(), 0
def admit(upto):
    global i
    while i < len(order) and procs[order[i]][0] <= upto:
        ready.append(order[i]); i += 1
admit(0)
while ready:
    p = ready.popleft()
    run = min(q, rem[p]); gantt.append((p, t, t + run))
    t += run; rem[p] -= run
    admit(t)                       # arrivals join before the preempted process
    if rem[p]: ready.append(p)
    else: done[p] = t
print(gantt)
wt = {p: done[p] - a - b for p, (a, b) in procs.items()}
print(done, wt, sum(wt.values()) / 4)`

Output:
`[('P1', 0, 2), ('P2', 2, 4), ('P3', 4, 5), ('P1', 5, 7), ('P4', 7, 9), ('P2', 9, 10), ('P1', 10, 11)]
{'P3': 5, 'P4': 9, 'P2': 10, 'P1': 11} {'P1': 6, 'P2': 6, 'P3': 2, 'P4': 4} 4.5`

P3 needs only one unit, so it leaves early. Average waiting time = **4.5**.

Lower number = higher priority. P1 (arrival 0, burst 4, priority 3), P2 (1, 2, 1), P3 (2, 3, 2).
Gantt: P1 0–1 | P2 1–3 | P3 3–6 | P1 6–9.
Completion: P1 9, P2 3, P3 6.
TAT: 9, 2, 4. Waiting: 9 − 4 = 5, 0, 1 → average **2**.
P2 preempts P1 at t = 1 because it has higher priority; at t = 2 P3 cannot preempt P2.
Strengths and weaknesses:
points: **SJF/SRTF**: best average waiting time; starvation possible; needs burst estimates.
**FCFS**: no starvation, convoy effect, poor for interactive systems.
**RR**: good response time; average waiting often higher than SJF; quantum should exceed most CPU bursts slightly.
**Priority**: starvation fixed by aging.
**HRRN**: non-preemptive, balances SJF with fairness.
**MLFQ**: approximates SJF without knowing bursts — CPU-hungry jobs sink to lower queues.

notes.p: Remember:
points: TAT = CT − AT; WT = TAT − BT; RT = first run − AT.
SJF optimal among non-preemptive; SRTF optimal overall for average WT.
RR: big quantum → FCFS; small → overhead.
HRRN ratio = (W + S)/S.
τₙ₊₁ = α tₙ + (1 − α) τₙ.
Starvation: SJF, SRTF, priority; cure: aging.
Always draw the Gantt chart and check idle gaps.

chapters.title: Process synchronisation: locks, semaphores & classic problems

cards.title: Race condition
cards.body: When processes update shared data concurrently and the result depends on the interleaving, there is a **race**. x++ is really load, add, store, so two concurrent increments can lose an update. The code touching shared data is the **critical section**.

cards.title: Critical-section requirements
points: Mutual exclusion: at most one process inside
Progress: if none is inside, the choice of who enters cannot be postponed forever by processes outside
Bounded waiting: a limit on how often others can enter before a waiting process gets in
No assumption about speeds or number of CPUs

cards.title: Peterson's algorithm
cards.body: flag[i] = true; turn = j; while (flag[j] && turn == j); → critical section → flag[i] = false. It satisfies all three requirements for **two** processes (on hardware with sequential consistency). Strict alternation (turn variable alone) violates **progress**.

cards.title: Hardware support
cards.body: **Test-and-set** and **compare-and-swap** are atomic. A simple TSL spin lock gives mutual exclusion and progress but **not bounded waiting**. Spin locks waste CPU (busy waiting) but are fine for very short sections on multiprocessors.

cards.title: Semaphores
points: wait(S)/P: S = S − 1; if S < 0 block
signal(S)/V: S = S + 1; if S ≤ 0 wake one waiting process
Final value = initial − (#P) + (#V)
Negative value −k → k processes blocked
Binary semaphore (mutex) initial 1; counting semaphore initial = number of resources

cards.title: Semaphore arithmetic
cards.body: A counting semaphore starts at 7. Then 20 P and 15 V operations complete. Final value = 7 − 20 + 15 = **2**. If instead it had reached −3 at some instant, 3 processes were blocked at that moment.

cards.q: Bounded buffer of size n with semaphores empty, full, mutex. Their initial values are:
cards.explain: All slots are empty, none full, and the buffer lock is free.

cards.q: Turn-based strict alternation between two processes violates:
cards.explain: A process outside its CS that does not want to enter can block the other.

cards.q: A counting semaphore is initialised to 10. Then 6 P and 4 V operations are done. Final value:

notes.p:
Two threads each run `x = x + 1` on shared x = 0. Each increment is three steps — R (load into a register), I (add 1), W (store). If both load 0 before either stores, both store 1 and one update is **lost**. Mutual exclusion around the three steps makes the result always 2.

**Worked example 1: enumerate every interleaving.**

`from itertools import permutations
def run(order):
    x, reg = 0, {}
    for p, step in order:
        if step == 'R': reg[p] = x
        elif step == 'I': reg[p] += 1
        else: x = reg[p]
    return x
steps = [('A', s) for s in 'RIW'] + [('B', s) for s in 'RIW']
results = set()
for perm in set(permutations(steps)):
    if [s for p, s in perm if p == 'A'] == list('RIW') and [s for p, s in perm if p == 'B'] == list('RIW'):
        results.add(run(perm))
print(sorted(results))`

Output:
`[1, 2]`

Only 1 and 2 are possible.

**Producer–consumer (bounded buffer):** empty = n, full = 0, mutex = 1. Producer: wait(empty); wait(mutex); add; signal(mutex); signal(full). Consumer mirrors it. Swapping the two waits in the producer (wait(mutex) before wait(empty)) can **deadlock** when the buffer is full.

**Readers–writers:** many readers may read together; a writer needs exclusive access. The first reader locks `wrt`, the last reader releases it — writers may starve.

**Dining philosophers:** five philosophers, five chopsticks; if all pick up the left chopstick first, **deadlock**. Fixes: allow at most four at the table, pick both chopsticks atomically, or make one philosopher pick right first.

Ensure statement S1 in P1 runs before S2 in P2: semaphore s = 0. P1: S1; signal(s). P2: wait(s); S2.
If P2 arrives first, wait makes s = −1 and blocks it; P1's signal brings s to 0 and wakes P2. With several constraints (A before B, B before C), use one semaphore per edge of the precedence graph, each initialised to 0.

A **monitor** is a language construct where only one process is active inside at a time; **condition variables** with wait() and signal() handle ordering. Unlike a semaphore, signal() on a condition with no waiter does nothing (no memory). A **mutex** is owned: only the thread that locked it may unlock it.
points: Busy waiting (spin lock) vs blocking (sleep and wake).
Priority inversion: a low-priority holder blocks a high-priority waiter; fix with priority inheritance.
Deadlock and starvation are different: starvation means some process waits indefinitely while others progress.

notes.p: Remember:
points: CS requirements: mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting.
Peterson: correct for 2 processes; strict alternation fails progress.
TSL spin lock: no bounded waiting.
Semaphore final = initial − P + V; −k means k blocked.
Bounded buffer: empty = n, full = 0, mutex = 1; wait(empty) before wait(mutex).
Dining philosophers: all-left-first → deadlock.
Lost-update race on x++ gives 1 or 2 for two increments.

cards.title: Four necessary conditions
points: Mutual exclusion: a resource is held non-sharably
Hold and wait: holding one resource while waiting for another
No preemption: resources are released only voluntarily
Circular wait: P1 waits for P2 … Pn waits for P1
All four must hold together for deadlock

cards.title: Resource-allocation graph
cards.body: Request edges P → R, assignment edges R → P. **No cycle ⇒ no deadlock.** With a **single instance** of each resource, a cycle ⇒ deadlock. With **multiple instances**, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient.

cards.title: Prevention
cards.body: Break one condition: spool devices (mutual exclusion — rarely possible); request everything at once or release before requesting (hold and wait); allow preemption of resources whose state can be saved (no preemption); **number the resources and request in increasing order** (circular wait — the most practical).

cards.title: Avoidance
cards.body: The **Banker's algorithm** keeps the system in a **safe state**: one where some order lets every process get its maximum need and finish. Each request is granted only if the state after granting is still safe. Unsafe ≠ deadlocked, but deadlock is possible from an unsafe state.

cards.title: Resource-count formulas
points: n processes, each needs at most k units: deadlock-free iff units ≥ n(k − 1) + 1
Different maxima m₁ … mₙ: deadlock-free iff units ≥ Σ(mᵢ − 1) + 1
Banker's safety check: O(m × n²)

cards.title: Detection and recovery
cards.body: Run a safety-style algorithm on the **current requests** (not maximum needs); processes that cannot finish are deadlocked. Recovery: abort processes (all or one at a time) or preempt resources with rollback, choosing victims to minimise cost and avoid starvation.

cards.q: Three processes need at most 3, 4 and 5 units of one resource. The minimum number of units that guarantees no deadlock is:
Requesting resources only in increasing order of resource number prevents deadlock by eliminating:
cards.explain: A cycle would need some process to request a lower-numbered resource.

cards.q: In a resource-allocation graph where every resource has a single instance, a cycle means:
cards.explain: With single instances a cycle is both necessary and sufficient.

notes.p: **Deadlock**: a set of processes each waits for a resource held by another in the set — none can ever proceed. **Starvation**: a process waits indefinitely while others keep progressing (e.g. low priority). **Livelock**: processes keep changing state in response to each other without progress. GATE often asks which condition a given protocol breaks, so map each technique to the condition it removes.

Six processes each need at most 3 tape drives. Minimum drives for deadlock freedom?
Worst case: every process holds k − 1 = 2 drives and waits for one more → 6 × 2 = 12 drives are tied up. One extra drive lets someone finish → **13**.
Reverse question: with 13 drives and 6 processes, the largest per-process maximum k satisfying 6(k − 1) + 1 ≤ 13 is k = 3.

`def safe(avail, alloc, need):
    work, fin, seq = list(avail), [False] * len(alloc), []
    while True:
        for i in range(len(alloc)):
            if not fin[i] and all(n <= w for n, w in zip(need[i], work)):
                work = [w + a for w, a in zip(work, alloc[i])]
                fin[i] = True; seq.append('P%d' % i); break
        else:
            return seq if all(fin) else None
def request(i, req, st):
    avail, alloc, need = st
    if any(r > n for r, n in zip(req, need[i])): return 'error: exceeds claim', st
    if any(r > a for r, a in zip(req, avail)): return 'wait: not available', st
    av = [a - r for a, r in zip(avail, req)]
    al = [list(x) for x in alloc]; nd = [list(x) for x in need]
    al[i] = [a + r for a, r in zip(al[i], req)]; nd[i] = [n - r for n, r in zip(nd[i], req)]
    s = safe(av, al, nd)
    return (('grant %s' % s), (av, al, nd)) if s else ('deny: unsafe', st)
alloc = [[0, 1, 0], [2, 0, 0], [3, 0, 2], [2, 1, 1], [0, 0, 2]]
maxm  = [[7, 5, 3], [3, 2, 2], [9, 0, 2], [2, 2, 2], [4, 3, 3]]
need = [[m - a for m, a in zip(M, A)] for M, A in zip(maxm, alloc)]
st = ([3, 3, 2], alloc, need)
for p, req in [(1, [1, 0, 2]), (4, [3, 3, 0]), (0, [0, 2, 0])]:
    msg, st = request(p, req, st)
    print('P%d' % p, req, '->', msg, '| available', st[0])`

Output:
`P1 [1, 0, 2] -> grant ['P1', 'P3', 'P0', 'P2', 'P4'] | available [2, 3, 0]
P4 [3, 3, 0] -> wait: not available | available [2, 3, 0]
P0 [0, 2, 0] -> deny: unsafe | available [2, 3, 0]`

Requests are processed in order on the classic 5-process state. P1's request leaves a safe order, so it is granted and Available becomes (2, 3, 0). P4 then asks for (3, 3, 0), more than is available, so it **waits**. P0's (0, 2, 0) is available, but granting it would leave (2, 1, 0) — no process could finish, so it is **denied** as unsafe.

**Ignore** (ostrich): most general-purpose OSes, because deadlocks are rare and prevention is costly. **Prevent**: impose rules at design time (lock ordering is standard in kernels and databases). **Avoid**: needs every process's maximum claim in advance — rarely known in practice. **Detect and recover**: run detection periodically or when CPU utilisation drops; costs are rollback and lost work.
points: Detection with single instances = cycle detection in the wait-for graph, O(n²).
Holding a resource while waiting for I/O is not deadlock by itself.
An unsafe state is not yet a deadlock.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Mutual exclusion + hold and wait + no preemption + circular wait.
RAG: no cycle → no deadlock; single instances: cycle ⇔ deadlock.
Units needed: Σ(maxᵢ − 1) + 1.
Resource ordering breaks circular wait.
Banker's: grant only if the new state is safe.
Request > need → error; request > available → wait.
Unsafe ≠ deadlock; detection uses current requests.

cards.title: Contiguous allocation
cards.body: Variable partitions are allocated by **first fit**, **best fit** (smallest hole that fits) or **worst fit** (largest hole). Leftover gaps between processes are **external fragmentation** (cured by compaction or paging); unused space inside an allocated block is **internal fragmentation**.

cards.title: Paging arithmetic
points: Logical address = page number + offset; offset bits = log₂(page size)
Page-table entries = 2^(page-number bits); size = entries × PTE size
Frames = physical memory / frame size
Inverted page table: one entry per frame

cards.title: Multi-level paging
cards.body: If a page table does not fit in one page, page it too. 32-bit address, 4 KB pages, 4 B entries: one page holds 1024 entries → split as **10 | 10 | 12**. Each level adds one memory access on a TLB miss.

cards.title: Effective access times
points: TLB: EAT = h(t + m) + (1 − h)(t + (L + 1)m) for L-level tables
Page faults: EAT = (1 − p) × m + p × fault-service time
A fault costs milliseconds, memory nanoseconds — p must be tiny

cards.title: Replacement algorithms
cards.body: **FIFO** (can show **Belady's anomaly**: more frames, more faults), **Optimal** (evict the page used farthest in future — lowest faults, needs the future), **LRU** (evict least recently used — a stack algorithm, no anomaly). Clock/second-chance approximates LRU with a reference bit.

cards.title: Thrashing
cards.body: When processes do not have frames for their **working set**, they fault constantly, CPU utilisation collapses and the OS may wrongly admit more processes. Fixes: working-set model, page-fault-frequency control, reducing the degree of multiprogramming.

cards.q: Reference string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5 with FIFO: 3 frames give 9 faults and 4 frames give 10. This is:
cards.explain: FIFO is not a stack algorithm, so more frames can mean more faults.

cards.q: Physical memory 1 GB, frame size 4 KB. Entries in an inverted page table:
cards.explain: 2³⁰ / 2¹² = 2¹⁸ frames, one entry each.

cards.q: 32-bit virtual addresses with 8 KB pages give how many offset bits and pages?
cards.explain: 8 KB = 2¹³ → 13 offset bits; 32 − 13 = 19 page bits.

notes.p:
`def place(holes, procs, pick):
    holes, out = list(holes), []
    for p in procs:
        fits = [i for i, h in enumerate(holes) if h >= p]
        if not fits: out.append((p, 'waits')); continue
        i = pick(fits, holes); out.append((p, holes[i])); holes[i] -= p
    return out
holes, procs = [100, 500, 200, 300, 600], [212, 417, 112, 426]
print('first', place(holes, procs, lambda f, h: f[0]))
print('best ', place(holes, procs, lambda f, h: min(f, key=lambda i: h[i])))
print('worst', place(holes, procs, lambda f, h: max(f, key=lambda i: h[i])))`

Output:
`first [(212, 500), (417, 600), (112, 288), (426, 'waits')]
best  [(212, 300), (417, 500), (112, 200), (426, 600)]
worst [(212, 600), (417, 500), (112, 388), (426, 'waits')]`

Each pair is (process, size of the hole it went into). Here **best fit** places all four; first and worst fit leave the 426 KB process waiting.

`def faults(refs, frames, policy):
    mem, f = [], 0
    for i, r in enumerate(refs):
        if r in mem:
            if policy == 'LRU': mem.remove(r); mem.append(r)
            continue
        f += 1
        if len(mem) == frames:
            if policy == 'OPT':
                fut = refs[i + 1:]
                victim = max(mem, key=lambda p: fut.index(p) if p in fut else 10**9)
                mem.remove(victim)
            else:
                mem.pop(0)
        mem.append(r)
    return f
s = [7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 7, 0, 1]
print([faults(s, 3, p) for p in ('FIFO', 'LRU', 'OPT')])
b = [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(faults(b, 3, 'FIFO'), faults(b, 4, 'FIFO'), faults(b, 3, 'LRU'), faults(b, 4, 'LRU'))`

Output:
`[15, 12, 9]
9 10 10 8`

Optimal ≤ LRU ≤ FIFO on the first string (9, 12, 15). On the second, FIFO goes from 9 to 10 faults when frames increase; LRU improves from 10 to 8.

Memory access 100 ns, page-fault service 8 ms, fault rate p. EAT = (1 − p) × 100 + p × 8,000,000 ns.
For at most 10% slowdown, EAT ≤ 110: 100 + 7,999,900 p ≤ 110 → p ≤ **1.25 × 10⁻⁶**, i.e. fewer than about one fault per 800,000 accesses. This is why demand paging only works because of **locality of reference**.

**Segmentation** divides a program into logical units (code, stack, data) of different sizes; the segment table holds base and limit, and an offset ≥ limit traps. It has external fragmentation but no internal fragmentation. **Segmented paging** pages each segment. Page-table entries carry valid, dirty, reference and protection bits; the **dirty bit** lets a clean victim page be dropped without writing it to disk.
Remember:
points: First/best/worst fit; external vs internal fragmentation.
Offset bits = log₂(page size); PT size = entries × PTE size.
Multi-level paging: each level adds a memory access on a TLB miss.
Inverted page table: one entry per frame.
OPT ≤ LRU; FIFO can show Belady's anomaly.
EAT = (1 − p)m + p × fault time.
Thrashing: working set does not fit; reduce multiprogramming.

chapters.title: File systems, disk structure & I/O scheduling

cards.title: Allocation methods
cards.body: **Contiguous**: fast sequential and direct access, external fragmentation, hard to grow. **Linked**: no fragmentation, but direct access is slow and a broken pointer loses the rest of the file. **FAT**: the links kept in a table in memory. **Indexed**: an index block lists all data blocks — direct access without fragmentation.

cards.title: Unix inode file size
points: Pointers per block = block size / address size (= P)
Max blocks = direct + P + P² + P³ (single, double, triple indirect)
Max file size = max blocks × block size

cards.title: inode numbers
cards.body: 1 KB blocks, 4-byte addresses → P = 256. With 10 direct, 1 single, 1 double, 1 triple: 10 + 256 + 65,536 + 16,777,216 = 16,843,018 blocks ≈ **16 GB**.

cards.title: Disk timing
points: Capacity = surfaces × tracks per surface × sectors per track × bytes per sector
Rotation time = 60 / RPM seconds; average rotational latency = half of it
Access time = seek + rotational latency + transfer (+ controller overhead)
Transfer time = bytes / transfer rate

cards.title: Disk scheduling
cards.body: **FCFS** fair but slow; **SSTF** serves the nearest request (can starve far ones); **SCAN** sweeps to the end then reverses; **LOOK** reverses at the last request; **C-SCAN/C-LOOK** serve in one direction only and jump back, giving more uniform waits.

cards.title: Free-space management
cards.body: **Bit vector**: one bit per block — easy to find runs of free blocks. **Linked free list**: no wasted space but slow to traverse. **Grouping/counting** store addresses or (start, count) runs. Directories can be single-level, two-level, tree-structured or acyclic-graph (links).

cards.q: Average rotational latency of a 7200 rpm disk is about:
cards.explain: One rotation = 60/7200 s = 8.33 ms; average = half = 4.17 ms.

cards.q: A 1 TB disk with 4 KB blocks uses a bitmap for free space. Bitmap size:
cards.explain: 2⁴⁰ / 2¹² = 2²⁸ blocks → 2²⁸ bits = 2²⁵ bytes = 32 MB.

cards.q: 4 KB blocks, 4-byte block addresses, 12 direct pointers and one single-indirect pointer. Maximum file size:

notes.p:
A file system maps names to blocks. The **directory** maps a name to an inode (Unix) or a directory entry with the first block (FAT). The **inode** stores metadata (owner, permissions, size, times, link count) and block pointers — but not the name, which is why one file can have several **hard links**.

**Worked example 1: direct access cost.** To read block 100 of a file: contiguous needs 1 disk read (compute the address); linked needs 101 reads (follow 100 pointers); indexed needs 2 (index block + data block, or 1 if the index is cached).

notes.h: Worked example 2: inode and disk geometry
notes.p:
`def max_file(block, addr, direct, single=1, double=1, triple=1):
    p = block // addr
    blocks = direct + single * p + double * p**2 + triple * p**3
    return blocks, blocks * block
b, size = max_file(1024, 4, 10)
print(b, size / 2**30, 'GiB')
print(max_file(4096, 4, 12, 1, 0, 0)[1] // 1024, 'KiB')
surfaces, tracks, sectors, bps = 16, 512, 1024, 512
print(surfaces * tracks * sectors * bps // 2**30, 'GiB disk')
rpm, seek_ms, rate = 7200, 4.0, 100e6
lat = 0.5 * 60 / rpm * 1000; xfer = 4096 / rate * 1000
print(round(lat, 2), round(xfer, 3), round(seek_ms + lat + xfer, 2), 'ms per 4 KB read')`

Output:
`16843018 16.062753677368164 GiB
4144 KiB
4 GiB disk
4.17 0.041 8.21 ms per 4 KB read`

A random 4 KB read is dominated by seek and rotation (≈ 8.2 ms); the transfer itself is about 0.04 ms. That is why scheduling and contiguous layout matter.

`reqs, head, top = [98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67], 53, 199
up = sorted(r for r in reqs if r >= head); down = sorted((r for r in reqs if r < head), reverse=True)
look   = (up[-1] - head) + (up[-1] - down[-1])
cscan  = (top - head) + top + max(r for r in reqs if r < head)   # counts the return sweep
clook  = (up[-1] - head) + (up[-1] - min(reqs)) + (max(r for r in reqs if r < head) - min(reqs))
print('LOOK', look, 'C-SCAN', cscan, 'C-LOOK', clook)`

Output:
`LOOK 299 C-SCAN 382 C-LOOK 322`

Head at 53 moving toward 199. These totals **include** the return jump; some questions exclude it (C-SCAN would then be 146 + 37 = 183), so read the convention stated.

**Buffering** smooths speed mismatch, **caching** keeps copies of hot blocks, **spooling** queues output for devices like printers. **RAID**: RAID 0 stripes (speed, no redundancy), RAID 1 mirrors, RAID 5 stripes with distributed parity (survives one disk failure), RAID 6 adds a second parity.
Remember:
points: Contiguous, linked, FAT, indexed allocation — know access costs.
inode max blocks = direct + P + P² + P³.
Rotational latency = half a rotation.
Access = seek + latency + transfer.
SSTF can starve; C-SCAN/C-LOOK give uniform waits.
Bitmap size = number of blocks bits.
Check whether the return sweep is counted.

cards.title: Relational algebra
cards.body: σ (select rows), π (project columns, removes duplicates), ⋈ (join), ∪, −, ×, ρ (rename), ÷ (division for 'for all' queries).

cards.title: SQL subtleties
cards.body: Comparisons with NULL give UNKNOWN, so WHERE x = NULL matches nothing; use IS NULL. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs. NOT IN with a NULL in the subquery returns no rows.

cards.title: Functional dependencies
cards.body: Compute attribute closure X⁺ by repeatedly applying FDs. X is a super key if X⁺ = all attributes; a candidate key if also minimal. Armstrong's axioms: reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity.

cards.title: Find all candidate keys
cards.body: R(A, B, C, D), F = {AB → C, C → D, D → A}. B is on no right side, so every key contains B. AB⁺ = ABCD, BC⁺ = BCDA, BD⁺ = BDAC; B⁺ = B. Keys: AB, BC, BD.

cards.title: Decomposition
cards.body: Lossless if the common attributes form a key of at least one part. 3NF decomposition can always be lossless and dependency-preserving; BCNF is always lossless but may lose dependencies.

cards.title: Serialisability
cards.body: Draw the precedence graph from conflicting operations (RW, WR, WW on the same item by different transactions). Acyclic ⇒ conflict serialisable. Basic 2PL guarantees conflict serialisability but not freedom from deadlock.

cards.title: Recoverability
cards.body: Recoverable: a transaction commits only after those it read from commit. Cascadeless: read only committed data. Strict: no read or write of uncommitted data. Strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable.

cards.q: R(A, B, C, D) with F = {AB → C, C → D, D → A}. How many candidate keys?
cards.explain: AB, BC and BD.

cards.q: Basic two-phase locking (2PL) guarantees:
cards.explain: 2PL ensures serialisability; deadlocks are still possible.

cards.q: A schedule's precedence graph contains a cycle. The schedule is:
cards.explain: Conflict serialisability ⇔ acyclic precedence graph.

notes.p:
A **functional dependency** X → Y means equal X values force equal Y values. The **attribute closure** X⁺ is everything X determines (apply Armstrong's axioms: reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity). X is a **super key** if X⁺ contains all attributes; a **candidate key** is a minimal super key. **Prime attributes** belong to some candidate key.

Shortcut for keys: attributes that never appear on any right side **must** be in every key; attributes only on the right side never are.

notes.h: Worked example: keys and normal form
notes.p:
R(A, B, C, D, E) with F = {A → B, BC → E, ED → A}. C and D never appear on a right side, so every key contains CD. (CD)⁺ = CD, not a key. Try adding one attribute:

`from itertools import combinations

R = set("ABCDE")
F = [("A", "B"), ("BC", "E"), ("ED", "A")]

def closure(X):
    X = set(X)
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for lhs, rhs in F:
            if set(lhs) <= X and not set(rhs) <= X:
                X |= set(rhs); changed = True
    return X

keys = []
for k in range(1, len(R) + 1):
    for combo in combinations(sorted(R), k):
        if closure(combo) == R and not any(set(c) <= set(combo) for c in keys):
            keys.append("".join(combo))
print(keys)
print("".join(sorted(closure("AC"))))`

Output:
`['ACD', 'BCD', 'CDE']
ABCE`

Candidate keys: **ACD, BCD, CDE**, so every attribute is prime. For each FD the right side is prime, so R is in **3NF**. But A → B has a left side A that is not a super key, so R is **not in BCNF**.

**2NF:** no non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of a candidate key. **3NF:** for every X → A, X is a super key **or** A is prime. **BCNF:** for every non-trivial X → A, X is a super key. BCNF ⊂ 3NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 1NF.

Decomposition of R into R1, R2 is **lossless** iff R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R1 ∩ R2 → R2. It is **dependency preserving** if the union of the projected FDs implies F. 3NF synthesis always gives a lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition; BCNF is always lossless but may lose dependencies.

A schedule is **conflict serializable** iff its **precedence graph** is acyclic. Two operations conflict if they belong to different transactions, touch the same item, and at least one is a write. For S: r1(X), r2(X), w1(X), w2(X): r1(X) before w2(X) gives T1 → T2, and r2(X) before w1(X) gives T2 → T1 — a cycle, so S is **not** conflict serializable. **View serializability** is weaker (every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable). **Recoverable** schedules commit a reader only after the writer it read from; **cascadeless** schedules read only committed data. **2PL** guarantees conflict serializability; strict 2PL also avoids cascading aborts.

**B+ tree order:** with block size 1024 B, key 9 B and block pointer 6 B, an internal node with p pointers needs 6p + 9(p − 1) ≤ 1024, so **p = 68**. B+ trees keep all records at the leaves, which are linked for range queries.

**Q: R(ABCD), F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}. Highest normal form?** A: Key A; B → C is transitive on a non-key → 2NF.

**Q: Is every BCNF relation in 3NF?** A: Yes.

**Q: Relational algebra for 'employees in every project' uses which operator?** A: Division (÷).

**Q: Does 2PL prevent deadlocks?** A: No; conservative 2PL does.

**Q: Number of super keys of R(A, B, C, D) with key A only?** A: 2³ = 8.
Remember:
points: Attributes never on a right side are in every key.
3NF: LHS super key or RHS prime; BCNF: LHS super key.
Lossless: common attributes form a key of one side.
Precedence graph acyclic ⇔ conflict serializable.
2PL → conflict serializable; strict 2PL → cascadeless.
B+ tree order from block, key and pointer sizes.

chapters.title: ER model, relational model, keys & integrity constraints

cards.title: ER building blocks
cards.body: **Entity sets** (rectangles) have **attributes**: simple or composite, single- or **multivalued** (double oval), stored or **derived** (dashed). A **weak entity** has no key of its own; it is identified by its owner's key plus a **partial key** (discriminator) through an identifying relationship.

cards.title: Relationships
cards.body: **Cardinality ratio**: 1:1, 1:N, M:N. **Participation**: total (every entity takes part — double line) or partial. **Degree**: binary, ternary. A relationship can have its own attributes (e.g. the date of an enrolment).

cards.title: ER → tables (minimum count)
points: Each strong entity → one table
M:N relationship → its own table with both keys
1:N → put the 1-side key as a foreign key in the N-side table (no new table)
1:1 → merge into either side (into the total-participation side if one exists)
Multivalued attribute → separate table (owner key + value)
Weak entity → table with owner key + partial key

cards.title: Keys
points: Superkey: any attribute set that uniquely identifies tuples
Candidate key: a minimal superkey
Primary key: the chosen candidate key (no NULLs)
Foreign key: refers to a key of another (or the same) relation
With n attributes and one single-attribute candidate key: 2ⁿ⁻¹ superkeys

cards.title: Integrity constraints
cards.body: **Domain** (values from the attribute's type/range), **key** (no duplicates), **entity integrity** (primary key not NULL), **referential integrity** (each foreign-key value matches a referenced key or is NULL). On delete of a referenced row: RESTRICT/NO ACTION, CASCADE, SET NULL or SET DEFAULT.

cards.title: Counting superkeys
cards.body:
R(A, B, C, D) with candidate keys A and B.
Supersets of A: 2³ = 8. Supersets of B: 8. Supersets of both (contain AB): 2² = 4.
Superkeys = 8 + 8 − 4 = **12** (inclusion–exclusion).

cards.q: An ER diagram has entities E1 and E2 joined by an M:N relationship, with no multivalued attributes. Minimum number of tables:
cards.explain: E1, E2 and a table for the M:N relationship.

cards.q: R(A, B, C, D, E) has exactly one candidate key, A. Number of superkeys:
cards.explain: Any set containing A: 2⁴ = 16.

cards.q: The primary key of a weak entity's table is:
cards.explain: The discriminator is unique only within one owner.

notes.h: From requirements to an ER diagram
notes.p:
Nouns become **entities**, verbs become **relationships**, and properties become **attributes**. For each relationship decide cardinality (how many on each side) and participation (must every entity take part?). A ternary relationship is not always replaceable by three binary ones without losing information.

**Specialisation/generalisation** (ISA): subclasses inherit the superclass key; constraints are disjoint/overlapping and total/partial.

notes.h: Worked example 1: minimum number of tables
notes.p:
Entities: Student (roll, name, phones — multivalued), Course (cid, title), Department (did, dname).
Relationships: Student –enrols (M:N, attribute grade)– Course; Department –offers (1:N)– Course.
Tables: Student(roll, name); Student_Phone(roll, phone); Course(cid, title, did) with did as a foreign key for 'offers'; Department(did, dname); Enrols(roll, cid, grade).
Minimum = **5**. The 1:N relationship adds no table; the M:N relationship and the multivalued attribute each need one.

Dept(did) is referenced by Emp(eid, did) with ON DELETE CASCADE, and Emp(eid) is referenced by Project(pid, lead_eid) with ON DELETE SET NULL. Deleting department 10, which has 3 employees who lead 2 projects:
Step 1: the department row is deleted.
Step 2: CASCADE deletes its 3 employee rows.
Step 3: SET NULL sets lead_eid = NULL in the 2 project rows (they stay).
Total rows **deleted = 4**; rows **updated = 2**. With RESTRICT instead of CASCADE, the department delete would be rejected.

A **relation** is a set of tuples (no duplicates, no order); its **schema** is the relation name plus attributes; the **degree** is the number of attributes and the **cardinality** the number of tuples. Attribute values are atomic (1NF). NULL means unknown or inapplicable and is not equal to anything, including another NULL.
points: A foreign key may be NULL unless declared NOT NULL.
A relation can reference itself (employee → manager).
Candidate keys are minimal; superkeys need not be.
An M:N relationship with total participation still needs its own table.

notes.p:
**Q: E1 and E2 have a 1:1 relationship with total participation on both sides. Minimum tables?** A: **1** — both entities and the relationship merge into one table. With total participation on only one side the usual answer is **2** (the total side carries the other's key as a foreign key).

**Q: R(A, B, C) has candidate keys AB and BC. How many superkeys?** A: Supersets of AB: 2; of BC: 2; of ABC: 1 → 2 + 2 − 1 = **3**.

**Q: Can a foreign key reference a non-key attribute?** A: No — it must reference a primary key or a UNIQUE (candidate) key.

**Q: A ternary relationship among three entities with no attributes needs how many tables in total?** A: 4 — three entity tables plus one relationship table holding all three keys.
Remember:
points: Weak entity key = owner key + discriminator.
1:N → foreign key on the N side; M:N → new table.
Multivalued attribute → separate table.
Superkeys with one candidate key of size 1 in n attributes: 2ⁿ⁻¹.
Inclusion–exclusion for several candidate keys.
Entity integrity: PK not NULL; referential integrity: FK matches or NULL.
CASCADE deletes children; SET NULL keeps them.

cards.title: Basic operators
points: σ (select): filters rows
π (project): keeps columns and removes duplicates
ρ (rename)
∪, −, ∩: need union-compatible relations
× (Cartesian product): |R| × |S| tuples
Complete set: {σ, π, ∪, −, ×, ρ}

cards.title: Joins
cards.body: **Theta join** R ⋈θ S = σθ(R × S). **Equi-join** uses only =. **Natural join** equates all common attributes and keeps one copy. **Left/right/full outer joins** keep unmatched tuples padded with NULLs. **Semi-join** keeps R tuples that have a match.

cards.title: Cardinality bounds
points: σ: 0 … |R|;  π: 1 … |R| (if R non-empty)
R × S: exactly |R| × |S|
R ⋈ S (natural): 0 … |R| × |S|
If R's common attributes form a non-NULL foreign key to S's key: |R ⋈ S| = |R|

cards.title: Division
cards.body: R(A, B) ÷ S(B) gives the A values paired with **every** B in S — 'students who took all courses'. In basic operators: π_A(R) − π_A((π_A(R) × S) − R).

cards.title: Tuple relational calculus
cards.body: { t | P(t) } — the set of tuples t satisfying formula P, built with ∧, ∨, ¬, ∃, ∀. A **safe** expression only produces values from the database (e.g. { t | ¬R(t) } is unsafe — infinite). Safe TRC, safe DRC and relational algebra have the same expressive power (**relationally complete**).

cards.title: Same query three ways
cards.body:
Names of employees in dept 5:
RA: π_name(σ_dno=5(Emp))
TRC: { t.name | t ∈ Emp ∧ t.dno = 5 }
SQL: SELECT DISTINCT name FROM Emp WHERE dno = 5 — DISTINCT matches π's duplicate removal.

cards.q: R has 10 tuples and S has 20, with some common attributes. The maximum size of R ⋈ S (natural join) is:
cards.explain: If every tuple matches every tuple (same common values), the join is as large as R × S.

cards.q: Which query needs the division operator (or its equivalent)?
cards.explain: 'For all' queries map to ÷.

cards.q: { t | ¬(t ∈ Emp) } is:
cards.explain: It describes infinitely many tuples outside Emp.

notes.p: RA is the procedural language query optimisers use internally. GATE questions give an expression and ask what it returns, or ask for a tuple count. Read inside out and track the schema after each operator. Remember RA works on **sets** (π removes duplicates), while SQL works on **multisets** unless DISTINCT is used.

notes.h: Worked example 1: division by hand and in code

notes.p:
Emp(eid, dno) has 100 tuples; dno is a NOT NULL foreign key to Dept(dno), which has 10 tuples.
Emp ⋈ Dept: each employee matches exactly one department → **100** tuples.
Emp × Dept: 100 × 10 = **1000** tuples.
π_dno(Emp): between 1 and 10 tuples (only departments that have employees).
Dept ⟕ Emp (left outer): at least 100 tuples, plus one NULL-padded tuple for every department with no employees (at most 100 + 9 = 109, since at least one department has employees).

Push selections down: σ_c(R ⋈ S) = σ_c(R) ⋈ S when c uses only R's attributes. Cascade selections: σ_c1∧c2(R) = σ_c1(σ_c2(R)). Joins are commutative and associative. Projections can be pushed down as long as join attributes are kept. These rewritings shrink intermediate results before expensive joins.
points: σ commutes with σ; π of π keeps the outer list.
R − S ≠ S − R; ∩ can be written R − (R − S).
Outer joins are not associative in general.
TRC ∀ is written as ¬∃¬ when needed.

notes.p:
**Q: What does π_A(R) − π_A(σ_B=5(R)) return?** A: A values none of whose tuples has B = 5.

**Q: R(A, B) has 6 tuples, S(B, C) has 4 tuples, and B is the key of S. Maximum tuples in R ⋈ S?** A: 6 — each R tuple matches at most one S tuple.

**Q: Is R ⋈ S = R × S possible?** A: Yes, when R and S share no attributes.

**Q: Express R ∩ S using only − .** A: R − (R − S).
Remember:
points: π removes duplicates; SQL needs DISTINCT.
|R × S| = |R| × |S|; natural join 0 … |R||S|.
FK (NOT NULL) to a key: |R ⋈ S| = |R|.
Division answers 'for all' queries.
R ÷ S = π_A(R) − π_A((π_A(R) × S) − R).
Safe TRC = safe DRC = RA in power.
Outer joins keep unmatched tuples with NULLs.

chapters.title: SQL queries, NULLs & nested subqueries (GATE style)

cards.title: Query skeleton
cards.body: SELECT [DISTINCT] … FROM … WHERE … GROUP BY … HAVING … ORDER BY. Logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY. WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups. Every non-aggregated SELECT column must appear in GROUP BY.

cards.title: Three-valued logic
cards.body: Any comparison with NULL is **UNKNOWN**. WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. UNKNOWN AND FALSE = FALSE; UNKNOWN OR TRUE = TRUE; NOT UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN. Test with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

cards.title: Aggregates and NULL
points: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs
SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX ignore NULLs
AVG(col) = SUM(col)/COUNT(col), not /COUNT(*)
On an empty set: COUNT gives 0, the others give NULL

cards.title: Subquery operators
points: IN / NOT IN: membership
EXISTS: true if the subquery returns any row
x > ALL (S): greater than every value; TRUE if S is empty
x > ANY (S): greater than at least one; FALSE if S is empty
NOT IN with a NULL in the list never returns TRUE

cards.title: Correlated subqueries
cards.body: A subquery that refers to the outer row runs (logically) once per outer row: employees earning more than their own department's average. EXISTS/NOT EXISTS with correlation expresses 'some' and 'all' (double NOT EXISTS = division).

cards.title: Second highest salary
cards.body:
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Emp);
Works with duplicates of the top salary, and returns NULL if every salary is equal.

cards.q: Column x holds 5, NULL, 3, 7. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM T WHERE x <> 5 returns:
cards.explain: 3 and 7 qualify; NULL <> 5 is UNKNOWN and is dropped.

cards.q: SELECT name FROM A WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM B), where B.id contains a NULL, returns:
options: Rows of A not in B
cards.explain: id NOT IN (…, NULL) is never TRUE — at best UNKNOWN.

cards.q: salary > ALL (subquery) when the subquery returns no rows is:
cards.explain: A universal condition over an empty set is vacuously true.

notes.p: Questions give small tables and a query and ask for the number of rows or the output. The traps are always the same: NULLs, duplicates (SQL keeps them unless DISTINCT), GROUP BY semantics, and how IN, EXISTS, ANY and ALL behave on empty or NULL-containing subqueries. Evaluate step by step in logical order.

`import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE T(x INT); INSERT INTO T VALUES (5),(NULL),(3),(7);
CREATE TABLE A(id INT, name TEXT); INSERT INTO A VALUES (1,'p'),(2,'q'),(3,'r');
CREATE TABLE B(id INT); INSERT INTO B VALUES (1),(NULL);
""")
q = lambda s: db.execute(s).fetchall()
print(q("SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(x), SUM(x), AVG(x) FROM T"))
print(q("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM T WHERE x <> 5"))
print(q("SELECT name FROM A WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM B)"))
print(q("SELECT name FROM A WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE B.id = A.id)"))
print(q("SELECT COUNT(*), MAX(x) FROM T WHERE x > 100"))`

Output:
`[(4, 3, 15, 5.0)]
[(2,)]
[]
[('q',), ('r',)]
[(0, None)]`

AVG is 15/3 = 5, not 15/4. NOT IN returns nothing because of the NULL in B, while NOT EXISTS returns q and r — the safe way to write an anti-join. On an empty set COUNT is 0 and MAX is NULL (printed as None).

notes.h: Worked example 2: GROUP BY and HAVING
notes.p:
Emp(name, dept, sal): (A, 1, 100), (B, 1, 200), (C, 2, 300), (D, 2, NULL), (E, 3, 150).
SELECT dept, COUNT(*), COUNT(sal), AVG(sal) FROM Emp GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
Groups: dept 1 → (2, 2, 150); dept 2 → (2, 1, 300); dept 3 has one row and is removed by HAVING.
Result: **2 rows**. Note dept 2's average is 300 because D's NULL is ignored.

UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT remove duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them. A **view** is a stored query; it is updatable only in simple cases (one base table, no aggregates or DISTINCT). Outer joins in SQL: LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows; a WHERE condition on the right table after a LEFT JOIN silently turns it into an inner join — put such conditions in the ON clause.
points: ORDER BY may use aliases; WHERE may not.
DISTINCT treats NULLs as equal to each other for de-duplication.
GROUP BY puts all NULLs in one group.
x = ANY (S) is the same as x IN S.

notes.p:
**Q: SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM Emp WHERE sal > ALL (SELECT sal FROM Emp WHERE dept = 9), and dept 9 has no employees — what is returned?** A: Every department that has an employee (ALL over an empty set is TRUE).

**Q: Does SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT x) count NULL?** A: No.

**Q: Can HAVING be used without GROUP BY?** A: Yes — the whole table is then one group.
Remember:
points: Logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY.
Comparisons with NULL are UNKNOWN; WHERE keeps only TRUE.
COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col); aggregates skip NULLs.
NOT IN with a NULL returns no rows; prefer NOT EXISTS.
> ALL(empty) is TRUE; > ANY(empty) is FALSE.
SQL keeps duplicates unless DISTINCT.
Double NOT EXISTS expresses division.

cards.title: Armstrong's axioms
points: Reflexivity: if Y ⊆ X then X → Y
Augmentation: X → Y ⇒ XZ → YZ
Transitivity: X → Y, Y → Z ⇒ X → Z
Derived: union, decomposition, pseudo-transitivity

cards.title: Attribute closure
cards.body: X⁺ = all attributes determined by X: start with X and keep adding the right side of any FD whose left side is inside the set. X is a **superkey** iff X⁺ = all attributes. Attributes never on any right side must be in **every** candidate key.

cards.title: Normal forms
points: 1NF: atomic values
2NF: no non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of a candidate key
3NF: for every X → A, X is a superkey or A is prime
BCNF: for every non-trivial X → A, X is a superkey
4NF: BCNF and no non-trivial MVD whose left side is not a superkey

cards.title: Minimal (canonical) cover
cards.body: 1) Make every right side a single attribute. 2) Remove extraneous attributes from left sides. 3) Remove redundant FDs (those implied by the rest). The result is not always unique.

cards.title: Decomposition tests
points: Lossless (binary): R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R1 ∩ R2 → R2
Dependency preserving: (F₁ ∪ F₂ …)⁺ = F⁺
3NF synthesis: always lossless and dependency preserving
BCNF decomposition: always lossless, not always dependency preserving

cards.title: Highest normal form
cards.body: R(A, B, C, D, E), F = {A → B, BC → E, ED → A}. Candidate keys: ACD, BCD, CDE — every attribute is prime, so R is in **3NF**. A → B violates BCNF (A is not a superkey).

cards.q: R(A, B, C, D) with F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}. Candidate keys:
cards.explain: A⁺ = ABCD; nothing else determines A.

cards.q: R(A, B, C) with A → B is split into R1(A, B) and R2(B, C). The decomposition is:
cards.explain: R1 ∩ R2 = B, and B is not a key of R1 or R2 (B → C is not given).

cards.q: Which normal form guarantees a lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition always exists?
cards.explain: 3NF synthesis achieves both; BCNF may lose dependencies.

notes.p:
Split attributes into: **only on left sides** (must be in every key), **only on right sides** (never in a key), **both** (maybe), **neither** (must be in every key). Start from the mandatory set; if its closure is everything, it is the only key. Otherwise add 'both' attributes one at a time, then pairs, keeping only **minimal** sets.

**Worked example 1.** R(A, B, C, D, E), F = {A → B, BC → E, ED → A}. C and D appear only on left sides → in every key. (CD)⁺ = CD. Try adding one more: (ACD)⁺ = ABCDE ✓, (BCD)⁺ = BCDE + A = ABCDE ✓, (CDE)⁺ = CDE + A + B ✓. Keys: **ACD, BCD, CDE**.

`from itertools import combinations
def closure(X, F):
    X = set(X); changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for l, r in F:
            if set(l) <= X and not set(r) <= X:
                X |= set(r); changed = True
    return X
def keys(R, F):
    found = []
    for k in range(1, len(R) + 1):
        for c in combinations(R, k):
            if closure(c, F) == set(R) and not any(set(f) <= set(c) for f in found):
                found.append(c)
    return [''.join(k) for k in found]
F = [('A', 'B'), ('BC', 'E'), ('ED', 'A')]
K = keys('ABCDE', F)
prime = set(''.join(K))
print(K, sorted(prime))
print('BCNF violations:', [l + '->' + r for l, r in F if closure(l, F) != set('ABCDE')])
print('3NF violations:', [l + '->' + r for l, r in F if closure(l, F) != set('ABCDE') and not set(r) <= prime])`

Output:
`['ACD', 'BCD', 'CDE'] ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E']
BCNF violations: ['A->B', 'BC->E', 'ED->A']
3NF violations: []`

Three FDs have non-superkey left sides, so R is not in BCNF; all right sides are prime, so R **is** in 3NF.

notes.h: Worked example 3: minimal cover and decomposition
notes.p:
F = {A → BC, B → C, A → B, AB → C}.
Split: A → B, A → C, B → C, AB → C.
AB → C: B alone gives C, so A is extraneous → B → C (duplicate).
A → C follows from A → B and B → C → redundant.
Minimal cover: **{A → B, B → C}**.
3NF synthesis gives R1(A, B), R2(B, C); A is a key of R(A, B, C), and R1 contains it, so no extra table is needed. The split is lossless (R1 ∩ R2 = B → C, a key of R2) and preserves both FDs.

Project F onto each part (compute closures inside each part) and see whether the union implies every original FD.

Example: R(A, B, C), F = {AB → C, C → B}. Keys AB and AC; C → B violates BCNF. BCNF split: R1(C, B), R2(A, C) — lossless (common C → B is a key of R1), but **AB → C is lost**: neither part contains A, B and C together. This is the classic case where 3NF (keep R as is) is preferred over BCNF.
points: 2NF matters only when a key is composite.
Every binary relation (two attributes) is in BCNF.
A relation whose candidate keys are all single attributes is in 2NF automatically.

notes.p: Remember:
points: X⁺ ⊇ all attributes ⇔ X is a superkey.
Left-only and absent attributes belong to every key.
3NF: X superkey or A prime; BCNF: X superkey.
Lossless binary split: common attributes form a key of one side.
3NF synthesis: lossless + dependency preserving.
BCNF: lossless, may lose dependencies (AB → C, C → B).
Minimal cover: single RHS, no extraneous LHS, no redundant FD.

cards.title: Blocking
points: Blocking factor bfr = ⌊block size / record size⌋ (unspanned)
Blocks for a file = ⌈records / bfr⌉
Binary search on a sorted file: ⌈log₂ blocks⌉ block accesses
Linear search: blocks/2 on average for a key, all blocks otherwise

cards.title: Index types
cards.body: **Primary index**: on the ordering key of a sorted file — sparse, one entry per block. **Clustering index**: on a non-key ordering field — one entry per distinct value. **Secondary index**: on a non-ordering field — dense, one entry per record (or per value with indirection). A file has at most one primary or clustering index, but many secondary indexes.

cards.title: Multilevel index
cards.body: Treat the index itself as a sorted file and index it again until the top level fits in one block. With fan-out fo = index bfr, levels = ⌈log_fo(first-level blocks)⌉ + 1 … simply keep dividing by fo. Access cost = levels + 1 (the data block).

cards.title: B+ tree node order
points: Internal: p × block pointer + (p − 1) × key ≤ block size
Leaf: n × (key + record pointer) + next-leaf pointer ≤ block size
Every node except the root at least half full
All data pointers are in leaves; leaves are linked for range queries

cards.title: B-tree vs B+ tree
cards.body: A **B-tree** stores record pointers in internal nodes too, so some searches stop early, but fan-out is smaller. A **B+ tree** keeps data pointers only in leaves: higher fan-out, shallower tree, and efficient range scans through the leaf chain — the standard DBMS index.

cards.title: Order calculation
cards.body:
Block 1024 B, key 9 B, block pointer 6 B, record pointer 7 B.
Internal: 6p + 9(p − 1) ≤ 1024 → 15p ≤ 1033 → **p = 68**.
Leaf: 16n + 6 ≤ 1024 → **n = 63** keys per leaf.

cards.q: Records of 100 bytes are stored unspanned in 1024-byte blocks. Blocking factor:
cards.explain: ⌊1024/100⌋ = 10; the remaining 24 bytes are wasted.

cards.q: A B-tree of order m (max m children) has non-root nodes with at least how many children?
cards.explain: Non-root internal nodes are at least half full: ⌈m/2⌉ children.

cards.q: Which index is always dense?
cards.explain: The file is not ordered on that field, so every record needs an entry.

notes.p: **Heap** (unordered): fast insert, linear search. **Sorted**: binary search on the ordering field, costly inserts. **Hashed**: one or two block accesses for equality search on the hash field, useless for ranges; overflow chains or dynamic schemes (extendible, linear hashing) handle growth. **Spanned** records may cross block boundaries — no wasted space, more complex reads.

`import math
records, rec_size, block = 30000, 100, 1024
bfr = block // rec_size; blocks = math.ceil(records / bfr)
print('data bfr', bfr, 'blocks', blocks, 'binary search', math.ceil(math.log2(blocks)))
entry = 9 + 6                                  # key + block pointer
fo = block // entry; l1 = math.ceil(blocks / fo)
print('index fan-out', fo, 'first-level blocks', l1, 'binary search on index + 1', math.ceil(math.log2(l1)) + 1)
levels, n = 1, l1
while n > 1:
    n = math.ceil(n / fo); levels += 1
print('multilevel levels', levels, 'accesses', levels + 1)`

Output:
`data bfr 10 blocks 3000 binary search 12
index fan-out 68 first-level blocks 45 binary search on index + 1 7
multilevel levels 2 accesses 3`

A sparse primary index (one entry per data block) shrinks 12 accesses to 7; making it multilevel cuts that to 3.

`p, leaf = 68, 63                    # from the order calculation
for levels in (1, 2, 3):           # levels of internal nodes above the leaves
    full = p ** levels * leaf
    fill = 0.69                    # typical average occupancy
    avg = round((p * fill) ** levels * leaf * fill)
    print(levels, 'internal levels -> max', full, 'records, about', avg, 'at 69% fill')`

Output:
`1 internal levels -> max 4284 records, about 2040 at 69% fill
2 internal levels -> max 291312 records, about 95699 at 69% fill
3 internal levels -> max 19809216 records, about 4490179 at 69% fill`

Three internal levels plus leaves already index about 2 × 10⁷ records at full capacity — so search cost stays at 4–5 block accesses even for very large tables.

For a B-tree of order m (max m children, m − 1 keys): **max keys** with height h (levels h + 1, root at level 0) = m^(h+1) − 1. The **minimum** keys: the root has at least 1 key, every other node at least ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 keys, giving 2⌈m/2⌉ʰ − 1 keys. Insertion splits a full node at its median and pushes the median up; the tree grows only at the root, so all leaves stay at the same depth.
points: Splitting a leaf in a B+ tree copies the middle key up; splitting an internal node moves it up.
Deletion merges or redistributes when a node falls below half full.
Order definitions differ across books — read whether order means max children or max keys.

notes.p: Remember:
points: bfr = ⌊B/R⌋; blocks = ⌈r/bfr⌉.
Primary: sparse, on ordering key; secondary: dense.
Multilevel index: divide by fan-out until one block.
B+ internal: p·P + (p − 1)·K ≤ B.
B+ leaf: n(K + Pr) + P ≤ B.
B+ trees: data in leaves, linked leaves, range-friendly.
Hashing: great for equality, useless for ranges.

cards.title: ACID
points: Atomicity: all or nothing (undo via the log)
Consistency: constraints hold before and after
Isolation: concurrent execution looks serial
Durability: committed changes survive crashes (redo via the log)

cards.title: Conflicts
