cards.body: Two operations **conflict** if they belong to different transactions, access the same item, and at least one is a **write** (RW, WR, WW). Swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations gives a **conflict-equivalent** schedule.

cards.title: Conflict serializability
cards.body: Build the **precedence graph**: an edge Ti → Tj for each conflict where Ti's operation comes first. The schedule is conflict serializable iff the graph is **acyclic**; any topological order is an equivalent serial schedule.

cards.title: View serializability
cards.body: View equivalence needs the same initial reads, the same reads-from pairs and the same final writes. Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable. A view-serializable schedule that is not conflict serializable must contain a **blind write** (write without a prior read).

cards.title: Recoverability ladder
points: Recoverable: Tj commits only after every Ti it read from commits
Cascadeless (ACA): read only committed data
Strict: no read or write of an item until the last writer commits/aborts
Strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable

cards.title: Locking and timestamps
cards.body: **2PL** (growing then shrinking phase) guarantees conflict serializability but not freedom from deadlock or cascading aborts. **Strict 2PL** holds exclusive locks until commit → strict schedules. **Timestamp ordering** is deadlock-free; **Thomas write rule** ignores obsolete writes, allowing some view-serializable schedules. **Wait-die** and **wound-wait** prevent deadlock using timestamps.

cards.q: S: r1(A) r2(A) w1(A) w2(A). The schedule is:
options: View serializable but not conflict serializable
cards.explain: Edges T1→T2 and T2→T1 (cycle); no blind writes, so it is not view serializable either (a lost update).

cards.q: S: r1(X) w2(X) w1(X) w3(X). The schedule is:
options: View serializable but not conflict serializable
cards.explain: Cycle T1⇄T2, but it is view-equivalent to T1 T2 T3 thanks to the blind writes.

cards.q: Basic two-phase locking guarantees:
cards.explain: Deadlocks and cascading aborts are still possible with basic 2PL.

notes.h: Worked example 1: precedence graph in code

notes.p:
S: w1(A) r2(A) w2(B) c2 c1.
T2 reads A written by T1 and commits **before** T1. If T1 now aborts, T2 has committed a value derived from data that never existed → **not recoverable**. Moving c2 after c1 makes it recoverable; making T2 read A only after c1 makes it cascadeless.

In S: w1(A) r2(A) a1 (abort), T2 must also be rolled back — a **cascading abort**, which strict 2PL prevents.

Older transaction = smaller timestamp. **Wait-die** (non-preemptive): an older requester waits; a younger requester dies (aborts and restarts with its original timestamp). **Wound-wait** (preemptive): an older requester wounds (aborts) the younger holder; a younger requester waits. In both, the older transaction never aborts, so no starvation.

**Timestamp ordering rules**: read(X) by T is rejected if TS(T) < W-TS(X); write(X) is rejected if TS(T) < R-TS(X) or TS(T) < W-TS(X) — except that the Thomas write rule simply skips the obsolete write in the last case.

The **write-ahead log** records old and new values before data pages reach disk. After a crash: **redo** transactions that committed after the last checkpoint, **undo** those that had not committed. With deferred update only redo is needed; with immediate update both undo and redo may be needed. A **checkpoint** limits how far back recovery must scan.
points: Number of serial schedules of n transactions: n!.
Conflict-equivalent serial schedules = topological orders of the precedence graph.
Shadow paging avoids a log but fragments data.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Conflict: different transactions, same item, at least one write.
Acyclic precedence graph ⇔ conflict serializable.
CS ⊂ VS; VS-but-not-CS needs a blind write.
Strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable.
2PL ⇒ CS; strict 2PL ⇒ strict schedules; deadlocks still possible.
Wait-die: young dies; wound-wait: old wounds young.
WAL: undo uncommitted, redo committed.

cards.title: Subnetting & CIDR
cards.body: A /p prefix leaves 32 − p host bits: 2^(32−p) addresses, 2^(32−p) − 2 usable hosts. Routers forward using longest-prefix match.

cards.title: Sliding window
points: a = propagation delay / transmission time
Stop-and-wait efficiency = 1 / (1 + 2a)
Go-Back-N window ≤ 2ᵏ − 1 (k-bit sequence numbers)
Selective Repeat window ≤ 2ᵏ⁻¹

cards.title: TCP congestion control
cards.body: Slow start: cwnd doubles each RTT until ssthresh. Congestion avoidance: +1 MSS per RTT. On timeout: ssthresh = cwnd/2, cwnd = 1 MSS. On 3 duplicate ACKs (Reno): fast retransmit, cwnd halves.

cards.title: Error control
points: Minimum Hamming distance d: detect up to d − 1 errors
Correct up to ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋ errors
CRC: append r bits where the generator has degree r

cards.title: CSMA/CD
points: Minimum frame size = 2 × propagation delay × bandwidth
Efficiency ≈ 1 / (1 + 6.44a) for Ethernet

cards.title: Routing
cards.body: Distance vector (Bellman–Ford, neighbours exchange vectors, count-to-infinity problem; RIP). Link state (flooded LSAs, each router runs Dijkstra; OSPF).

cards.title: Headers & ports
cards.body: IPv4 header 20–60 bytes; TCP header 20–60 bytes; UDP header 8 bytes. DNS over UDP 53, HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SMTP 25.

cards.q: A code has minimum Hamming distance 5. It can correct up to:
Maximum Go-Back-N sender window with 3-bit sequence numbers:
CSMA/CD at 10 Mbps with 25.6 µs one-way propagation delay. Minimum frame size:
cards.explain: 2 × 25.6 µs × 10⁷ bps = 512 bits.

notes.p:
With CIDR /n, a block has 2^(32 − n) addresses and 2^(32 − n) − 2 usable hosts. To find a host's network, AND the address with the mask. **Longest-prefix match** decides the forwarding entry when several prefixes match. **Supernetting** combines contiguous blocks (four /24s starting at a multiple of 4 make a /22).

Routing: **distance vector** (Bellman–Ford, shares the table with neighbours, suffers **count-to-infinity**, fixed partly by split horizon/poisoned reverse; RIP) vs **link state** (each router floods link info and runs Dijkstra; OSPF). BGP is a path-vector protocol between autonomous systems.

notes.h: Flow control and sliding window formulas
notes.p:
Let **Tt = frame size / bandwidth** and **Tp = distance / propagation speed**, **a = Tp/Tt**. **Stop-and-wait efficiency = 1/(1 + 2a)**. With window size W, efficiency = min(1, W/(1 + 2a)). For **Go-Back-N**, window ≤ 2ᵏ − 1 with k sequence bits; for **Selective Repeat**, window ≤ 2^(k − 1). Throughput = efficiency × bandwidth.

**Example.** Tt = 1 ms, Tp = 10 ms → a = 10 → stop-and-wait efficiency = 1/21 ≈ **4.76%**. Full utilisation needs W ≥ 21, so k ≥ 5 bits for GBN (2⁵ − 1 = 31) and k ≥ 6 for SR.

**CSMA/CD** needs Tt ≥ 2Tp so a sender detects a collision before it finishes: minimum frame = 2 × Tp × bandwidth. For 10 Mbps with Tp = 25.6 µs: **512 bits = 64 bytes** — the classic Ethernet minimum.

**Q: Usable hosts in 200.10.10.0/27?** A: 2⁵ − 2 = 30.

**Q: Which layer handles end-to-end reliability?** A: Transport.

**Q: Max window for Selective Repeat with 3-bit sequence numbers?** A: 4.

**Q: Efficiency of pure ALOHA and slotted ALOHA?** A: 18.4% and 36.8%.

**Q: TCP header minimum size?** A: 20 bytes (UDP: 8 bytes).
Remember:
points: Usable hosts = 2^(32 − n) − 2.
Stop-and-wait efficiency = 1/(1 + 2a).
GBN window ≤ 2ᵏ − 1; SR ≤ 2^(k − 1).
CSMA/CD minimum frame = 2 × Tp × B.
CRC: append r zeros, XOR-divide, append remainder.
Slow start doubles; congestion avoidance adds 1; timeout halves ssthresh.
ALOHA 18.4%, slotted 36.8%.

cards.title: Layered models
cards.body: **OSI** (7): physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application. **TCP/IP** (5-layer teaching model): physical, link, network, transport, application. Each layer adds a header (**encapsulation**): segment (transport) → packet/datagram (network) → frame (link) → bits.

cards.title: Devices by layer
points: Hub, repeater: physical (one collision domain)
Switch, bridge: data link (each port its own collision domain)
Router: network (separates broadcast domains)
Gateways/proxies: up to application layer

cards.title: Delay components
points: Transmission delay = L / R (packet bits ÷ link rate)
Propagation delay = d / s (distance ÷ signal speed, ≈ 2 × 10⁸ m/s)
Queuing + processing delays at each node
RTT = time to send a tiny message and get a tiny reply

cards.title: Three ways to switch
cards.body: **Circuit switching**: reserve a path (setup delay), then a dedicated rate — no queuing. **Packet switching** (datagram): each packet routed independently, store-and-forward, statistical multiplexing. **Virtual circuit**: a setup phase installs per-connection state; packets carry a short VC identifier and follow the same path in order.

cards.title: Throughput formulas
points: Bandwidth-delay product = R × one-way propagation delay (bits in flight)
Utilisation (stop-and-wait) = Tt / (Tt + 2Tp)
End-to-end throughput = min of link rates on the path
n packets over k store-and-forward links: (n + k − 1) × L/R (+ k × Tp)

cards.title: Pipelining through routers
cards.body:
3 packets of 1000 bits cross 2 links (one router) at 1 Mbps; ignore propagation. Each transmission takes 1 ms.
Time = (3 + 2 − 1) × 1 ms = **4 ms**, not 3 × 2 = 6 ms — the router forwards packet 1 while packet 2 is arriving.

cards.q: Transmission delay of a 1500-byte frame on a 10 Mbps link:
One 1-Mbit packet crosses 3 store-and-forward links, each 1 Mbps, propagation ignored. Delay:
cards.explain: Each link must receive the whole packet before forwarding: 3 × 1 s.

cards.q: Which device separates broadcast domains?
cards.explain: Routers do not forward link-layer broadcasts.

notes.p:
Each layer offers a service to the one above and uses the one below, so technologies can change independently (Wi-Fi or Ethernet below, the same IP above). The cost is header overhead and some duplicated functionality. **Peer layers** talk through headers: the transport header on one host is read only by the transport layer on the other.

Which layer does what: link — framing, error detection, MAC; network — addressing, routing, fragmentation; transport — process-to-process delivery, reliability, flow and congestion control; application — the protocol the user cares about (DNS, HTTP).

notes.h: Worked example 1: circuit vs packet switching
notes.p:
`L_msg = 8e6                 # 1 MB message in bits
R, links, tp = 1e6, 3, 0.01   # 1 Mbps links, 3 links, 10 ms propagation per link
setup = 0.5                    # circuit setup time (s)
circuit = setup + L_msg / R + links * tp
whole = links * (L_msg / R) + links * tp                # one big message, store-and-forward
pkt = 8000; n = int(L_msg // pkt)                       # 1000-byte packets, headers ignored
packets = (n + links - 1) * pkt / R + links * tp
print(round(circuit, 3), round(whole, 3), round(packets, 3))`

Output:
`8.53 24.03 8.046`

Sending the message as one unit through store-and-forward routers takes 3 × 8 s. Splitting it into packets pipelines the links and nearly matches the circuit (8.046 s vs 8.53 s) without any setup. In practice per-packet headers add overhead, so very small packets become worse again.

A 100 Mbps link, 2000 km long, signal speed 2 × 10⁸ m/s.
Tp = 2 × 10⁶ / 2 × 10⁸ = **10 ms**.
BDP = 10⁸ × 0.01 = 10⁶ bits = **125 KB** in flight one way; a sender needs a window of about 2 × BDP = 250 KB (one RTT's worth) to keep the pipe full.
Stop-and-wait with 1000-byte frames: Tt = 8000 / 10⁸ = 0.08 ms; utilisation = 0.08 / (0.08 + 20) ≈ **0.4%** — the reason for sliding windows.
Watch the units and assumptions:
points: 1 KB in data sizes is usually 1024 bytes, but 1 kbps is 1000 bits per second.
Bytes vs bits: multiply by 8.
Store-and-forward means each hop adds a full transmission delay.
Propagation does not depend on packet size; transmission does not depend on distance.
Throughput is limited by the slowest link (bottleneck).

notes.p: Remember:
points: OSI 7 layers; TCP/IP 5-layer model.
Hub L1, switch L2, router L3.
Tt = L/R; Tp = d/s.
n packets, k links: (n + k − 1) L/R + k Tp.
BDP = R × Tp; window ≥ R × RTT to fill the pipe.
Stop-and-wait utilisation = Tt / (Tt + 2Tp).
Circuit: setup + dedicated rate; VC: setup + per-flow state; datagram: none.

chapters.title: Data link: framing, error detection, MAC & Ethernet

cards.title: Framing
cards.body: **Byte stuffing**: a flag byte marks frame boundaries; an ESC byte is inserted before any flag or ESC inside the data. **Bit stuffing** (HDLC flag 01111110): after five consecutive 1s in the data, insert a 0; the receiver removes it.

cards.title: Error detection and correction
points: Detect up to d errors: minimum Hamming distance d + 1
Correct up to d errors: distance 2d + 1
Single parity: detects any odd number of bit errors
CRC with generator of degree r: append r bits; detects all bursts ≤ r
Internet checksum: 16-bit one's-complement sum

cards.title: Random access
points: Pure ALOHA: S = G e^(−2G), max 1/(2e) ≈ 18.4% at G = 0.5
Slotted ALOHA: S = G e^(−G), max 1/e ≈ 36.8% at G = 1
N stations, each sends with prob p per slot: P(success) = Np(1 − p)^(N−1)
Vulnerable time: pure 2 × frame time, slotted 1 frame time

cards.title: CSMA/CD
points: Collision must be detected while still transmitting: Tt ≥ 2Tp
Minimum frame = 2 × Tp × bandwidth
Classic Ethernet: 64-byte minimum, 1518-byte maximum frame
Binary exponential backoff: after the k-th collision wait r × slot time, r ∈ [0, 2^min(k,10) − 1]

cards.title: Ethernet and bridging
cards.body: 48-bit MAC addresses; FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF is broadcast. A **learning switch/bridge** records the source MAC of each incoming frame against its port, forwards known destinations on one port and floods unknown ones. Redundant links create loops, so bridges run the **spanning tree protocol**, blocking ports to leave a loop-free tree rooted at the lowest bridge ID.

cards.title: Minimum frame size
cards.body:
10 Mbps Ethernet segment of 2 km, signal speed 2 × 10⁸ m/s → Tp = 10 µs.
Minimum frame = 2 × 10 µs × 10⁷ bps = **200 bits** (25 bytes).

cards.q: To correct up to 2 bit errors, the minimum Hamming distance of the code must be:
Maximum throughput of slotted ALOHA:
cards.explain: 1/e at G = 1.

cards.q: A switch receives a frame whose destination MAC is not in its table. It:
options: Floods it on all ports except the incoming one
cards.explain: Unknown unicast is flooded; replies then let the switch learn.

notes.h: What the data link layer guarantees
notes.p:
It moves a frame across **one hop**: it delimits frames, adds link-layer addresses, detects errors with CRC, and on shared media decides who may transmit (**medium access control**). Reliability (retransmission) is optional at this layer — Ethernet just drops bad frames and leaves recovery to TCP.

Error detection is cheaper than correction; correction (forward error correction) is used where retransmission is expensive, such as wireless or storage.

notes.h: Worked example 1: bit stuffing and CRC
Worked example 2: ALOHA and CSMA/CD numbers
notes.p:
**Slotted ALOHA**, 5 stations, each transmits in a slot with p = 0.2.
P(success) = 5 × 0.2 × 0.8⁴ = 1 × 0.4096 = **0.41**. This is the best p for N = 5 because p = 1/N maximises Np(1 − p)^(N−1).

**CSMA/CD**: 1 Gbps link, minimum frame 512 bytes = 4096 bits, signal speed 2 × 10⁸ m/s. Tt = 4.096 µs must be ≥ 2Tp → Tp ≤ 2.048 µs → maximum length = 2.048 × 10⁻⁶ × 2 × 10⁸ ≈ **409.6 m**. Faster Ethernet shrinks the collision domain unless the minimum frame grows — modern switched full-duplex Ethernet avoids collisions altogether.

Stop-and-wait sends one frame and waits for its ACK. **Go-Back-N** with k sequence bits allows a window of 2ᵏ − 1 and resends everything after a loss; **Selective Repeat** allows 2ᵏ⁻¹ and resends only lost frames (receiver buffers out-of-order frames). Efficiency = window × Tt / (Tt + 2Tp), capped at 1. These ideas reappear in TCP.
points: Collision domain: switch port; broadcast domain: whole switched LAN (VLANs split it).
CRC catches all single-bit, double-bit and odd-count errors when the generator is chosen well.
Parity cannot detect an even number of flipped bits.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Bit stuffing: 0 after five 1s; flag 01111110.
Detect d: distance d + 1; correct d: 2d + 1.
Pure ALOHA 18.4%, slotted 36.8%.
CSMA/CD: min frame = 2 Tp × R.
Ethernet: 48-bit MAC, 64 B minimum frame, binary exponential backoff.
Learning switch: learn source, forward known, flood unknown.
STP removes loops between bridges.

cards.title: Forwarding vs routing
cards.body: **Forwarding** moves a packet from input to output port using the forwarding table (longest-prefix match). **Routing** is the control-plane algorithm that builds those tables. Intra-domain protocols: RIP (distance vector), OSPF (link state); BGP connects autonomous systems.

cards.title: Distance vector
cards.body: Each router keeps a vector of best-known costs and periodically sends it to **neighbours only**. Update (Bellman-Ford): Dₓ(y) = min over neighbours v of { c(x, v) + Dᵥ(y) }. Simple and distributed, but slow to converge after failures.

cards.title: Count to infinity
cards.body: When a link fails, routers can keep believing each other's stale routes, raising the cost by one step each exchange. Fixes: **split horizon** (do not advertise a route back to the neighbour you learnt it from), **poison reverse** (advertise it as ∞), and a small 'infinity' (RIP uses 16).

cards.title: Link state
cards.body: Each router **floods** link-state advertisements (its neighbours and link costs) to **all** routers, so every router has the full topology and runs **Dijkstra** locally. Faster convergence, no count-to-infinity, more memory and computation. OSPF uses this.

cards.title: Compare
points: DV: talks to neighbours, sends whole vector, Bellman-Ford
LS: talks to everyone (flooding), sends neighbour list, Dijkstra
DV message complexity per round: O(neighbours); LS flooding: O(N·E)
Dijkstra with a heap: O(E log V)

cards.title: One DV update
cards.body: A's neighbours: B at cost 2 advertises D = 5; C at cost 1 advertises D = 7. A's cost to D = min(2 + 5, 1 + 7) = **7**, via B.

cards.q: The count-to-infinity problem affects:
cards.explain: DV routers only know neighbours' distances, not the topology.

cards.q: In link-state routing each router computes routes using:
cards.explain: It has the full map and computes a shortest-path tree.

cards.q: Split horizon with poison reverse means a router advertises a route learnt from neighbour N back to N with cost:
cards.explain: Poison reverse tells N not to route through this router.

notes.p: Each router starts knowing only direct links. In every round it receives neighbours' vectors and recomputes. After at most N − 1 rounds (N routers) all costs are correct when nothing changes — good news travels fast. Bad news (a cost increase or failure) travels slowly, which is the count-to-infinity problem.

`INF = float('inf')
links = {('A','B'): 1, ('B','C'): 2, ('C','D'): 1, ('A','D'): 7}
nodes = 'ABCD'
cost = lambda u, v: links.get((u, v), links.get((v, u), INF))
D = {u: {v: (0 if u == v else cost(u, v)) for v in nodes} for u in nodes}
for rnd in range(1, 4):
    new = {u: {v: min([D[u][v]] + [cost(u, n) + D[n][v] for n in nodes if cost(u, n) < INF])
               for v in nodes} for u in nodes}
    changed = new != D; D = new
    print('round', rnd, 'A:', D['A'], 'changed' if changed else 'stable')`

Output:
`round 1 A: {'A': 0, 'B': 1, 'C': 3, 'D': 7} changed
round 2 A: {'A': 0, 'B': 1, 'C': 3, 'D': 4} changed
round 3 A: {'A': 0, 'B': 1, 'C': 3, 'D': 4} stable`

In round 1 A learns C via B (1 + 2 = 3) but keeps D at 7, because B did not yet know a route to D. In round 2 B advertises D = 3 (via C), so A's cost drops to 1 + 3 = **4**. Round 3 changes nothing — the tables have converged.

Chain A — B — C with costs 1, 1. B reaches C at 1, A reaches C at 2 (via B). Now link B–C fails.
B looks for another route: A advertises C at 2, so B sets cost 1 + 2 = 3 via A.
A hears B's 3 and sets 1 + 3 = 4 via B. B then sets 5, A 6, …
The costs keep climbing, one exchange at a time, until they hit 'infinity' (16 in RIP). With **split horizon**, A would never advertise its C-route back to B, and B would correctly mark C unreachable at once (for this simple chain; longer loops can still count up).

Steps: discover neighbours (hello packets), measure link costs, build an LSA, **flood** it reliably with sequence numbers and ages so stale information is discarded, then run Dijkstra on the complete graph. Each router computes the same shortest-path tree rooted at itself and installs the first hop for each destination.
points: Flooding: every router forwards an LSA on all links except the one it came from; duplicates are dropped using sequence numbers.
Oscillation is possible if link costs depend on load.
Hierarchical routing (OSPF areas, BGP between ASes) keeps tables manageable.

notes.p: Remember:
points: DV: Bellman-Ford, neighbours only, whole vector.
Good news fast, bad news slow (count to infinity).
Split horizon, poison reverse, max hop count 16 (RIP).
LS: flood LSAs to all, Dijkstra locally (OSPF).
DV converges in ≤ N − 1 rounds when costs only decrease.
Forwarding = data plane lookup; routing = control plane.
Longest-prefix match chooses among overlapping routes.

chapters.title: IPv4: header, fragmentation, CIDR, NAT, ARP, DHCP & ICMP

cards.title: IPv4 header facts
points: Header 20–60 bytes; HLEN counts 4-byte words (5 … 15)
Total length (16 bits) counts header + data, max 65,535 bytes
TTL decremented at each router; packet dropped at 0
Protocol field: 6 = TCP, 17 = UDP, 1 = ICMP
Header checksum covers the header only and is recomputed at each hop

cards.title: Fragmentation
points: Fragment data size = multiple of 8 (except the last), ≤ MTU − header
Fragment offset counts 8-byte units
MF = 1 on every fragment except the last; DF = 1 forbids fragmenting
Fragments share the Identification field; only the destination reassembles

cards.title: CIDR
points: a.b.c.d/n: n network bits, 32 − n host bits
Usable hosts = 2^(32 − n) − 2 (network and broadcast addresses excluded)
Aggregation: 2ᵏ contiguous, aligned blocks of /n → one /(n − k)
Longest-prefix match picks the most specific route

cards.title: NAT
cards.body: A **NAT** router lets many hosts with private addresses (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) share one public address. It rewrites the source IP and port on the way out, remembers the mapping in a translation table, and reverses it for replies. Unsolicited inbound connections fail unless a port is forwarded.

cards.title: ARP, DHCP, ICMP
cards.body: **ARP** maps an IP address to a MAC address on the local link (broadcast request, unicast reply, cached). **DHCP** leases an address: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge (DORA), over UDP 67/68. **ICMP** reports errors and diagnostics: echo request/reply (ping), destination unreachable, time exceeded (used by traceroute).

cards.title: Subnet a /24
cards.body:
Split 192.168.10.0/24 into 4 equal subnets → borrow 2 bits → /26, 64 addresses each, 62 hosts.
Subnets: .0, .64, .128, .192. The third subnet's broadcast is 192.168.10.191.

cards.q: A 2400-byte datagram (20-byte header + 2380 data) crosses a link with MTU 1000. The offset field of the second fragment is:
cards.explain: Max data per fragment = 980 → round down to a multiple of 8 = 976. Second fragment starts at byte 976 → offset 976/8 = 122.

cards.q: Usable host addresses in a /27 network:
Which protocol maps an IP address to a MAC address on a LAN?
cards.explain: ARP resolves the next hop's link-layer address.

notes.p: IP gives **best-effort**, connectionless delivery of datagrams between hosts — no guarantee of delivery, order or no duplication. Routers forward using the destination address and longest-prefix match. Upper layers (TCP) add reliability. An IP address names an **interface**, not a host: a router has one per interface.

notes.h: Worked example 2: CIDR and longest-prefix match
notes.p:
`import ipaddress as ip
nets = [ip.ip_network('200.1.%d.0/24' % i) for i in range(4)]
print(list(ip.collapse_addresses(nets)))
table = {'0.0.0.0/0': 'default', '131.16.0.0/16': 'if1', '131.16.32.0/19': 'if2', '131.16.40.0/21': 'if3'}
def lookup(addr):
    a = ip.ip_address(addr)
    best = max((ip.ip_network(p) for p in table if a in ip.ip_network(p)), key=lambda n: n.prefixlen)
    return table[str(best)]
for a in ['131.16.41.7', '131.16.33.1', '131.16.200.1', '8.8.8.8']: print(a, lookup(a))
n = ip.ip_network('192.168.10.128/26'); print(n.network_address, n.broadcast_address, n.num_addresses - 2)`

Output:
`[IPv4Network('200.1.0.0/22')]
131.16.41.7 if3
131.16.33.1 if2
131.16.200.1 if1
8.8.8.8 default
192.168.10.128 192.168.10.191 62`

Four aligned /24s aggregate into one /22. 131.16.41.7 matches /16, /19 and /21 — the /21 wins.

notes.h: NAT, ARP, DHCP and ICMP in a real exchange
notes.p: A laptop joins Wi-Fi: **DHCP** gives it 192.168.1.23/24, gateway 192.168.1.1 and a DNS server. To reach a web server it needs the gateway's MAC, so it sends an **ARP** request (broadcast) and caches the reply. The packet leaves with source 192.168.1.23:51000; the **NAT** router rewrites it to its public address, say 203.0.113.5:62001, and stores the mapping. If a router on the path finds TTL = 0 it returns **ICMP time exceeded** — traceroute sends probes with TTL 1, 2, 3, … to list every hop.
points: ARP is used only for the next hop, never for remote hosts directly.
NAT breaks the end-to-end principle; NAPT uses ports to multiplex.
DHCP Discover is sent from 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255.

notes.p:
**Q: An IP packet has HLEN = 6 and total length 500. How many data bytes?** A: Header = 6 × 4 = 24 bytes → 476 data bytes.

**Q: A fragment has offset 100, MF = 0 and total length 520 with a 20-byte header. What are its first and last data byte numbers?** A: First = 100 × 8 = 800; last = 800 + 500 − 1 = 1299 — so the original carried 1300 data bytes.

**Q: How many /26 subnets fit in a /22?** A: 2⁴ = 16.
Remember:
points: IPv4 header 20–60 B; TTL, protocol, header checksum.
Fragment data multiple of 8; offset in 8-byte units; MF on all but last.
Hosts in /n: 2^(32 − n) − 2.
Aggregate aligned blocks; longest prefix wins.
NAT rewrites IP and port; private ranges 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16.
ARP: IP → MAC; DHCP: DORA; ICMP: ping, traceroute.
Only the destination reassembles fragments.

chapters.title: UDP, TCP, flow & congestion control, socket API

cards.title: UDP
cards.body: Connectionless, unreliable, message-oriented. 8-byte header: source port, destination port, length, checksum. No handshake, no congestion control — used by DNS queries, DHCP, streaming and games where low latency beats retransmission.

cards.title: TCP connection management
cards.body: **Three-way handshake**: SYN (seq = x), SYN-ACK (seq = y, ack = x + 1), ACK (ack = y + 1). SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number. Close: FIN → ACK, FIN → ACK; the side that closes first waits in **TIME_WAIT** for 2 × MSL.

cards.title: TCP numbers
points: Header 20–60 bytes; sequence and ACK numbers count bytes
ACK number = next byte expected (cumulative)
Effective window = min(rwnd, cwnd)
Throughput ≤ window / RTT
Sequence wrap-around time = 2³² bytes ÷ bandwidth in bytes/s

cards.title: Congestion control (Reno)
points: Slow start: cwnd doubles every RTT (+1 MSS per ACK) until ssthresh
Congestion avoidance: cwnd + 1 MSS per RTT
Timeout: ssthresh = cwnd/2, cwnd = 1 MSS, slow start again
3 duplicate ACKs: fast retransmit; ssthresh = cwnd/2, cwnd = ssthresh (fast recovery)
Tahoe treats 3 dup ACKs like a timeout

cards.title: Socket API
cards.body: TCP server: **socket → bind → listen → accept** (blocks until a client connects, returns a new socket) → recv/send → close. TCP client: **socket → connect** → send/recv → close. UDP: socket → (bind) → sendto/recvfrom, no listen/accept/connect needed.

cards.title: Window-limited throughput
cards.body:
rwnd = 64 KB (65,535 bytes), RTT = 100 ms.
Max throughput = 65,535 × 8 / 0.1 ≈ **5.24 Mbps**, whatever the link speed. The window-scale option raises the limit on long fat networks.

cards.q: Which socket call makes a TCP server block until a client connects?
cards.explain: accept() returns a new connected socket for each client.

cards.q: cwnd = 16 MSS when a timeout occurs (TCP Tahoe/Reno). New ssthresh and cwnd:
cards.explain: ssthresh = 16/2 = 8; cwnd restarts at 1 MSS.

cards.q: Size of the UDP header:
cards.explain: Four 2-byte fields.

notes.h: Worked example 1: a real TCP exchange
notes.p:
`import socket, threading
srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
srv.bind(('127.0.0.1', 0)); srv.listen(1)          # socket -> bind -> listen
port = srv.getsockname()[1]
def serve():
    conn, addr = srv.accept()                        # blocks until a client connects
    data = conn.recv(1024)
    conn.sendall(b'ECHO ' + data.upper()); conn.close()
t = threading.Thread(target=serve); t.start()
cli = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
cli.connect(('127.0.0.1', port))                     # three-way handshake happens here
cli.sendall(b'hello gate'); print(cli.recv(1024).decode()); cli.close()
t.join(); srv.close()
u1, u2 = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM), socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
u2.bind(('127.0.0.1', 0)); u1.sendto(b'datagram', u2.getsockname())
print(u2.recvfrom(100)[0].decode()); u1.close(); u2.close()`

Output:
`ECHO HELLO GATE
datagram`

The server needs four calls before it can talk; the client's connect() triggers the handshake. UDP just sends a datagram to an address — no connection exists.

`def reno(rounds, ssthresh, events):
    cwnd, out = 1, []
    for r in range(1, rounds + 1):
        out.append(cwnd)
        ev = events.get(r)
        if ev == 'timeout': ssthresh, cwnd = max(cwnd // 2, 2), 1
        elif ev == '3dup': ssthresh = max(cwnd // 2, 2); cwnd = ssthresh
        elif cwnd < ssthresh: cwnd = min(cwnd * 2, ssthresh)
        else: cwnd += 1
    return out
print(reno(14, 16, {7: 'timeout'}))
print(reno(14, 16, {7: '3dup'}))`

Output:
`[1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 17, 18, 1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 10, 11]
[1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 17, 18, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]`

cwnd (in MSS) per RTT with ssthresh = 16. Slow start goes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, then linear growth to 18. A timeout at 18 sets ssthresh = 9 and cwnd = 1; triple duplicate ACKs instead resume at 9 and grow linearly. Many textbook questions cap slow start exactly at ssthresh as done here — check the stated convention.

A TCP connection starts with ISN 1000 (SYN uses 1000). The client then sends segments of 500, 300 and 200 bytes.
First data byte = 1001. Segment sequence numbers: **1001, 1501, 1801**. After all arrive, the ACK number is **2001**. If the 300-byte segment is lost, the receiver keeps acknowledging 1501 (duplicate ACKs).
Wrap-around: at 1 Gbps (1.25 × 10⁸ B/s), 2³² bytes are sent in about **34.4 s**, so timestamps protect against old duplicates on fast links.

**Flow control** protects the **receiver**: it advertises rwnd, the free buffer space; rwnd = 0 stops the sender (it probes with persist-timer segments). **Congestion control** protects the **network**: cwnd is the sender's own estimate. The sender may have min(rwnd, cwnd) unacknowledged bytes in flight.
points: Nagle's algorithm batches small writes; delayed ACKs reduce ACK count.
RTO is computed from smoothed RTT and RTT variance (Jacobson); retransmissions back off exponentially.
TCP is a byte stream — message boundaries are not preserved.

notes.p: Remember:
points: UDP header 8 B; TCP header 20–60 B.
SYN and FIN consume a sequence number each.
ACK = next byte expected.
Window = min(rwnd, cwnd); throughput ≤ window/RTT.
Slow start doubles; avoidance +1 per RTT.
Timeout → cwnd 1; 3 dup ACKs → cwnd = ssthresh (Reno).
Server: socket, bind, listen, accept; client: socket, connect.

chapters.title: Application layer: DNS, HTTP, SMTP, FTP & e-mail

cards.title: DNS
cards.body: A distributed, hierarchical database: **root** → **TLD** (.com, .in) → **authoritative** servers. Clients ask a **local resolver**, which queries recursively on their behalf; the resolver itself usually asks the hierarchy **iteratively**. Answers are cached for their TTL. Queries normally use **UDP port 53** (TCP for large replies and zone transfers).

cards.title: DNS records
points: A: name → IPv4;  AAAA: name → IPv6
NS: domain → its name server
CNAME: alias → canonical name
MX: domain → mail server
PTR: reverse lookup (IP → name)

cards.title: HTTP
cards.body: Stateless request–response over TCP (port 80; HTTPS 443). Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, HEAD. Status: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error (404), 5xx server error. **Cookies** add state. HTTP/1.0 is non-persistent by default; **HTTP/1.1** uses persistent connections and allows pipelining.

cards.title: HTTP response-time model (ignore transmission)
points: Non-persistent: 2 RTT per object (TCP setup + request)
Persistent, no pipelining: 1 RTT setup + 1 RTT per object
Persistent with pipelining: 1 RTT setup + 1 RTT (base page) + ~1 RTT for all objects
Parallel non-persistent connections overlap the 2-RTT costs

cards.title: E-mail
cards.body: **SMTP** (TCP 25) pushes mail from the sender's agent to its server and between servers; it is a push protocol with 7-bit ASCII, so **MIME** encodes attachments. The recipient pulls mail with **POP3** (110, download-and-delete style) or **IMAP** (143, keeps folders on the server). Webmail uses HTTP to the user.

cards.title: FTP
cards.body: Two TCP connections: **control** on port 21 (persistent, carries commands such as USER, RETR) and **data** on port 20 (active mode) or a negotiated port (passive mode), one per file. Control is 'out-of-band' and the server keeps state about the session.

cards.q: A web page has a base HTML file and 10 small images. With non-persistent HTTP and no parallel connections (ignore transmission time), the total time is:
cards.explain: 11 objects × 2 RTT = 22 RTT.

cards.q: Which DNS record type identifies the mail server for a domain?
cards.explain: MX = mail exchanger.

cards.q: Which protocol does a mail client use to retrieve mail while keeping it organised in folders on the server?
cards.explain: IMAP keeps state on the server; SMTP only sends.

notes.p:
Base page + 10 images, RTT = 50 ms, transmission ignored.
Non-persistent, serial: 11 × 2 RTT = 22 RTT = **1100 ms**.
Non-persistent with up to 10 parallel connections: 2 RTT (base) + 2 RTT (all images together) = 4 RTT = **200 ms**.
Persistent without pipelining: 1 RTT (TCP) + 1 (base) + 10 × 1 (images) = 12 RTT = **600 ms**.
Persistent with pipelining: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 RTT = **150 ms**.
If DNS must be resolved first, add its lookup time (e.g. local resolver plus iterative queries) once.

notes.h: Worked example 2: an HTTP exchange on a local server
notes.p:
`import http.server, threading, urllib.request class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler): def do_GET(self): body = b'

GATE

' if self.path == '/' else b'missing' self.send_response(200 if self.path == '/' else 404) self.send_header('Content-Type', 'text/html'); self.send_header('Content-Length', str(len(body))) self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(body) def log_message(self, *a): pass srv = http.server.HTTPServer(('127.0.0.1', 0), H) threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start() url = 'http://127.0.0.1:%d' % srv.server_port r = urllib.request.urlopen(url + '/') print(r.status, r.headers['Content-Type'], r.read().decode()) try: urllib.request.urlopen(url + '/x') except urllib.error.HTTPError as e: print(e.code) srv.shutdown()` Output: `200 text/html

GATE

404` The client sends `GET / HTTP/1.1` with a Host header; the server answers with a status line, headers and a body. A missing path gets **404**.

A host asks its local resolver for www.example.in (nothing cached).
Resolver → root server: referral to .in TLD servers.
Resolver → .in TLD: referral to example.in's authoritative servers.
Resolver → authoritative: the A record.
Resolver → host: the answer (and caches it).
The host made **1** recursive query; the resolver made **3** iterative queries. With fully recursive resolution, each server would query the next on the client's behalf instead.
Application protocols and their usual ports:
points: DNS 53 (UDP, TCP for zone transfers); DHCP 67/68 (UDP).
HTTP 80, HTTPS 443 (TCP).
SMTP 25, POP3 110, IMAP 143 (TCP).
FTP 21 control, 20 data in active mode; Telnet 23; SSH 22.
SNMP 161 (UDP).
HTTP is stateless; FTP keeps session state.

notes.p:
**Q: Which transport protocol does DNS normally use for queries, and why?** A: UDP port 53 — a single small request and reply, no handshake needed; TCP is used for zone transfers and replies too large for UDP.

**Q: A browser fetches a page whose base file references 4 images on the same server, using persistent HTTP with pipelining. Minimum RTTs, ignoring transmission?** A: 1 (TCP) + 1 (base) + 1 (all images) = 3 RTT.

**Q: Why does SMTP need MIME?** A: SMTP carries 7-bit ASCII only; MIME encodes binary attachments and non-ASCII text (e.g. base64) and labels content types.

**Q: Is FTP's control information in-band or out-of-band?** A: Out-of-band — commands use a separate control connection from the data.
Remember:
points: DNS hierarchy: root → TLD → authoritative; caching with TTL.
A, AAAA, NS, CNAME, MX records.
Non-persistent HTTP: 2 RTT per object.
Persistent + pipelining ≈ 3 RTT for a page with small objects.
SMTP pushes; POP3/IMAP pull; MIME for attachments.
FTP: control 21 (out-of-band), data 20.
HTTP status classes: 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, 5xx.

cards.title: What GA is
cards.body: 10 questions worth 15 marks (5 × 1 mark + 5 × 2 marks), common to all GATE papers. These are the easiest marks in the exam — never skip GA practice.

cards.title: Four areas
points: Verbal: grammar, vocabulary, sentence completion, analogies
Quantitative: percentages, ratios, data interpretation, mensuration
Analytical: logical deduction, critical reasoning
Spatial: rotation, folding, paper cutting, mirror images

cards.title: Quant sample
cards.body: Boys : girls = 3 : 2 (take 60 and 40). 20% of boys and 30% of girls hold scholarships: 12 + 12 = 24. So 76% do not.

cards.title: Clock angle
points: Angle = |30H − 5.5M| degrees
Take 360 − angle if the result exceeds 180 for the smaller angle

cards.title: Painted cube
cards.body: A painted n × n × n cube is cut into unit cubes: 3 faces painted = 8 (corners), 2 faces = 12(n − 2), 1 face = 6(n − 2)², none = (n − 2)³.

cards.title: Time plan
cards.body: Do GA first in about 15–20 minutes; the NAT and MSQ items there have no negative marking, so answer every one.

cards.q: Angle between the hands of a clock at 3:15:
A painted 3 × 3 × 3 cube is cut into 27 unit cubes. How many have exactly two painted faces?
Boys:girls = 3:2; 20% of boys and 30% of girls have scholarships. Percentage without scholarship:
cards.explain: Of 100 students, 12 + 12 = 24 have one, so 76% don't.

notes.h: Structure and why GA decides ranks
notes.p:
**General Aptitude** carries **15 of 100 marks** in every GATE paper: 5 one-mark and 5 two-mark questions. Negative marking for MCQs is −1/3 (1-mark) and −2/3 (2-mark); NAT questions have no negative marks. GA is the easiest 15 marks in the paper, and a 3–4 mark difference here can move your rank by hundreds or thousands. Pattern as reported for recent GATE papers; confirm in the official information brochure for your year.

Topics: **verbal** (grammar, vocabulary, sentence completion, verbal analogies, critical reasoning), **quantitative** (percentages, ratios, averages, data interpretation, basic algebra/geometry), **analytical** (deduction, inference, puzzles) and **spatial** (paper folding, rotations, counting shapes, patterns).

**1.** 'She is one of those people who ____ always on time.' Options: is / are. The relative clause refers to 'people', so **are**.

**2. Analogy.** Pen : Write :: Knife : ? → **Cut** (tool : function).

**3. Critical reasoning.** 'All successful startups had strong teams. X has a strong team. So X will succeed.' This is the fallacy of **affirming the consequent** — the conclusion does not follow.

Read every option; GA verbal questions often have two near-correct choices that differ by one word like 'only' or 'all'.

**4.** A price rises 20% and then falls 20%. Net change = 20 − 20 − 4 = **−4%**.

**5.** The ratio of boys to girls is 3 : 2. If 10 more girls join, it becomes 1 : 1. Then 3x = 2x + 10 → x = 10 → **30 boys, 20 girls**.

**6. Data interpretation.** Sales were 120, 150, 180 units in three years. Average growth from year 1 to year 3 is (180 − 120)/120 = **50%** in total, 25% and 20% year-on-year. Always check whether the question asks for total or year-on-year growth.

**7. Logic.** 'If it rains, the match is cancelled. The match was not cancelled.' Valid conclusion: **it did not rain** (contrapositive).

**8. Spatial.** A square sheet folded in half twice and punched once in the middle of the folded square shows **4 holes** when unfolded — count one hole per layer.
A simple plan used by toppers:
points: Attempt GA first or last, but give it a fixed 20–25 minutes.
Solve every 1-mark question; skip a 2-mark question only if it is clearly long.
NAT questions have no negative marks — always enter an answer.
For spatial questions, draw quickly on the scribble pad instead of imagining.
Practise last 8–10 years of GA questions; styles repeat.
Use the virtual calculator only when arithmetic is heavy — it is slower than you think.

notes.p: Where students lose GA marks:
points: Misreading 'not' or 'except' in the question.
Using percentage points vs percent interchangeably.
Assuming real-world facts in logic questions.
Rushing two-mark DI questions without checking units.

notes.p: Remember:
points: MCQ negative marking; NAT none.
Verbal: grammar, vocabulary, analogies, reasoning.
Quant: percentages, ratios, DI basics.
Contrapositive is valid; converse is not.
Practise past GA papers — the easiest marks in GATE.

chapters.title: GA: verbal aptitude — grammar, vocabulary, reading & sequencing

cards.title: What is tested
cards.body: Basic English grammar (tenses, articles, adjectives, prepositions, conjunctions, verb–noun agreement and other parts of speech), vocabulary (words, idioms and phrases **in context**), reading comprehension and **narrative sequencing** (ordering sentences into a coherent paragraph).

cards.title: Agreement rules
points: Neither/either … nor/or: verb agrees with the nearer subject
Each, every, either, neither, everyone: singular verb
One of the + plural noun + singular verb ('One of the students is…')
A number of → plural; the number of → singular
Subject + 'as well as/along with' + noun: verb follows the first subject

cards.title: Articles and prepositions
points: 'a' before a consonant sound, 'an' before a vowel sound: an hour, a university, an MBA
'the' for something specific or unique: the sun, the best
Comply with, consist of, prefer to, superior to, capable of, interested in
Since + point in time; for + duration

cards.title: Tense traps
cards.body: Use the **present perfect** for an action continuing to now with since/for ('I have lived here since 2020'), not the simple present. In reported speech, past reporting verbs shift tenses back. Avoid two past markers: 'did not went' → 'did not go'.

cards.title: Vocabulary in context
cards.body: Read the whole sentence before choosing. Look for **contrast signals** (but, although, despite → opposite idea) and **continuation signals** (moreover, and, because → similar idea). For idioms, test the literal meaning against the context — 'to beat around the bush' = to avoid the main point.

cards.title: Reading comprehension
cards.body: Answer from the passage, not from outside knowledge. **Inference** questions ask what must be true given the text; eliminate options that are too strong ('always', 'all') or only partly supported. For 'main idea', pick the option that covers the whole passage, not one paragraph.

cards.q: Choose the correct sentence:
options: Neither the manager nor the clerks was present.
Neither the manager nor the clerks were present.
Neither the manager nor the clerks is present.
Neither the manager or the clerks were present.
cards.explain: The verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'clerks' (plural); and 'neither' pairs with 'nor'.

cards.q: Fill in: She has been working here ___ five years.
cards.explain: 'for' with a duration; 'since' with a starting point.

cards.q: 'The new policy was a red herring.' Here 'red herring' means:
options: Something that distracts from the real issue
cards.explain: A red herring diverts attention from what matters.

notes.p:
General Aptitude carries 15 of the 100 marks, and verbal questions are usually the quickest to answer. A few seconds of grammar checking per option avoids silly losses — MCQs carry negative marking, so guess only after eliminating options.

The standard approach: read the full sentence, find the subject and verb, check agreement, tense, articles and prepositions in that order, then reread the chosen sentence as a whole.

**Sentence:** 'Each of the candidates have submitted their forms on time.'
Step 1 — subject: 'Each' (singular), not 'candidates'.
Step 2 — verb must be singular: 'has submitted'.
Step 3 — formal pronoun agreement: 'his or her form' (many modern style guides also accept singular 'their').
Correct: **'Each of the candidates has submitted his or her form on time.'**

**Sentence:** 'The committee have reached its decision.' A collective noun acting as one unit takes a singular verb and pronoun: **'The committee has reached its decision.'**

Arrange: (P) The results surprised everyone. (Q) A small team began testing the new drug in 2019. (R) Within two years, it had reduced symptoms in most patients. (S) Encouraged, they expanded the trial to three hospitals.
The opening sentence introduces the subject without a pronoun: **Q**. 'Encouraged' needs an earlier success, so S must follow R (the first results). P comments on the outcome of the whole story, so it comes last. Order: **Q → R → S → P**. Check pronouns ('they' needs 'a small team' before it) and time markers ('within two years').
Easily mixed-up pairs and idioms:
points: affect (verb) / effect (noun); principal (main) / principle (rule).
complement (complete) / compliment (praise); stationary (still) / stationery (paper).
fewer (countable) / less (uncountable); between (two) / among (many).
'Bite the bullet' = face something unpleasant bravely; 'cut corners' = do something cheaply or carelessly.
'Once in a blue moon' = rarely; 'hit the nail on the head' = describe exactly.

notes.p:
**Q: Fill in: The news ___ good.** A: 'is' — 'news' is uncountable and singular.

**Q: Choose the correct preposition: He is senior ___ me.** A: 'to' (senior to, junior to, superior to, prefer A to B).

**Q: Pick the word closest in meaning to 'ephemeral'.** A: short-lived (transient).

**Q: Correct the error: I am knowing him for ten years.** A: I have known him for ten years — stative verbs such as know are not used in continuous tenses, and a duration up to now needs the present perfect.

**Q: a European or an European?** A: a European, because the word begins with a y sound.
Remember:
points: Find the true subject before choosing the verb.
Neither…nor / either…or: agree with the nearer subject.
Each/every/one of the … : singular verb.
a/an by sound; 'the' for specific or unique things.
Since + point in time; for + duration.
Contrast words flip meaning; continuation words keep it.
RC: answer from the passage; avoid extreme options.

chapters.title: GA: quantitative aptitude — DI, logs, mensuration & statistics

cards.title: Percentages and ratios
points: Percent change = (new − old) / old × 100
Successive changes a% and b%: a + b + ab/100
Pie chart: sector angle = share × 360°
Ratio of totals ≠ average of ratios — always go back to totals

cards.title: Powers and logs
points: log(ab) = log a + log b;  log(aⁿ) = n log a
logₐ b = log b / log a
Digits in N = ⌊log₁₀ N⌋ + 1

cards.title: Mensuration
points: Circle: area πr², circumference 2πr
Cylinder: volume πr²h, curved area 2πrh
Cone: volume πr²h/3;  Sphere: volume 4πr³/3, area 4πr²
Scaling by k: lengths × k, areas × k², volumes × k³

cards.title: Statistics
points: Mean = sum / n; median = middle value of sorted data
Mode = most frequent value
Variance = mean of squares − square of mean
Adding a constant changes the mean, not the SD; multiplying by c scales the SD by |c|

cards.title: Successive change
cards.body:
A price rises 20% and then falls 20%.
Net = 20 − 20 + (20 × −20)/100 = **−4%**. The fall applies to a larger base, so the price ends below where it started.

cards.q: In a pie chart, a sector of 72° represents what share of the total?
If the radius of a sphere is doubled, its volume becomes:
cards.explain: Volume ∝ r³ → 2³ = 8.

cards.q: Data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9. The median is:
cards.explain: Sorted, 8 values: average of the 4th and 5th = (4 + 5)/2.

notes.p: Data interpretation (bar graphs, pie charts, line graphs, tables, 2-D and 3-D plots, maps), numerical computation and estimation (ratios, percentages, powers, exponents and logarithms, permutations and combinations, series), mensuration and geometry, and elementary statistics and probability. Many questions are numerical-answer type, so calculate cleanly and round only at the end.

A company's sales (₹ crore): 2022 — A 40, B 60; 2023 — A 50, B 66.
Growth of A = 10/40 = **25%**; growth of B = 6/60 = **10%**.
Total growth = (116 − 100)/100 = **16%** — not the average (17.5%) of the two growth rates, because B is the larger base.
Share of A in 2023 = 50/116 ≈ **43.1%** → pie-chart angle = 0.431 × 360 ≈ **155°**.

`import math, statistics as st
print(len(str(2**50)), math.floor(50 * math.log10(2)) + 1)
print(round((1.2 * 0.8 - 1) * 100, 2), '% net change')
data = [2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]
print(st.mean(data), st.median(data), st.mode(data), st.pstdev(data))
print(round(50 / 116 * 360, 1), 'degrees')
r = 3; print(round(4 / 3 * math.pi * r**3, 2), round(4 * math.pi * r**2, 2))
print(math.comb(10, 3), math.perm(5, 2), sum(range(1, 101)))`

Output:
`16 16
-4.0 % net change
5 4.5 4 2.0
155.2 degrees
113.1 113.1
120 20 5050`

The dataset has mean 5, median 4.5, mode 4 and population SD 2. A sphere of radius 3 has volume 36π ≈ 113.1 and surface area 36π as well — a coincidence of r = 3.

When options are far apart, **approximate**: 49 × 51 ≈ 2500 (exactly 2499). For series, look at differences, ratios, squares/cubes ± a constant, or two interleaved series. Sum of the first n natural numbers = n(n + 1)/2; of squares = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6; geometric series a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1).
points: Probability of at least one = 1 − P(none).
Expected value of a fair die = 3.5.
Average speed over equal distances = harmonic mean 2ab/(a + b).
Compound growth over n years: (1 + r)ⁿ.

notes.p:
**Q: If log₁₀ x = 2.5, what is x?** A: 10^2.5 = 100√10 ≈ 316.2.

**Q: A cylinder and a cone have the same base and height. Ratio of volumes?** A: 3 : 1.

**Q: Two fair coins are tossed. P(at least one head)?** A: 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.

**Q: Next term: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ?** A: 42, since the terms are n(n + 1).

**Q: The mean of 10 numbers is 20. Each is increased by 5 and then doubled. New mean?** A: (20 + 5) × 2 = 50.
Remember:
points: Successive % change: a + b + ab/100.
Work with totals, not averages of percentages.
Digits = ⌊log₁₀N⌋ + 1.
Area ∝ k², volume ∝ k³.
Median of even count = average of middle two.
SD unchanged by adding a constant.
Pie angle = share × 360°.

cards.title: Deduction vs induction
cards.body: **Deduction** draws conclusions that must follow from the premises (All A are B; x is A ⇒ x is B). **Induction** generalises from examples — likely, never certain. GATE asks which conclusion is **necessarily** true: pick only what the premises force.

cards.title: Syllogism shortcuts
points: All A are B + All B are C ⇒ All A are C
All A are B + Some B are C ⇒ no definite A–C conclusion
Some A are B ⇒ Some B are A (converse valid)
No A is B ⇒ No B is A
All A are B does NOT give All B are A

cards.title: Analogy and numerical relations
cards.body: Identify the exact relation in the first pair (part–whole, cause–effect, tool–user, degree) and apply it to the second. For ordering puzzles (taller than, older than), draw a line diagram; for age or number relations, write equations immediately.

cards.title: Spatial transformations (about the origin)
points: Rotate 90° anticlockwise: (x, y) → (−y, x)
Rotate 90° clockwise: (x, y) → (y, −x)
Rotate 180°: (x, y) → (−x, −y)
Mirror in the y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y); in the x-axis: (x, −y)
Scaling by k multiplies every coordinate (and length) by k

cards.title: Painted-cube counts (n × n × n)
points: 3 faces painted: 8 (corners)
2 faces: 12(n − 2) (edges)
1 face: 6(n − 2)² (face centres)
0 faces: (n − 2)³ (interior)

cards.title: Paper folding and cutting
cards.body: Each fold doubles the layers. A hole punched through k layers gives k holes when unfolded, mirrored across each fold line. Unfold in reverse order, reflecting the holes at every step.

cards.q: A 4 × 4 × 4 painted cube is cut into unit cubes. How many have exactly two faces painted?
The point (2, 3) is rotated 90° anticlockwise about the origin. The image is:
Premises: All engineers are graduates. Some graduates are artists. Which conclusion follows?
cards.explain: The artists among graduates may or may not include engineers; nothing definite follows.

notes.p: The syllabus lists logic (deduction and induction), analogy, and numerical relations and reasoning. Most questions are short puzzles: decide what must be true, what could be true, and what cannot be true. Draw Venn diagrams for 'all/some/no' statements, and tables for multi-attribute puzzles.

Three people: P says 'Q is lying'; Q says 'R is lying'; R says 'P and Q are both lying'.
Assume R tells the truth → P and Q lie → Q's statement 'R is lying' is false ✓, but P's statement 'Q is lying' would then be true ✗ (P was supposed to lie). Contradiction, so **R lies**.
Then Q ('R is lying') tells the truth, so P ('Q is lying') lies. Check R: 'P and Q both lie' is false since Q is truthful ✓.
Answer: **only Q tells the truth**.

notes.h: Worked example 2: cubes and grids by brute force
notes.p:
`from itertools import product
n = 4
counts = {}
for x, y, z in product(range(n), repeat=3):
    faces = sum(c in (0, n - 1) for c in (x, y, z))
    counts[faces] = counts.get(faces, 0) + 1
print(dict(sorted(counts.items())))
print(sum(k * k for k in range(1, 6)), 'squares in a 5x5 grid')
print((6 * 5 // 2) ** 2, 'rectangles in a 5x5 grid')
rot = lambda p: (-p[1], p[0])
print(rot((2, 3)), rot(rot((2, 3))))`

Output:
`{0: 8, 1: 24, 2: 24, 3: 8}
55 squares in a 5x5 grid
225 rectangles in a 5x5 grid
(-3, 2) (-2, -3)`

For n = 4: 8 corners, 24 edge cubes, 24 face cubes, 8 interior cubes — matching the formulas. A 5 × 5 grid of unit squares contains 55 squares of all sizes and C(6, 2)² = 225 rectangles.

A square sheet is folded in half vertically, then in half horizontally, and a hole is punched near the folded corner (the centre of the original sheet).
Layers at the punch = 2 × 2 = 4 → **4 holes** when unfolded, placed symmetrically about both fold lines — all four close to the centre. If the punch were made near the open corners instead, the four holes would sit near the four corners of the sheet.
points: Mirror images swap left and right but not up and down (vertical mirror).
Water images flip top and bottom.
Opposite faces of a standard die sum to 7.
On an unfolded cube net, faces separated by one square in a straight line are opposite.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Deduction = must follow; induction = probable.
All A are B + Some B are C → nothing definite about A and C.
90° anticlockwise: (x, y) → (−y, x).
Painted cube: 8, 12(n − 2), 6(n − 2)², (n − 2)³.
Squares in an n × n grid: Σk²; rectangles: C(n + 1, 2)².
Each fold doubles layers; unfold in reverse.
Test every assumption in truth-teller puzzles.
